# Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on March 12, 2025 at 11:00 AM GMT+2
## On this page
  * [What is a transient ischemic attack?](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#what-is-a-transient-ischemic-attack)
  * [Symptoms](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#symptoms)
  * [Causes](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#causes)
  * [Risks factors](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#risks-factors)
    * [Uncontrollable risk factors](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#uncontrollable-risk-factors)
    * [Medical conditions](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#medical-conditions)
    * [Controllable risk factors](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#controllable-risk-factors)
  * [Diagnosis](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#diagnosis)
  * [Treatment and prevention](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#treatment-and-prevention)
    * [Medication](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#medication)
    * [Lifestyle](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#lifestyle)
    * [Surgery](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#surgery)
  * [Complications](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#complications)
  * [Other names for transient ischemic attack](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#other-names-for-transient-ischemic-attack)

Share this article:
## What is a transient ischemic attack?
A transient ischemic attack (TIA), sometimes called a mini-stroke, is a sudden, short-lived neurological condition.
Common transient ischemic attack signs and symptoms include temporary loss of vision, slurred speech, and weakness of the face, arm or legs.[1](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
Think you might be experiencing transient ischemic attack (TIA)
The swift recovery time of a TIA (transient ischemic attack) is what differentiates it from an [ischemic stroke](https://ada.com/conditions/ischemic-stroke/). In an ischemic stroke, the blockage tends to last for more than a few minutes and can cause long-term damage to the brain. This is why a transient ischemic attack is often referred to as a mini-stroke
Although a TIA does not usually cause permanent damage to the brain, in some cases it can be a warning sign that a full-blown stroke may occur in the near future.
## What are the symptoms of a transient ischemic attack?
The symptoms of a transient ischemic attack (TIA) tend to arrive and leave quickly. Symptoms usually peak within the first minute of their appearance and then disappear within an hour.[1](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [3](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [4](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
  * Weakness or paralysis of the face, arm or leg, usually on one side of the body
  * Loss of vision
  * Slurred speech, also known as dysarthria
  * Difficulty finding words, also known as dysphasia
  * Loss of balance
  * Impaired memory
  * Confusion
  * Behavioral changes
  * Headache


However, it should be noted that these symptoms are usually different from person to person,[1](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
Although transient ischemic attack symptoms typically disappear within an hour and leave no lasting neurological damage, an attack signifies a greater risk of a stroke happening in the future.
Good to know:[ischemic stroke](https://ada.com/conditions/ischemic-stroke/). It is crucial to visit a doctor without delay, even if symptoms appear to have passed.
## What causes transient ischemic attack?
A TIA is most often caused by a small, temporary blockage in an artery that carries oxygenated blood to the brain.
The blockage is usually a blood clot that becomes lodged in the artery.[1](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
The cause of a transient ischemic attack is identical to the cause of an ischemic stroke. However, in a TIA, the blood clot tends to break up quickly[3](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
## Transient ischemic attack risk factors
A transient ischemic attack can affect anyone,
### Uncontrollable risk factors
The following risk factors for a TIA or mini-stroke cannot be modified, but it is still important to know what they are in order to assess overall risk: [3](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [6](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
  * Age.
  * Genetics.
  * Gender.
  * Ethnicity.


### Medical conditions
Transient ischemic attacks are also more likely to occur in people with certain medical conditions,[2](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [3](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [6](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
  * High blood pressure, known as [hypertension](https://ada.com/conditions/essential-hypertension/)
  * [Diabetes](https://ada.com/conditions/diabetes/)
  * Obesity
  * Heart disease
  * Abnormal heart rhythm, known as atrial fibrillation
  * High cholesterol
  * [Sickle cell disease](https://ada.com/conditions/sickle-cell-disease/)
  * Carotid artery disease (CAD) and [peripheral vascular disease](https://ada.com/conditions/peripheral-vascular-disease/) (PVD)
  * High levels of fats or lipids in the blood, known as dyslipidemia
  * Predisposition to the formation of blood clots, known as thrombophilia or hypercoagulability
  * Inflammation of the blood vessels, known as vasculitis


### Controllable risk factors
In addition to the above, there are a number of controllable lifestyle factors[2](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [3](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [6](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [7](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
  * Smoking.
  * Diet.
  * Excess alcohol.
  * Lack of exercise.
  * Birth control pills.


  * Good to know:


## Diagnosing a transient ischemic attack
As symptoms of a transient ischemic attack usually resolve within an hour, diagnosis is often made retrospectively.[2](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") Even if symptoms appear to have passed, it is crucial to visit the doctor for a prompt, proper diagnosis.
The diagnosis of a transient ischemic attack often begins with questions about the symptoms experienced and a physical examination.[1](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [9](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") [10](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
  * Tests for the existence of known risk factors such as high blood pressure
  * Neurological tasks to test coordination, strength, and understanding
  * Eye examination to detect any blockage in the blood vessels at the back of the eye
  * Audial examination of the neck using a stethoscope, to detect a murmuring sound in the arteries known as a bruit


Referral to a specialist doctor or neurosurgeon might be made for further tests[1](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [9](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") [10](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
  * Neuroimaging tests,
  * Blood tests
  * Vascular ultrasound,
  * Echocardiogram,
  * Electrocardiogram (ECG),


Diagnostic procedures will vary from person to person, depending on their individual circumstances and medical history. However, the aims of these procedures are: [1](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * To confirm the diagnosis of a transient ischemic attack, rather than a stroke
  * To determine which underlying medical factors may have caused the attack
  * To identify and prevent factors which may increase the risk of a mini-stroke or stroke happening in the future


Think you might be experiencing transient ischemic attack (TIA)
## Transient ischemic attack treatments and prevention
Once a transient ischemic attack diagnosis has been made, treatment methods usually aim to reduce both the short and long-term risk of another attack taking place[11](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
### Medication
Prescription drugs are typically used to reduce the possibility of blood clots forming.[1](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [9](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9")
  * Antiplatelet drugs
  * Anticoagulant drugs
  * Medication for other risk factors


### Lifestyle
Certain risk factors for transient ischemic attacks can be reduced through simple lifestyle alterations, such as: [12](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12") [9](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") [13](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:13 "See Footnote 13")
  * Stopping smoking,
  * Eating more fresh fruit and vegetables
  * Reducing alcohol intake.
  * Exercising more often.
  * Control of other existing medical conditions


### Surgery
In some cases, a surgical procedure called a carotid endarterectomy[14](https://ada.com/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14")
Narrowing of the carotid artery is typically due to fatty deposits, known as atheroma or plaque, building up in the arterial walls and restricting blood flow to the brain. A carotid endarterectomy involves opening up the affected artery and removing the buildup of plaque. The procedure usually takes between one and two hours and is done under anesthetic. 
## Complications of a transient ischemic attack
Although a TIA typically lasts only a few minutes and causes no permanent damage, it can be a warning sign that the affected person may suffer a more severe ischemic stroke in the near future.
## Other names for transient ischemic attack
Transient ischemic attacks may also be referred to as:
  * TIAs
  * Mini-strokes
  * With the slight spelling variation of transient ischaemic attacks

# Micronutrients Guide
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on May 21, 2025 at 11:30 AM GMT+3
## On this page
  * [What are micronutrients?](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#what-are-micronutrients)
  * [Why are micronutrients important?](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#why-are-micronutrients-important)
  * [What symptoms can a deficiency of micronutrients cause?](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#what-symptoms-can-a-deficiency-of-micronutrients-cause)
  * [When should you test your blood for micronutrients?](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#when-should-you-test-your-blood-for-micronutrients)
  * [FAQs](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#faqs)


* * *
Share this article:
Micronutrients are chemical substances that support growth and development in your body
You should get the right amount of these vitamins and minerals from a healthy and varied diet. Although you only need a small amount of micronutrients, there are many people around the world who suffer from deficiencies.
As these substances have important roles like supporting the immune system, metabolism and DNA repair, micronutrient deficiencies can have an impact on your health. They can cause conditions ranging from blindness to slowed growth and lower our defenses against viruses and bacteria.
Are you concerned your micronutrients level
## What are micronutrients?
Micronutrients are a group of vitamins and minerals[1](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
Micronutrients can be divided into three main typesvitamins
Minerals
Trace minerals[2](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [3](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [4](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
We get our micronutrients from the food that we eatexception to this is vitamin D[2](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [3](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [4](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
Each micronutrient has its own specific properties and can cause different symptoms when there’s a deficiency. Some of the most crucial vitamins in the human body are
  * Vitamin A
  * Vitamins B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, and B7
  * Vitamin B9
  * [Vitamin B12](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-b12/) assists nerve function, metabolism, and the blood system.
  * Vitamin C
  * [Vitamin D](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-d/) keeps bones healthy and supports the immune system.
  * [Vitamin E](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/) supports the immune system and nerve function.
  * [Vitamin K](https://ada.com/conditions/vitamin-k-deficiency/) is important for blood clotting.


Some important minerals
  * Calcium
  * Chromium
  * [Copper](https://ada.com/micronutrients/copper/) for cell energy and the nervous system.
  * Fluoride
  * Iodine[thyroid hormones](https://ada.com/thyroid/).
  * Iron for metabolism
  * [Magnesium](https://ada.com/micronutrients/magnesium/) for bones, metabolism, and nervous system.
  * Phosphorus
  * Potassium
  * [Selenium](https://ada.com/micronutrients/selenium/) supports proper function of the thyroid.
  * Sodium
  * [Zinc](https://ada.com/micronutrients/zinc/) supports the immune system and blood system.


Besides the micronutrients listed above, there are others such as vitamin B4 and B8[5](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [6](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [7](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
Are you concerned your micronutrients level 
## Why are micronutrients important?
Micronutrients are involved in a number of crucial processes in the body. They play a vital role in our metabolism[8](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
Micronutrients also reduce the amount of free radicals in the body[8](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [9](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9")
Micronutrients like vitamins B6, C, and E, as well as magnesium and zinc support our immune system[10](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
Micronutrients also modulate gene transcription[8](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [11](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11") [12](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
## What symptoms can a deficiency of micronutrients cause?
Micronutrient deficiencies present in a variety of different ways. You may only need small amounts of micronutrients, but a deficiency can result in serious conditions. As diet is responsible for many deficiencies, they tend to be more present in underdeveloped countries. Some of the most common deficiencies in the world are:
  * [Iron deficiency](https://ada.com/conditions/iron-deficiency-anemia/) can cause [anemia](https://ada.com/conditions/anemia/) with symptoms like tiredness, fatigue, breathlessness, feeling faint, and headaches.
  * Vitamin A deficiency
  * [Vitamin D deficiency](https://ada.com/conditions/vitamin-d-deficiency/) can cause bone problems like [osteoporosis](https://ada.com/conditions/osteoporosis/) and [osteomalacia](https://ada.com/conditions/osteomalacia/). Vitamin D is also important for the immune system and muscle and nerve functions.
  * Iodine deficiency
  * **[Folate](https://ada.com/conditions/folate-deficiency/) or [vitamin B12](https://ada.com/conditions/vitamin-b12-deficiency/)**[ deficiency](https://ada.com/conditions/vitamin-b12-deficiency/)[2](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [13](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:13 "See Footnote 13")
  * Zinc deficiency[14](https://ada.com/micronutrients/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14")


## When should you test your blood for micronutrients?
If you think you have symptoms of micronutrient deficiency, you should consider [testing your blood for micronutrients](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-deficiency-test/). Your doctor can interpret your symptoms and confirm the diagnosis with a blood test.
## Find out more about your symptoms
## Micronutrient FAQs
Q: What are macronutrients and micronutrients?  
A: Macronutrients are fats, proteins and carbohydrates. The body uses them in large amounts. Micronutrients, on the other hand, are vitamins and minerals which are only necessary in smaller amounts.
Q: Why are vitamins and minerals called micronutrients?  
A: Vitamins and minerals are called micronutrients because we only need a very small dose of them to keep our body healthy.
Q: Is water a micronutrient?  
A: Water is seen as a macronutrient, together with fats, proteins and carbohydrates. However, some micronutrients are soluble in water.

# Asma infantil
Escrito por nuestro [Equipo de Profesionales Médicos](https://ada.com/es/team/medical/)
Actualizado el 15 de febrero de 2022, 10:01 EET

## Resumen
El asma es un trastorno inflamatorio crónico que afecta las vías respiratorias. Cuando este problema se manifiesta en la infancia, suele llamarse asma infantil. El asma ocasiona un estrechamiento o bloqueo repentino y reversible (no permanente) de las vías respiratorias y una disminución del flujo de aire. La contaminación del aire y los alérgenos pueden ser disparadores de ataques de asma, los cuales se caracterizan por silbidos, rigidez en el pecho y dificultad para respirar. Los episodios graves de asma pueden reconocerse por una dificultad para respirar estando en reposo y cuando no es posible comer o decir una oración entera sin tener que detenerse para respirar. El asma infantil puede empeorar por la exposición al humo del cigarrillo, infecciones en las vías respiratorias o por alergias. Los síntomas suelen controlarse bien con medicamentos y evitando aquello que se sabe empeora los síntomas.
## Riesgos
Los niños cuyos padres tienen asma y los niños con alergias son más propensos a contraer asma. Los niños expuestos a humos irritantes tales como el de cigarrillo y aire contaminado también son más propensos al asma que otros niños.
## Síntomas
Los síntomas típicos son dificultad para respirar, silbidos al respirar, tos y sensación de estrechez en el pecho. Durante un fuerte episodio de asma, los niños pueden tener dificultad para respirar en reposo, hablar entrecortado por la tos, y toser flema clara o transparente. Los síntomas pueden aparecer de repente o en respuesta a un disparador, y pueden empeorar durante la noche. Algunas personas notan que sus síntomas empeoran a lo largo de 1 o 2 semanas antes de tener un episodio de asma especialmente fuerte. Los síntomas son resultado de la inflamación que produce estrechamiento de las vías respiratorias, lo que dificulta el paso normal del aire a los pulmones.
## Diagnóstico
El diagnóstico suele hacerse luego de evaluar los síntomas, haciendo un examen físico y descartando otras condiciones tales como infecciones en las vías respiratorias. También se realiza una prueba respiratoria, llamada espirometría, para medir el flujo de aire a través de los pulmones y las vías respiratorias.
## Tratamiento
Para mejorar los síntomas, se utilizan medicamentos que se inhalan para reducir la inflamación de las vías respiratorias. Dichos medicamentos pueden tomarse periódicamente o sólo cuando el niño está produciendo silbidos o tiene dificultad para respirar. En momentos de síntomas graves de asma, los niños pueden necesitar oxígeno u otros tratamientos de emergencia que los ayuden a respirar.
## Prevención
Tomar medidas para prevenir el contagio de resfriados o gripe en el hogar y la comunidad puede ayudar a evitar episodios de asma. Evitar aquello que empeora el asma (alergias, zonas de aire contaminado, ejercicio) puede ayudar a controlar los síntomas. No permitir que se fume en la casa o cerca de los niños puede ayudar a prevenir o reducir la cantidad de ataques de asma.
## Pronóstico
En algunos niños con asma moderada los síntomas pueden desaparecer a medida que crecen. Los niños con asma infantil grave tienen más probabilidades de continuar teniendo asma en su vida adulta.

# COVID-19 Symptom: Rash in Adults
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on February 4, 2025 at 10:00 AM GMT+2
## On this page
  * [Overview](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#overview)
  * [What is a COVID-19 rash in adults?](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#what-is-a-covid-19-rash-in-adults)
  * [What does covid rash look like](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#what-does-covid-rash-look-like)
  * [Duration](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#duration)
  * [Is covid rash contagious?](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#is-covid-rash-contagious)
  * [Diagnosis](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#diagnosis)
  * [Treatments](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#treatments)
  * [Wrapping up](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#wrapping-up)
  * [FAQs](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#faqs)

Share this article:
## Overview
  * COVID rashes can develop on any part of the body.
  * There is no distinct shape or size of a COVID rash.
  * The typical COVID-19 rash usually doesn’t last very long - often a few days to a few weeks. 
  * A COVID rash can be treated with various types of over-the-counter medications.


Think you might be experiencing COVID-19 symptoms
A COVID-19 rashin adults
COVID-19 is a virus that does not cause rashes like many conditions, such as Lyme or chickenpox. This makes it hard for doctors to diagnose it. COVID rashes can take on various shapes and forms and may feel itchy or painful. In addition, COVID rashes can affect any part of the body. Reports indicate the presence of a rash on various body parts, including the arms, legs, trunk, face, and toes.
## What is a COVID-19 rash in adults?
The exact cause of COVID rash is not yet fully understood[1](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") This immune response can cause inflammation in various parts of the body, including the skin. The inflammation can cause the blood vessels in the skin to dilate, leading to the formation of the rash.
It’s not present in all adults[1](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [3](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
Concerned that you or a loved one may have COVID-19? Start your symptom assessment in the [app](https://ada.com/app/) first.
## What does a COVID rash in adults look and feel like?
A COVID skin rash can present itself in many ways and on different body parts
COVID rashes may be itchy or painful and can cause skin discoloration or swelling of some parts of the skin. The appearance of COVID-19 rashes can include the following[2](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [3](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [4](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") [5](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
  * Rose-red flat or slightly elevated eruptions resembling measles
  * Raised red or skin-colored bumps on the skin or hives
  * Small fluid-filled blisters
  * Painful red and swollen fingers or toes
  * Rashes [due to blood clots in small blood vessels](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-blood-clots/) that cause reduced blood flow in the affected skin area


## How long does COVID rash last in adults?
If you develop a rash with COVID-19, it will usually take about a week to clear
In rare instances, people with COVID skin reactions, such as **[COVID toes](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-toes-symptoms/)** , have symptoms that last 6 to 12 months, but such cases are rare. [1](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
## Is a COVID rash in adults contagious?
It’s important to note that a COVID rash itself is not contagious. The rash occurs because of the body's immune response to the virus and cannot be spread to other people
However, a person with a COVID rash will have the virus in the system and can spread it. It’s important to still take precautions against spreading COVID-19, even if a rash is your only symptom. 
## How can a COVID-19 rash be diagnosed?
As a COVID-19 rash always clusters with [other symptoms of COVID-19](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptoms/), your doctor will ask you about any other symptoms you might be experiencing if they suspect your rash stems from a COVID-19 infection. 
As a COVID-19 rash can look similar to some other viral rashes[chickenpox](https://ada.com/conditions/acute-varicella-zoster/), [measles](https://ada.com/conditions/measles/), or [herpes simplex](https://ada.com/conditions/herpes-simplex/), your doctor will have to consider all your symptoms and test you for COVID-19 to confirm the diagnosis. [2](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
## Is there a treatment for a COVID-19 rash in adults?
COVID rash is not typically considered a serious condition and does not pose a significant risk to overall health. However, it can be uncomfortable or painful and can cause some people to feel self-conscious about their appearance. Treatment for a COVID-19 rash
[In addition to COVID-19 treatment](https://ada.com/covid/treatment-guide/), specific treatment for the rash includes: [7](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-rash-in-adults/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
  * Corticosteroids
  * Antihistamines
  * Anticoagulants (blood thinners)


As with any medical symptom, it’s essential to [seek medical advice if you have any concerns about a COVID](https://ada.com/covid/) rash or other symptoms.
## Wrapping up
COVID rash is a less common COVID-19 symptom. It can occur as a standalone symptom or may be accompanied by other symptoms, [such as fever](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-fever-range/) and [muscle or joint pain](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-joint-pain/), and it's not contagious.
The exact cause of the rash is not yet fully understood, but it’s believed to be related to the immune response to the virus. The rash is typically not serious and can be treated with over-the-counter creams or lotions. The American Academy of Dermatology has set up a 
## Skin rash and COVID-19 FAQs
Q: Does COVID-19 cause a rash in adults?  
A: An infection with the coronavirus may cause a rash in some cases.
Q: Is a rash a sign of COVID-19 in adults?  
A: A rash may be a sign of COVID-19 in adults, although it’s not present in all cases of COVID-19. Your healthcare provider will take your other symptoms into account as well. 
Q: Can a COVID-19 vaccine cause a rash in adults?  
A: In some cases, it’s possible to develop a rash after the COVID-19 vaccine. This happens because the vaccine can cause an allergic reaction in the skin, presenting itself with hives and swelling. 
Q: Does COVID make you itch all over?  
A: Some people diagnosed with COVID-19 report itching all over their body, while others may experience itching only in certain areas, such as the face or limbs. The itchiness can vary in intensity and may be accompanied by a rash.
Q: How long after COVID can you get a rash?  
A: The timing of when a COVID rash appears varies by case. Some people may develop a rash soon after contracting the virus, while others may not develop a rash until several days or even weeks after the onset of COVID-19 symptoms. Additionally, some people [who test positive for COVID](https://ada.com/covid/what-to-do-if-you-test-positive-for-covid/) may never develop a rash.

# Genital Warts
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on June 16, 2025 at 12:59 PM GMT+3

## What are genital warts?
Genital warts (condylomata acuminata or anogenital warts) are the most common sexually transmitted disease (STD) and a symptom of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection
Although HPV comes in over 100 different types, 90 percent of all cases of genital warts are caused by strains 6 and 11. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/genital-warts/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") Accordingly, only 10 percent of those who contract the virus will develop visible warts.
Think you might be experiencing symptoms of genital warts
Even if they are unaware of its presence, most sexually active people will contract HPV at some point during their lifetime. It is passed on through skin-to-skin contact, most commonly through oral, vaginal or anal intercourse.
Although the warts rarely cause any long-term harm,
## Symptoms of genital warts
Most people who contract HPV will not develop any visible symptoms. If genital warts do appear, it can sometimes be a significant amount of time
Genital warts generally form in clusters, though a single wart can also appear.
Genital warts usually take the form of small bumps of roughly two to three centimeters in diameter
If you are concerned you may have genital warts or another sexually transmitted disease, start your free symptom assessment by downloading the 
## Causes of genital warts
**[Human papillomavirus (HPV) causes genital warts](https://ada.com/conditions/human-papillomavirus-hpv-infection/).** This is a skin infection that comes in over 100 different types, each affecting a different part of the body. There are roughly 30 types of HPVbut only twocause the vast majority of all cases of genital warts.
### Transmission
Genital warts are spread through skin-to-skin contact,[3](https://ada.com/conditions/genital-warts/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") Penetrative sex, however, is not necessary for contraction; close genital contact can be enough for HPV to be passed on between two sexual partners.
Although human papillomavirus (HPV) is extremely contagious, infection cannot occur through such physical interactions as hugging or kissing, nor through items of clothing or towels.[4](https://ada.com/conditions/genital-warts/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
Worried you may have contracted genital warts or another sexually transmitted disease? Start your free symptom assessment with the 
### Latency and reappearance
HPV naturally clears from the body
## Diagnosing genital warts
Most commonly, visible genital warts will be diagnosed through a routine doctor’s examination and the review of the patient’s medical history.
If, however, there is a suspicion of HPV infection without any visible symptoms, other diagnostic routes may be explored.
### Gynecological exam / Pap test
For women without visible genital warts, diagnosing the presence of HPV will often involve undergoing a gynecological exam. This exam will typically include a Pap test (sometimes called a Pap smear). [5](https://ada.com/conditions/genital-warts/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") A procedure usually used to test for [cervical cancer](https://ada.com/conditions/cervical-cancer/), the Pap test screens the cervix for abnormal cells, which are a possible sign of HPV infection. If abnormal cells are found on the cervix, further tests will be carried out to screen for HPV infection, as well as the presence of cervical cancer.
Think you might be experiencing symptoms of genital warts?
## Genital warts treatment
There is no cure for genital warts – no way to remove HPV from the patient's system – meaning that treatment is focussed on removing the warts or preventing them from spreading.
Some patients will choose to undergo no treatment for genital warts. This option is perfectly safe but will generally prolong the problem. If the patient does opt for treatment, there are a number of different options to explore:
  * Application of antiviral gels or creams.
  * Cryotherapy (freezing).
  * Excision.
  * Electrosurgery.
  * Laser surgery.


## Prevention of genital warts
Although they are not 100 percent reliable, the use of condoms remains the most effective way of preventing the contraction genital warts.
### Condoms
To help protect against genital warts, condoms should be used every time vaginal, anal or oral intercourse is engaged in.[effective prevention method](https://ada.com/editorial/how-to-prevent-sexually-transmitted-diseases/) currently known of. However, using a condom does not guarantee full protection. The virus may be able to spread from genital skin not covered by the condom.
### Vaccines
A HPV vaccine can be effective in preventing genital warts, as well as other conditions including cervical cancer.
There are a number of vaccines available (Gardasil and Cervarix, for example), each protecting against a number of different HPV strains. No vaccine is able to protect against all strains of HPV,
## The HPV virus and cancer
The human papillomavirus (HPV) that causes genital warts can also cause several forms of cancers, including: [8](https://ada.com/conditions/genital-warts/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
  * Cervical cancer.
  * Anal cancer:[anal cancer](https://ada.com/conditions/anal-cancer/) are caused by HPV, with most of these caused by type 16.
  * Oropharyngeal cancer:[oropharyngeal cancers](https://ada.com/conditions/oropharyngeal-cancer/) (cancers of the middle throat) are caused by HPV.
  * Other forms of cancer:

# Hypertensive Retinopathy
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on April 7, 2025 at 1:00 PM GMT+2
## On this page

## What is hypertensive retinopathy
Hypertensive retinopathy (HR) is a possible complication of
The condition can lead to symptoms including double or dim vision, loss of vision andlifestyle changes, medication and careful monitoring.
Think you might be experiencing hypertensive retinopathy
## Causes of hypertensive retinopathy
Hypertensive retinopathy is an eyesight disorder that occurs as a result of high blood pressure.
Hypertensive retinopathy occurs when the blood vessels supplying blood to the retina in the back of the eye become damaged. The likelihood of damage to the retina increases with the severity of high blood pressure and the length of time over which the condition is experienced. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/hypertensive-retinopathy/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
Older people are most at risk of developing high blood pressure and are therefore also most at risk of developing hypertensive retinopathy.
Other factorsdeveloping high blood pressure [2](https://ada.com/conditions/hypertensive-retinopathy/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
  * Being overweight
  * A sedentary lifestyle
  * A diet high in salt
  * Stress
  * A family history of high blood pressure
  * [Diabetes](https://ada.com/conditions/diabetes/)
  * Moderate to high [alcohol intake](https://ada.com/conditions/alcohol-intoxication/)


## Signs and symptoms of hypertensive retinopathy
Most people will only develop symptoms of hypertensive retinopathy after there has already been significant damage to the retina. Before this, it may take a doctor or ophthalmologist 
Symptoms
  * Double or cloudy vision
  * [Headaches](https://ada.com/conditions/headache/)
  * Loss of vision, when the condition has progressed significantly


If these symptoms come on very quickly, this can be a sign of severely high blood pressure and should be considered a medical emergency. Call a doctor immediately.
Think you might be experiencing hypertensive retinopathy
## Hypertensive retinopathy stages
Ophthalmologists grade hypertensive retinopathy using four categories or stages. The classification system is known as the Keith Wagener Barker (KWB) grades.[2](https://ada.com/conditions/hypertensive-retinopathy/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [1](https://ada.com/conditions/hypertensive-retinopathy/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * Grade 1:
  * Grade 2:
  * Grade 3:
  * Grade 4:


Some medical professionals may prefer to use the Mitchell-Wong grading system;
## Hypertensive retinopathy diagnosis
Diagnosing hypertensive retinopathy typically involves an examination by an ophthalmologist based on the symptoms present.
In some cases, an ophthalmoscope
More rarely, a test known as a fluorescein angiography[2](https://ada.com/conditions/hypertensive-retinopathy/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
## Hypertensive retinopathy treatment
The only way to treat hypertensive retinopathy is by controlling high blood pressure.
  * Giving up smoking
  * Losing weight
  * Taking regular exercise
  * Dietary changes
  * Reducing [alcohol intake](https://ada.com/conditions/alcohol-intoxication/)


Medication, such as ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-2 receptor blockers (ARBs), thiazide diuretics, calcium channel-blockers and beta-blockers may also be prescribed to help lower blood pressure levels. These medications can help to allow the retina to heal and stop further damage from occurring.
The type of medication chosen will depend on the affected person’s medical history and a consideration of the possible side-effects.
## Hypertensive retinopathy prevention
Preventing hypertensive retinopathy is possible through careful management of high blood pressure and related conditions, such as diabetes. Lifestyle changes, such as losing weight or giving up smoking,
## Hypertensive retinopathy complications
Individuals with hypertensive retinopathy are at risk of various complications, including:
  * Retinal vein occlusion
  * Retinal artery occlusion
  * Ischemic optic neuropathy
  * Malignant hypertension


Hypertensive retinopathy is also linked to an increased risk of [stroke](https://ada.com/conditions/ischemic-stroke/) and [heart attack](https://ada.com/conditions/myocardial-infarction/).
## Prognosis
The outlook for people with mild (grade 1 or 2) hypertensive retinopathy is relatively positive,[3](https://ada.com/conditions/hypertensive-retinopathy/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
## Other names for hypertensive retinopathy
  * Fundus hypertonicus

Q: What is the difference between hypertensive retinopathy and diabetic retinopathy?  
A:[type 2 can potentially develop the condition](https://ada.com/conditions/diabetes-mellitus-type-2/). Like hypertensive retinopathy, diabetic retinopathy causes damage to the retina at the back of the eye and can, if left untreated, lead to blindness. [4](https://ada.com/conditions/hypertensive-retinopathy/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")

# Thyroid Guide
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on June 16, 2025 at 12:41 PM GMT+3
## On this page
  * [About the Thyroid](https://ada.com/thyroid/#about-the-thyroid)
  * [Thyroid disease symptoms](https://ada.com/thyroid/#thyroid-disease-symptoms)
  * [Thyroid nodules](https://ada.com/thyroid/#thyroid-nodules)
  * [When to worry about thyroid nodules?](https://ada.com/thyroid/#when-to-worry-about-thyroid-nodules)
  * [Thyroid diseases](https://ada.com/thyroid/#thyroid-diseases)
  * [Thyroid test](https://ada.com/thyroid/#thyroid-test)
  * [Treatment](https://ada.com/thyroid/#treatment)
  * [Thyroid FAQ](https://ada.com/thyroid/#thyroid-faq)


* * *
Share this article:
The thyroid is a gland that forms part of the hormonal system
As the thyroid gland is involved in such crucial processes, its health can considerably impact the body.
Thyroid conditions such as hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism, auto-immune disorders, and cancers may all cause different symptoms. Fortunately, thyroid diseases are treatable, although they often require lifelong treatment.
You can read more about the different thyroid conditions, symptoms, and possible treatments as well as thyroid hormones like T4, T3, or [TPO antibodies](https://ada.com/thyroid/tpo-antibodies/) on this page and in the linked articles.
Feeling unwell? Get a symptom assessment
## What is the thyroid, and why do we need it?
The thyroid is a small gland in the neckconsisting of 2 lobes These also produce important hormones.
The thyroid covers most of the cricoid cartilage, touching the thyroid cartilage with the upper part of its lobes. The thyroid and cricoid cartilages are important as they help protect the windpipe. [1](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [3](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [4](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
The thyroid is an integral part of your hormonal system, as [it produces hormones](https://ada.com/hormones/) that regulate crucial body functions such as metabolism, fertility, and heart rate. On top of that, thyroid hormones play a vital part in growth and development. The thyroid gland's main hormones are[triiodothyronine (T3)](https://ada.com/thyroid/triiodothyronine-t3/) and [thyroxine (T4)](https://ada.com/thyroid/thyroxine-t4/), also known as tetraiodothyronine. Besides these hormones, the thyroid produces calcitonin and reverse triiodothyronine (RT3). [5](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [6](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
The thyroid produces these hormones in response to signals sent from 2 other important hormonal glands, the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary gland[5](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
Iodine is a trace element that's necessary for the production of thyroid hormones. When you do not get enough iodine from food sources such as iodized table salt, seafood, and vegetables, this could lead to underproduction and a deficiency of thyroid hormones. [5](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
Feeling unwell? Get a symptom assessment with the symptom checker works.
## What are typical thyroid disease symptoms?
Thyroid disease symptoms
With hyperthyroidism,[5](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [7](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
  * Tiredness
  * Nervousness and mood swings
  * Difficulty sleeping
  * Sensitivity to heat
  * A goiter, which is an enlarged thyroid gland
  * Irregular heartbeat
  * Tremors
  * Palpitations
  * Weight loss


With hypothyroidism,[8](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [9](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") [10](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
  * Tiredness
  * Sensitivity to the cold
  * Weight gain
  * Depression
  * Forgetfulness
  * Low libido
  * Irregular periods
  * Cessation of periods
  * Constipation
  * Dry skin
  * Low heart rate


With thyroid cancers[11](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
  * A painless lump in the neck area
  * Hoarseness that doesn’t improve
  * A sore throat that doesn’t improve
  * Difficulty swallowing
  * Swollen neck glands


## What are thyroid nodules?
A thyroid nodule is a small lump on the thyroid, which is caused by an abnormal growth of thyroid cells
## When to worry about thyroid nodules?
Sometimes thyroid nodules can be felt or cause problems with swallowing or breathing
Thyroid nodules can be singular, meaning there's only 1 on the thyroid. When there are several nodules on the thyroid gland, it's called a multinodular goiter.
An enlarged thyroid is called a diffuse goiter and is often related to auto-immune conditions such as Hashimoto’s thyroiditis and Graves’ disease. The goiter can also grow down to the breastbone. In this case, it’s called a retrosternal goiter. [12](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
## Which thyroid diseases exist?
Thyroid diseases can be divided into groups:[3](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
  1. Hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism
  2. [Thyroiditis](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/), which is an inflammation of the thyroid gland.
  3. Autoimmune processes[Graves’ disease](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/) and [Hashimoto’s thyroiditis](https://ada.com/conditions/hashimotos-thyroiditis-hypothyroidism/). Normally, your immune system detects viruses and bacteria that have invaded the body and attacks them. With autoimmune diseases, the immune system mistakes the body’s own healthy tissues for intruders and starts to attack them. Graves’ disease often goes hand in hand with thyroid eye disease. This is a condition where the immune system attacks the tissues behind the eye, causing bulging of the eyes and other eye symptoms. Despite the name, this condition can also occur without the thyroid being affected. [13](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:13 "See Footnote 13")
  4. Thyroid cancer


Feeling unwell? Get a symptom assessment
## When should thyroid function be tested?
Thyroid function should be tested when you’re experiencing symptoms of hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism.
This is done utilizing a blood test[hyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)](https://ada.com/thyroid/thyroid-stimulating-hormone-tsh/) and T4 in the blood. Less frequently, blood work can also be used to check for the amount of T3 in the blood or to check for a condition called Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, which is a disorder where the immune system attacks the thyroid. [14](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14")
The thyroid should also be tested when you feel an enlargement in the throat area, if you have problems swallowing, or if you experience continuous hoarseness. Apart from blood work to check your thyroid hormones, a thyroid ultrasound
A thyroid biopsy[11](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
## What treatment is available for thyroid issues?
If you are diagnosed with a condition of the thyroid[15](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:15 "See Footnote 15") [16](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:16 "See Footnote 16")
Thyroid medication can also help with hyperthyroidism. Certain medications prevent the thyroid from producing too much thyroid hormone. Other ways to treat hyperthyroidism are radiotherapy to destroy some of the hormone-producing cells in the thyroid or thyroid surgery to remove the thyroid either completely or partially. [7](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
For other conditions of the thyroid, such as thyroid cancer, the treatment strategy depends on which type of cancer is present. Treatment options may include medication, surgery, and chemotherapy. [11](https://ada.com/thyroid/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
## Find out more about your symptoms
## Thyroid FAQ
Q: What is a thyroid doctor called?  
A: An endocrinologist is a doctor that specializes in the hormonal system and its conditions. Endocrinologists can help you with conditions of the thyroid.
Q: Are thyroid problems curable?  
A: Thyroid problems are treatable, but they often require lifelong use of medication to keep a healthy level of thyroid hormones.
Q: Do thyroid problems run in families?  
A: If you have a blood relative that suffers from a thyroid condition, then you'll have a greater chance of developing thyroid problems as well.
Q: What is a thyroid storm?  
A: A thyroid storm is also known as a thyrotoxic crisis, and is a life-threatening complication of hyperthyroidism. During a thyroid storm, the thyroid suddenly releases large amounts of thyroid hormone.
Q: What happens if thyroid hormones are imbalanced?  
A: Imbalanced thyroid hormones may lead to problems with metabolism, growth, and fertility.
Q: What are early warning signs of thyroid problems?  
A: Early warning signs are fatigue, weight loss or gain without any known cause, and sensitivity to changes in temperature.
Q: How to prevent thyroid problems?  
A: Thyroid problems may be prevented in some cases by maintaining a healthy diet with a sufficient amount of iodine. Avoiding alcohol and smoking is also beneficial.
Q: When is thyroid surgery necessary?  
A: The thyroid, or a part of it, may be surgically removed in the case of hyperthyroidism, nodules, cysts, or cancer.

# Accidente cerebral hemorrágico
Escrito por nuestro [Equipo de Profesionales Médicos](https://ada.com/es/team/medical/)
Actualizado el 4 de febrero de 2022, 12:01 EET
## En esta página
  * [Resumen](https://ada.com/es/conditions/hemorrhagic-stroke/#resumen)
  * [Riesgos](https://ada.com/es/conditions/hemorrhagic-stroke/#riesgos)
  * [Síntomas](https://ada.com/es/conditions/hemorrhagic-stroke/#sintomas)
  * [Diagnóstico](https://ada.com/es/conditions/hemorrhagic-stroke/#diagnostico)
  * [Tratamiento](https://ada.com/es/conditions/hemorrhagic-stroke/#tratamiento)
  * [Prevención](https://ada.com/es/conditions/hemorrhagic-stroke/#prevencion)
  * [Pronóstico](https://ada.com/es/conditions/hemorrhagic-stroke/#pronostico)
  * [Otras denominaciones](https://ada.com/es/conditions/hemorrhagic-stroke/#otras-denominaciones)


* * *
Comparte este artículo:
## Resumen
El derrame cerebral hemorrágico es una emergencia en la que se produce un sangrado en el cerebro, lo que provoca daño y muerte de las células nerviosas del cerebro. Esta condición médica requiere una consulta médica urgente. Los signos comunes del derrame cerebral son la caída de una parte de la cara, debilidad de un costado del cuerpo, dificultad en el habla o pérdida de cualquier otra función controlada por el cerebro. Las probabilidades de sufrir un derrame cerebral aumentan con la edad. El derrame cerebral es una de las principales causas de discapacidad y muerte en todo el mundo.
¿Te sientes mal? Revisa tus síntomas con la app verificador de síntomas antes de probar nuestra app.
## Riesgos
El riesgo de sufrir un derrame cerebral aumenta con la edad. Si bien los derrames cerebrales hemorrágicos pueden afectar a adultos jóvenes, la mayoría ocurre en personas mayores de 70 años y muchos factores pueden aumentar el riesgo de derrame cerebral. Algunas condiciones médicas, como por ejemplo tener presión alta o tomar medicamentos para diluir la sangre, aumentan el riesgo de sufrir un derrame cerebral. Otros problemas de salud que puede aumentar el riesgo de derrame cerebral son los desórdenes de coagulación, el cáncer (en especial los tumores cerebrales), los aneurismas en el cerebro y otras causas que debiliten los vasos sanguíneos. Las personas que ya sufrieron un derrame cerebral son más propensas a tener un derrame cerebral hemorrágico. Beber alcohol, fumar o tomar cocaína o anfetaminas aumenta el riesgo de tener un derrame cerebral hemorrágico.
## Síntomas
Los síntomas del derrame cerebral hemorrágico dependen de la parte del cerebro afectada. Los más comunes son una repentina debilidad muscular unilateral del brazo, la pierna y la cara, falta de equilibrio, dificultades para hablar o balbuceo. Algunas personas pueden tener convulsiones y presentar otros síntomas como náuseas y vómitos o marearse y perder la conciencia.
## Diagnóstico
El diagnóstico se realiza en base a los síntomas, exámenes físicos y una tomografía computarizada (TAC) o resonancia magnética (RM) del cerebro.
## Tratamiento
El derrame cerebral hemorrágico es una emergencia que se atiende en un hospital. Puede ser necesario un tratamiento urgente para tratar una hemorragia activa en el cerebro. Además, algunas complicaciones como las convulsiones, también pueden requerir tratamiento urgente. Los tratamientos a largo plazo incluyen un buen manejo de la presión arterial alta y rehabilitación (por lo general, fisioterapia y terapia ocupacional intensiva). La rehabilitación es importante para mejorar la fuerza y ayudar a las personas a aprender a vivir con las discapacidades que hayan quedado a raíz del derrame cerebral.
## Prevención
Mantener un buen control de la presión arterial puede ayudar a prevenir el derrame cerebral hemorrágico. Reducir el consumo de alcohol puede contribuir a prevenir un derrame cerebral hemorrágico o un derrame recurrente.
## Pronóstico
El pronóstico tras un derrame cerebral hemorrágico depende del tamaño, la duración y la zona afectada del cerebro. La mayoría de las personas que tienen un derrame cerebral hemorrágico quedan con alguna discapacidad y es por ello que la rehabilitación es importante para mejorar el pronóstico. Si el derrame cerebral es grande o se diagnostica tardíamente, puede producir una discapacidad grave o la muerte.
## Otras denominaciones
  * sangrado en el cerebro que conduce a un derrame cerebral

  * [Wrapping up](https://ada.com/covid/smoking-and-covid-19/#wrapping-up)

Share this article:
## Overview: smoking and the risk of severe COVID-19
  * Smoking puts you at risk of severe COVID-19 complications
  * Smoking decreases lung function, creates circulation problems, and impairs the immune system
  * Exposure to second-hand smoke may also increase the risk of severe COVID-19 symptoms 


Think you might be experiencing COVID-19 symptoms
Smoking and COVID-19 [of the ongoing pandemic](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-is-the-pandemic-over/). There’s increasing evidence that smokers may be at a higher risk of experiencing severe symptoms due to an infection with the coronavirus. This article will explore the relationship between COVID-19 and smoking and its impact on your risk profile. 
## COVID-19 and smoking: what is the risk?
COVID-19 can affect anyone, but several factors, including smoking, heavily impact the progression and outcome of the disease. In assessing your risk, it's essential to understand that there's a distinction between a risk of getting COVID-19 and a [risk of getting very sick from COVID-19.](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-high-risk-groups/)
Whether or not you’ll get COVID-19[1](https://ada.com/covid/smoking-and-covid-19/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * Length of time
  * Coughing or heavy breathing
  * Symptoms[symptoms of COVID-19](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptoms/), the odds of you getting COVID-19 increase significantly.
  * Masks
  * Ventilation
  * Distance


To assess how ill you might get from an infection with the coronavirus[2](https://ada.com/covid/smoking-and-covid-19/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
  * Older adults and elderly
  * Chronic conditions of the lungs, such as **[asthma](https://ada.com/covid/asthma-and-covid-19/) **and [COPD](https://ada.com/covid/copd-and-covid-19/)
  * Chronic kidney, heart, liver, or certain neurological diseases
  * Diseases that affect your immunity
  * [Diabetes](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-diabetes/)
  * Obesity
  * [Pregnancy](https://ada.com/conditions/pregnancy/)
  * Smoking
  * Use of immunosuppressive medicationstransplantcancer treatment


The severity of COVID-19 among smokers is elevated for those still active smokers who get infected with the coronavirus and those who used to smoke in the past. Past smokers also have an increased [risk of severe symptoms due to the existing lung damage](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-lungs-symptoms/). It’s important to note that exposure to second-hand smoke
Apart from regular cigarettes, electronic cigarettes also affect the outcome of COVID-19 significantly, as smokers of any type of cigarette are more likely to experience severe complications compared to people that do not smoke. [3](https://ada.com/covid/smoking-and-covid-19/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [4](https://ada.com/covid/smoking-and-covid-19/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
Concerned that you or a loved one may have COVID-19? Start your symptom assessment in the [app](https://ada.com/app/) first.
## Are smokers more heavily impacted by COVID-19?
Smokers impacted by COVID-19 may experience more severe symptoms and face a higher hospitalization risk than non-smokers. This is because smoking causes damage to the heart, blood vessels, and lungs, which is why it increases the risk of heart and lung disease in general. [3](https://ada.com/covid/smoking-and-covid-19/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
Smoking and COVID-19 have been the subject of many studies, which suggested that smokers have a greater chance of requiring mechanical ventilationpassing awayheart failure or stroke[3](https://ada.com/covid/smoking-and-covid-19/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
Smoking could also affect COVID-19 in another way, as tobacco compromises the function of the immune system
## What to do if you’re a smoker and you get COVID-19
The treatment of COVID-19 for smokers is comparable to treatment for other risk groups and can be different for everyone, depending on your situation. In most cases, infections with the coronavirus can be treated at home. If you notice any symptoms related to COVID-19, then it’s crucial to get tested as soon as possible[to get more information regarding treatment](https://ada.com/covid/treatment-guide/).   
  
Your doctor will assess your risk profile and ask questions to determine if you are at risk of severe symptoms or hospitalization. [If you are eligible for antiviral treatment](https://ada.com/covid/antiviral-medication/), your doctor will prescribe you medication that you can take at home. For this medication to be effective, it needs to get started up as soon as possible, so you shouldn’t postpone contacting your doctor. This medication will help your immune system fight the virus by decreasing the amount of virus in your body. [5](https://ada.com/covid/smoking-and-covid-19/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
If you aren’t eligible for this medication, then there are still other things that you can do to alleviate your symptoms[6](https://ada.com/covid/smoking-and-covid-19/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
  * Opt for painkillers such as Paracetamol, Ibuprofen, or Naproxen
  * Rest as much as possible
  * Drink enough water
  * Reduce your cough by taking cough medicine and sitting upright instead of lying on your back 


If you are a smoker with COVID-19, keep track of your symptoms[6](https://ada.com/covid/smoking-and-covid-19/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
  * You’re gradually feeling worse
  * You're having difficulty breathing
  * You feel very weak, and basic tasks feel too difficult
  * You’re shaking or shivering
  * You still feel unwell after a 2 weeks


## Smoking and COVID-19: prevention guidelines
To reduce your chances of getting severely ill, we’ve listed some things you can do to reduce your risks of severe COVID-19 as a smoker[3](https://ada.com/covid/smoking-and-covid-19/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
The most crucial thing smokers can do to reduce the impact of COVID-19 is to quit smoking and stop using products containing tobacco. Quitting will immediately impact your health, and after a few weeks, your circulation and lung function will start to improve again. Apart from protecting yourself, you’ll also protect those around you by reducing their exposure to second-hand smoke. To help yourself quit, you can make use of nicotine replacement therapies or try an intervention program. [7](https://ada.com/covid/smoking-and-covid-19/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
Other [ways of preventing COVID-19](https://ada.com/covid/) both apply to smokers and non-smokers. You can drastically decrease your chances of getting infected by adhering to the following prevention measures: [8](https://ada.com/covid/smoking-and-covid-19/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
  * Wash your hands 
  * Use a mask that fits well
  * Get vaccinated and keep your vaccination up-to-date
  * Keep a safe distance from others
  * Improve indoor spaces
  * Avoid contact with people who are experiencing COVID-19 symptoms
  * Get tested for COVID-19 


## Wrapping up
The evidence linking smoking to COVID-19 has been attributed to the negative impact that smoking has on lung health and the immune system, which may make smokers more vulnerable to respiratory infections such as COVID-19. It’s crucial that smokers take proactive measures to protect themselves. If you are experiencing symptoms of the coronavirus, then it’s important to monitor yourself to see how your situation is evolving.

# Bilirubin
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on July 1, 2025 at 12:59 PM GMT+3
## On this page
  * [What is bilirubin?](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/#what-is-bilirubin)
  * [Conjugated vs unconjugated bilirubin](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/#conjugated-vs-unconjugated-bilirubin)
  * [What is Gilbert’s syndrome?](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/#what-is-gilbert-s-syndrome)
  * [What is a bilirubin nomogram?](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/#what-is-a-bilirubin-nomogram)
  * [How to lower bilirubin?](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/#how-to-lower-bilirubin)
  * [FAQs](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/#faqs)


* * *
Share this article:
Bilirubin is a yellowish substance that is formed by the body when red blood cells are broken down.[1](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") Bilirubin is toxic to the body, so under usual circumstances, it gets processed by the liver and then leaves the body through the stools. When this process doesn’t work well due to conditions of the blood, the liver or the gallbladder, it can cause jaundice
As the liver plays a big part in the excretion of bilirubin
Do you think your bilirubin levels
## What is bilirubin?
Bilirubin is a pigmented substance[2](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
Bilirubin is formed as a by-product during the breakdown process of red blood cells. During our lifespan, new red blood cells are continuously being produced by the bone marrow, and old red blood cells are broken down. While breaking down a specific part of the red blood cells, called [hemoglobin](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hemoglobin/), bilirubin is formed.
This bilirubin is toxic, but our body has mechanisms to excrete this substance.[1](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
This is a normal process, but in some cases the amount of bilirubin in the blood can increase, causing jaundice[liver cirrhosis](https://ada.com/conditions/liver-cirrhosis/), hepatitis (inflammation of the liver) and obstructions of the gallbladder can cause problems in the normal excretion of bilirubin. [1](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
Another frequent issue with bilirubin occurs in newborns. This is called [neonatal jaundice](https://ada.com/conditions/neonatal-jaundice/). Before birth, the mother’s liver takes care of the bilirubin excretion. After birth, the baby’s liver should take over. In some cases, the liver hasn’t fully developed yet and can’t excrete the bilirubin, causing jaundice. This is the most common cause why newborns get admitted to the hospital. Although neonatal jaundice isn’t always a serious condition, it can cause serious complications and should always be checked by a doctor or a midwife. [2](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
## What is conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin?
There are a few types of bilirubin
  * Conjugated bilirubindirect bilirubin
  * Unconjugated bilirubinindirect bilirubin
  * Total bilirubin


Unconjugated bilirubin is bilirubin that hasn’t been processed by the liver yet. This bilirubin is created when hemoglobin, a substance in the red blood cells, is broken down. The unconjugated bilirubin then binds to a protein in the blood and gets transported to the liver.
Once arrived in the liver, the bilirubin binds to an acid present in the liver and later on gets excreted. This bilirubin is called conjugated bilirubin. [3](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
## What is Gilbert’s syndrome?
Gilbert’s syndrome is a condition in which bilirubin levels in the blood are elevated
With Gilbert’s syndrome, unconjugated bilirubin is slower to convert into conjugated bilirubin and stays in the blood for longer. The condition is usually genetic
Symptoms often first appear in youth
However, since Gilbert’s syndrome can also alter the effect of certain medications, a visit to the doctor is still recommended to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other causes of jaundice.
## What is a bilirubin nomogram?
As neonatal jaundice is one of the most common disorders in newborns[2](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
The nomogram takes the baby’s age in hours into account, as well as the amount of bilirubin in the blood. Apart from that, there are also a few risk factors ([check here the causes of neonatal jaundice](https://ada.com/conditions/neonatal-jaundice/#causes)) that are taken into account to determine whether or not the newborn is at risk for developing jaundice.
Because of the bilirubin nomogram, doctors are able to determine how high the risk is for the baby to develop neonatal jaundice. By being able to react quickly when a baby is at high risk, serious complications may be avoided.
## How to lower bilirubin?
Bilirubin can be checked in the urine or through bloodworkthe normal range[4](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")

## Bilirubin FAQs 
Q: How is bilirubin defined?  
A: Bilirubin is an orange-yellowish pigment that is formed by the breakdown of hemoglobin in red blood cells. It gets excreted by the liver into the bile. It can be found in blood and urine, especially with certain conditions such as liver cirrhosis, hepatitis and gallstones.
Q: What does bilirubin do?  
A: Bilirubin is a by-product of the natural breakdown of red blood cells. It normally passes through the liver and gets excreted from the body.
Q: When do I need to seek medical help?  
A: When the skin or the white of the eyes starts turning yellow, it’s an indication that there is too much bilirubin present in the blood. This can be an indication that there is a problem with the liver, gallbladder, or the blood.

# Síndrome de Cushing
Escrito pelo nosso [Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/pt/team/medical/)
Atualizado em 15 de fevereiro de 2022 às 10:01 GMT+2
## Nesta página
  * [Visão geral](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/cushings-syndrome/#visao-geral)
  * [Riscos](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/cushings-syndrome/#riscos)
  * [Sintomas](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/cushings-syndrome/#sintomas)
  * [Diagnóstico](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/cushings-syndrome/#diagnostico)
  * [Tratamento](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/cushings-syndrome/#tratamento)
  * [Prevenção](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/cushings-syndrome/#prevencao)
  * [Prognóstico](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/cushings-syndrome/#prognostico)


* * *
Compartilhe esse artigo:
## Visão geral
A síndrome de Cushing é uma condição causada por um excesso de hormônio esteróide chamado cortisol. Isso pode ser causado por tomar muito de um medicamento que contém cortisol (esteróides) ou pelo corpo estar produzindo muito cortisol. Pessoas com síndrome de Cushing ganham peso ao redor do tronco e no rosto, e desenvolvem uma pele fina e esticada. Esta condição tende a afetar adultos entre 20 e 50 anos de idade. O tratamento desta condição depende da causa. Uma vez que a causa subjacente é reconhecida e removida, a maioria das pessoas com síndrome de Cushing se recuperará bem. A síndrome de Cushing não tratada pode causar osteoporose, diabetes, pressão alta e acidente vascular cerebral.
## Riscos
A síndrome de Cushing se desenvolve se houver muito cortisol no corpo. A causa mais comum é tomar medicação esteróide por um longo período de tempo. A síndrome de Cushing também pode ocorrer quando o corpo produz muito cortisol. Isso acontece quando um tumor ou câncer faz com que muito cortisol seja produzido. Esta condição geralmente afeta adultos entre as idades de 20 e 50 anos e afeta três vezes mais mulheres do que homens.
## Sintomas
Os sintomas típicos incluem um rosto vermelho, cheio (rosto de lua), ganho de peso em torno da barriga, um aumento da gordura entre o pescoço e os ombros, alterações da pele (desgaste, estrias, hematoma fácil, aumento do crescimento do cabelo) e fraqueza muscular. As mulheres podem apresentar um crescimento aumentado de pêlos diferente do padrão anterior. As crianças podem não crescer tão rápido quanto seus pares. O cortisol pode afetar a função sexual e alguns homens podem enfrentar problemas de ereção e diminuição do desejo sexual.
## Diagnóstico
O diagnóstico é feito através da avaliação do histórico médico de uma pessoa, com atenção especial aos medicamentos e exame físico, onde o médico verifica os sinais típicos da síndrome de Cushing. Se um medicamento não é a causa dos sintomas, testes de saliva, urina e sangue são feitos para testar os níveis de hormônio cortisol, e exames de imagem (ultrassonografia, tomografia computadorizada (TC) e ressonância magnética (MRI)) podem ser feitos para procurar uma causa para o excesso de cortisol.
## Tratamento
O tratamento depende da causa do alto nível de cortisol. Se for causado por uma alta ingestão de cortisol, a dosagem da medicação deve ser reduzida lentamente. As pessoas que tomam medicamentos esteróides nunca devem parar esses medicamentos repentinamente. Se um tumor é o motivo subjacente, poderá ter que ser removido por cirurgia. No caso de não ser possível remover a causa de níveis elevados de cortisol, o nível de cortisol pode ser bloqueado através de medicamentos.
## Prevenção
Ter cuidado e evitar o uso prolongado de medicamentos contendo cortisol pode ajudar a prevenir alguns casos de síndrome de Cushing.
## Prognóstico
O resultado depende da causa subjacente. Parar medicação que contém cortisol ou remover o tumor produtor de cortisol pode levar a uma recuperação total. Se a síndrome de Cushing não for tratada, pode levar a complicações como diabetes, osteoporose, pressão arterial alta, ataques cardíacos ou enfartes.

# Signs of Shingles: Herpes Zoster
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on May 14, 2025 at 9:59 AM GMT+3
