## Overview of the thyroid gland
The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland found in the lower neckThe hormones this gland releases control the body’s growth and metabolism.[1](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
When the levels of thyroid hormone are too high, symptoms of hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid) may presentwhen the levels are abnormally low, there may be symptoms of hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid)[depression](https://ada.com/signs-of-depression/).
If you are experiencing symptoms that may be linked to unusual thyroiditis levels.
## What is thyroiditis?
Thyroiditis is a term for inflammation of the thyroid gland, a condition which causes the levels of thyroid hormone in the body to go beyond the normal range.
Thyroiditis can be caused by several clinical disorders[Hashimoto’s thyroiditis](https://ada.com/conditions/hashimotos-thyroiditis-hypothyroidism/), postpartum thyroiditis and De Quervain’s thyroiditis.
Women are far more likely than men to experience thyroid problems. [3](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") Thyroiditis can be a serious condition, and requires management by a doctor.
If you are experiencing symptoms that may be linked to unusual thyroiditis levels, start a symptom assessment with the symptom checker works before you try it for yourself.
## What are the symptoms of thyroiditis?
The symptoms of thyroiditis depend on whether the levels of thyroid hormone in the blood are too high (hyperthyroidism or thyrotoxicosis) or too low (hypothyroidism).
Good to know:
### Symptoms of hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis) include:
  * Anxiety or nervousness
  * Irritability
  * Increased sweating
  * Heat intolerance
  * Weight loss or difficulty gaining weight, despite a good appetite
  * Insomnia (sleeplessness or sleep disturbances)
  * Racing heart or palpitations (pronounced awareness of one’s heartbeat) [4](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
  * High blood pressure [5](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
  * Increased frequency of bowel movements
  * Nausea and vomiting [6](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
  * Fatigue (generally feeling tired or weak)
  * Tremors (shaky hands)
  * Feeling of weakness in the muscles (particularly in the upper arms and thighs)
  * Difficulty exercising
  * Eye bulging and irritation
  * Light or no menstruation


Some people may experience weight gain due to increased appetite in hyperthyroidism. [7](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7") [8](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [9](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") [10](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10") [11](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
### Symptoms of hypothyroidism include:
  * Fatigue (generally feeling tired or weak)
  * [Depression](https://ada.com/signs-of-depression/)
  * Forgetfulness
  * Sensitivity to cold
  * Dry skin
  * Poor exercise tolerance
  * Constipation
  * Unexplained weight gain
  * Brittle nails
  * Hair loss
  * Tongue enlargement (swelling)


In addition, there may be menstrual irregularities. [12](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12") [13](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:13 "See Footnote 13") [14](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14")
### Thyroid goiter
People affected by thyroiditis may present with a goiter – the medical term for an enlarged thyroid gland
Thyroid goiters are usually painless, but can cause a tight feeling in the throat, hoarseness, coughing, and difficulty swallowing and breathing[15](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:15 "See Footnote 15")
## Types of thyroiditis
There are a number of different types of thyroiditis. Many of these thyroid problems seem to run in families, and they tend to affect a higher number of women than men. [3](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
### Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (Hashimoto’s disease)
Also known as chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, Hashimoto’s thyroiditis or disease - sometimes written as Hashimoto thyroiditis - is the most common type of thyroiditismore prevalent among women than men[16](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:16 "See Footnote 16")
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis tends to progress slowly and can take months or even years to be detected. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") Those affected may present with a painless goiter, symptoms of hypothyroidism and high levels of thyroid antibodies. Though less common, there may also be symptoms of hyperthyroidism. In some cases, the disease may begin with a period of hyperthyroidism, which leads to hypothyroidism as the thyroid gland becomes damaged. The hypothyroidism, which is often lifelong, is treated with thyroid hormone replacement. Sometimes, periods of thyroid over- and underactivity may alternate over the course of the disease. Regular monitoring and blood tests can help a person manage any thyroid hormone fluctuations that occur. [16](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:16 "See Footnote 16")
[Hashimoto’s thyroiditis](https://ada.com/conditions/hashimotos-thyroiditis-hypothyroidism/) is sometimes associated with other autoimmune conditions, including Addison’s disease, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, [celiac disease](https://ada.com/conditions/coeliac-disease/) and connective tissue disorders like [rheumatoid arthritis](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/). For more information, see the dedicated page on Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.
### Ord’s thyroiditis
Also known as Ord’s disease, this autoimmune condition is characterized by atrophy of the thyroid gland and hypothyroidism. It is very similar to Hashimoto’s disease, apart from the shrinking of the thyroid gland instead of the development of a goiter[17](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:17 "See Footnote 17")
### Silent thyroiditis
Also known as painless thyroiditis or subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis, this is an autoimmune disease
Silent thyroiditis generally resolves on its own within 12-18 months, [1](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") though in some cases the hypothyroidism may occasionally be permanent. Treatment may include beta-blockers to relieve the symptoms of hyperthyroidism and thyroid hormone replacement, when necessary, in the hypothyroid phase.
#### Postpartum thyroiditis
Sometimes classified as a type of silent thyroiditis, postpartum thyroiditis is a type of thyroiditis after pregnancy[18](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:18 "See Footnote 18") The condition is autoimmune in nature and typically manifests with an initial period of hyperthyroidism, followed by hypothyroidism that may be temporary or permanent. Not all people experience both phases. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") Postpartum thyroiditis most often affects people with a prior history of thyroid dysfunction, and resembles Hashimoto’s thyroiditis – as does regular silent thyroiditis. They are considered variants of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. [19](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:19 "See Footnote 19")
### Drug-induced thyroiditis
Some medications may cause hypothyroidism or, more rarely, hyperthyroidism. Treatment with lithium[20](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:20 "See Footnote 20") Iodine and iodine-containing medications[21](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:21 "See Footnote 21") Drugs used to treat hyperthyroidism can result in a hypothyroid state, and vice versa, if dosages are incorrect for a particular person. Treatment requires management of medications and dosages with a doctor.
### Riedel’s thyroiditis
Sometimes also called Riedel’s struma or invasive fibrous thyroiditis, this is an extremely rare type of thyroiditishard, painless mass in the front of the neck[22](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:22 "See Footnote 22") [23](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:23 "See Footnote 23")
### De Quervain’s thyroiditis (subacute thyroiditis)
Also known as painful subacute thyroiditis, subacute nonsuppurative thyroiditis, giant cell thyroiditis and subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, this is a relatively rare condition that mostly affects middle-aged women who have recently had a viral infection of the upper respiratory tractthe most common cause of a painful thyroid gland
The main symptoms of De Quervain’s thyroiditis are fever, pain in the throat and thyroid region of the neck (which may radiate to the jaw and ears) and an enlarged thyroid gland
De Quervain’s thyroiditis is usually self-limiting, with the condition clearing on its own within a few months. Treatment is aimed at minimizing pain and discomfort, and aspirin or another NSAID (Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drug), such as ibuprofen may be recommended. In severe cases, a corticosteroid may be prescribed as a potent anti-inflammatory measure. A beta-blocker may be given to ease some of the symptoms of hyperthyroidism, like a racing heart, high blood pressure, feeling agitated or having tremors. Antithyroid medication is not usually necessary. The temporary hypothyroidism that is often the last stage of the condition, before patients recover, may necessitate short-term treatment with thyroid hormone replacement.
Thyroid function generally returns to normal (a euthyroid state), though in a few cases De Quervain’s can recur and result in permanent hypothyroidism. [24](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:24 "See Footnote 24")
### Radiation-induced thyroiditis
A number of people who undergo radioactive iodine therapy for hyperthyroidism, develop radiation-induced thyroiditis after the procedure. Radiation therapy for certain cancers, such as lymphoma, head and neck cancers, can also trigger thyroiditis. [25](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:25 "See Footnote 25") Those affected may present with symptoms of hyper or hypothyroidism, ref1 as well as tenderness in the thyroid area. Treatment may involve beta-blockers to alleviate symptoms of temporary (transient) hyperthyroidism, painkillers ref17 and thyroid hormone replacement where necessary. [26](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:26 "See Footnote 26")
### Acute infectious thyroiditis
This very rare type of thyroiditiscaused by an infection of the thyroid gland[abnormality in the development of the thyroid gland](https://ada.com/conditions/congenital-hypothyroidism/). [1](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") Most people affected by acute infectious thyroiditis have a pre-existing thyroid disorder such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis or thyroid cancer. [27](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:27 "See Footnote 27")
Symptoms include pain in the front of the neck, soreness in the throat, fever and a rapid heart rate[28](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:28 "See Footnote 28")
## Diagnosis of thyroiditis (thyroid tests)
A number of diagnostic methods may be used to confirm that thyroiditis or another thyroid condition is present, including blood tests and ultrasound scans.
### Blood tests
Thyroiditis is typically diagnosed with a thyroid function test.[blood test](https://ada.com/blood-test-results/) that looks at levels of the following: [29](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:29 "See Footnote 29")
  * [TSH (thyroid stimulating hormone)](https://ada.com/thyroid/thyroid-stimulating-hormone-tsh/)
  * [FT4 (free thyroxine)](https://ada.com/thyroid/thyroxine-t4/)
  * [FT3 (free triiodothyronine)](https://ada.com/thyroid/triiodothyronine-t3/) – only occasionally


The amount of thyroxine (the thyroid’s main hormone) secreted by the thyroid gland is regulated by the pituitary gland (also called the hypophysis, a small hormone gland located at the base of the brain). The pituitary gland secretes TSH according to the amount of T4 (thyroxine) that is needed. T4 is converted into T3 (triiodothyronine), which is the biologically active form of thyroid hormone. [29](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:29 "See Footnote 29")
If the level of TSH is high and the FT4 low in a thyroid blood test, it indicates hypothyroidism.if the level of TSH is low and the FT4 high, hyperthyroidism is indicated.[29](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:29 "See Footnote 29")
Where the TSH level is slightly elevated, but the FT4 level is normal, subclinical or mild hypothyroidism is indicated.[29](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:29 "See Footnote 29")
When autoimmune thyroiditis is suspected, a doctor may order further blood tests to see whether thyroid antibodies are present at levels above the reference range. These include [thyroid peroxidase antibodies](https://ada.com/thyroid/tpo-antibodies/) (TPOAb) and thyroglobulin antibodies (TgAb) to confirm Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, and thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibodies (TSHR Ab), which are also called TSH receptor antibodies (TRAbs), in the case of Graves’ disease. [29](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:29 "See Footnote 29")
### Thyroid ultrasound
This non-invasive test may be ordered to check the thyroid gland for swelling and nodules, and blood circulation pattern. An ultrasound is also used to check the parathyroid glands (four glands that are situated on the back of the thyroid and produce parathyroid hormone, which affects the body’s calcium metabolism). [30](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:30 "See Footnote 30")
### Radioactive iodine uptake test
In some cases (particularly when hyperthyroidism is present), a radioactive iodine uptake test may be recommended – often together with a thyroid scan (a specialized imaging procedure). In both of these tests, a small amount of a weak radioactive substance is administered. [31](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:31 "See Footnote 31")A radioactive iodine uptake test allows the medical practitioner to determine whether the thyroid gland, which naturally takes up iodine, [32](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:32 "See Footnote 32") is functioning normally, and why thyroid hormone levels may be out of range. A scan can detect thyroid nodules and inflammation. ref20
### Fine needle aspiration
If a suspicious thyroid nodule is detected, a fine needle aspiration biopsy may be performed to determine whether it is benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous). [33](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:33 "See Footnote 33")
## Thyroiditis treatments
Treatment depends on the type of thyroiditis
### Hypothyroidism
An underactive thyroid is treated with thyroid hormone replacement.levothyroxine[34](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:34 "See Footnote 34") or remain too low. [35](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:35 "See Footnote 35")
### Hyperthyroidism
An overactive thyroid can be treated in a number of ways. There is no single preferred method – the chosen option usually depends on the type and severity of hyperthyroidism, as well as the age and general health of the affected person.
Treatment methods include antithyroid drugsradioactive iodinethyroid surgery[7](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
Because treatment will depend on the type of thyroiditis experienced, consultation with a medical professional is very important. Taking over-the-counter medication without advice from a healthcare provider is not recommended.
## Other thyroid conditions
### Graves’ disease
Also known as diffuse toxic goiter and [Basedow’s disease, Graves’ disease](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/) is an autoimmune condition in which the thyroid gland is stimulated to produce too much thyroid hormonemore prevalent among women than menone of the most common causes of hyperthyroidism[34](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:34 "See Footnote 34")
People affected by Graves’ disease may present with painless enlargement of the thyroid gland, symptoms of hyperthyroidism and high levels of thyroid antibodies. In addition, there may be symptoms of Graves’ ophthalmopathy, where the eyes are affected by a gritty sensation, pain or pressure. There may also be swollen eyelids, light sensitivity, double vision or bulging eyes, among other symptoms. Graves’ ophthalmopathy is seen in approximately 30 percent of people affected by Graves’ disease. There may also be reddening and thickening of the skin, most often on the shins or tops of the feet. This is called Graves’ dermopathy [36](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:36 "See Footnote 36") or pretibial myxedema, [37](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:37 "See Footnote 37") and is rare.
The hyperthyroidism is treated with antithyroid medication, radioactive iodine or thyroid surgery. Where permanent hypothyroidism results, levothyroxine is prescribed to replace the thyroid hormone and is typically taken for life. [34](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:34 "See Footnote 34")
### Thyroid nodules
Thyroid nodules are lumps in the thyroid gland[38](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:38 "See Footnote 38")
The majority of thyroid nodules do not cause any symptoms.
Thyroid nodules may be associated with iodine deficiency (rare in the United States, more common in many regions of Europe), overgrowth of normal thyroid tissue (thyroid adenomas) or Hashimoto’s disease, among other conditions. [39](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:39 "See Footnote 39") [40](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:40 "See Footnote 40")
A thyroid nodule may also be a sign of thyroid cancer. However, most thyroid nodules are benign (non-cancerous growths)[41](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:41 "See Footnote 41")
If a thyroid nodule is non-cancerous (benign) and not causing any symptoms, treatment may not be necessary. A doctor may simply opt to perform regular examinations and thyroid function tests to monitor its progress. Large nodules, and those that cause symptoms, may be removed surgically or treated with radioactive iodine (if they are producing thyroxine). [42](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:42 "See Footnote 42")
### Thyroid cancer
Thyroid cancer is relatively rareMost cases of thyroid cancer are treatable and can be cured[43](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:43 "See Footnote 43") [44](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:44 "See Footnote 44")
Early symptoms of thyroid cancer are rarely noticeable. However, in some cases, firm, painless nodules may be noted. Later symptoms may include rapid growth of a goiter, throat hoarseness or pain that does not go away, difficulty swallowing or breathing, pain in the front of the neck and an unexplained cough. [44](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:44 "See Footnote 44") [45](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:45 "See Footnote 45") [46](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:46 "See Footnote 46")
There are four main types of thyroid cancer:
  * Papillary
  * Follicular
  * Medullary
  * Anaplastic


Treatment depends on the type of thyroid cancer and may involve full (or, in rare cases, partial) removal of the thyroid gland during thyroid surgery, radioactive iodine therapy, radiotherapy and chemotherapy. Levothyroxine is prescribed to prevent hypothyroidism after treatment, and is taken for life. [44](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:44 "See Footnote 44")
## Find out more about your symptoms
## Thyroiditis FAQs
Q: Is there a special thyroid diet?  
A:no specific thyroid diet that is recommendedIt is not advisable to take special supplements, including iodine preparations, without first consulting a doctor.
Some foods and supplements can, however, interfere with the absorption of levothyroxine, so those taking this medication should keep in mind the following:
  * After taking calcium-rich foods or supplements, wait four hours before taking levothyroxine
  * After taking iron tablets, wait two hours before taking levothyroxine
  * Wait as long as possible after taking levothyroxine before eating soya or soy products


In addition, kelp and iodine supplements should be avoided unless otherwise recommended by a healthcare provider, as they can potentially aggravate thyroid disorders
Vegetables of the Brassica family, such as cabbage, broccoli and kale, may be implicated in the development of a goiter in some people, but only in very rare cases where consumption is extremely high. It is not a problem under normal dietary conditions. [47](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:47 "See Footnote 47")
Q: What is thyroid hair loss?  
A:
The hair typically grows back once the thyroid disorder has been successfully treated. However, this may take a few months, and regrowth is not always complete. [48](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:48 "See Footnote 48") Partial hair loss is listed as a possibility during the first few months of treatment with levothyroxine. [49](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:49 "See Footnote 49") In rare cases, antithyroid drugs may also be associated with hair loss. ref36
Q: What precautions need to be taken with the thyroid in pregnancy?  
A:
In some parts of the world, such as Germany, pregnant women may be encouraged to take iodine supplements to compensate for deficiencies in the soil and the lack of fortification of food products. A doctor will be able to advise on whether supplementation is necessary.
People who develop symptoms of hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism while pregnant need to seek immediate medical care.[postpartum depression](https://ada.com/signs-of-postpartum-depression/). [8](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
Q:  
A:[Hashimoto’s disease](https://ada.com/conditions/hashimotos-thyroiditis-hypothyroidism/), may be associated with an increase in a person’s risk of developing thyroid cancer and certain other types of cancer. [50](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:50 "See Footnote 50") [51](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:51 "See Footnote 51") It is advisable to speak to a doctor about any cancer concerns you may have.
Q: Can thyroiditis recur?  
A:
Q: Can thyroiditis cause a sore throat?  
A:[52](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:52 "See Footnote 52") [53](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:53 "See Footnote 53")
Q: Can thyroiditis cause swollen lymph nodes?  
A:[Hashimoto’s thyroiditis](https://ada.com/conditions/hashimotos-thyroiditis-hypothyroidism/), as well as in acute infectious thyroiditis. However, swollen lymph glands can also be a sign of many other conditions. If you have swollen lymph nodes and other signs of a thyroid problem, it is advisable to consult a doctor. [54](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:54 "See Footnote 54") [55](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/#fn:55 "See Footnote 55")

# Migraine with aura
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on October 22, 2024 at 4:00 PM GMT+3
## On this page

## Overview
  * Migraine with a visual aura refers to a classic form of migraine accompanied by visual disturbances.
  * An aura usually occurs before the migraine attack, although in some cases, you can also experience it during or after your migraine episode.
  * Treatment for aura migraine is focused on symptom relief and prevention.


Think you might be experiencing migraine with aura
Migraine with aura is a classic form of migraine affecting 10 to 30% of all people who experience migraine. This type of migraine is typically accompanied by visual disturbances, such as seeing flashing lights, zigzag lines, or black spots. In this guide by Ada’s medical team, you can find more information on aura migraines, the possible symptoms, and treatment options. 
## What is a migraine aura?
An aura migraine[type of migraine](https://ada.com/conditions/migraine-headache/#types-of-migraines) that occurs following warning signs known as an aura. This migraine is also referred to as a classic migraine and affects about 10 to 30% of people who experience migraines. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/migraine-with-aura/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
## What does a migraine with aura feel like?
Migraines with aura can cause several symptoms. You can experience the common signs of migraine[2](https://ada.com/conditions/migraine-with-aura/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
  * Throbbing, pulsating pain on one side of the head. This pain may affect the eye area but can occur anywhere in the head or the neck.
  * Sensitivity to light, sound, and/or smell
  * Vision changes
  * Nausea
  * Vomiting


Besides these common symptoms of a migraine, it’s also possible to experience: 
  * Loss of appetite 
  * Muscle tenderness 
  * Impaired concentration 
  * Fatigue 
  * Anxiety
  * Other symptoms


The aura that accompanies this type of migraine[2](https://ada.com/conditions/migraine-with-aura/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
  * Visual disturbances such as seeing zigzag lines, black spots, or flashing lights
  * Feeling numbness or a tingling feeling
  * Difficulty speaking
  * Dizziness


Although it’s more common to experience an aura before migraine, it’s also possible to experience the aura symptoms during the attack or afterward. In some cases, you can also experience an aura without migraine. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/migraine-with-aura/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
## What causes migraines with aura?
The causes of migraines with aura are not fully understood yet. We know that they result from inflammation near the nerves and blood vessels of the headtriggers for migraine with aura[2](https://ada.com/conditions/migraine-with-aura/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
  * Anxiety 
  * Depression
  * Stress
  * Fatigue
  * Menstruation 
  * Not eating regularly 
  * Certain foods
  * Caffeine
  * Not getting enough exercise


## How long can a migraine with aura last?
The aura preceding the migraine usually only lasts for an hour. The actual migraine episode can last anywhere between 2 hours and 3 days[3](https://ada.com/conditions/migraine-with-aura/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
## How can migraine with aura be diagnosed?
A healthcare provider can diagnose a migraine with aura by: [4](https://ada.com/conditions/migraine-with-aura/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
  * Checking symptomsmedical, family, and overall health history
  * Looking at headache details
  * Using CT or MRI
  * Performing a complete neurologic exam


A migraine diagnosis is given when other causes are ruled out. After diagnosing a migraine, a healthcare provider can recommend treatments to help reduce the impact on daily life.
## How to stop migraines with aura?
A migraine with typical aura symptoms can be treated in various ways. You can relieve your symptoms with medication as prescribed by your healthcare provider: [5](https://ada.com/conditions/migraine-with-aura/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
  1. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)  
NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and aspirin can help reduce headache pain. Their anti-inflammatory properties are thought to help relieve a migraine’s characteristic throbbing/pulsing sensation. Depending on the type and strength, they can be purchased over the counter or prescribed.
  2. However, NSAIDs are not suitable for long-term use, as they can cause complications, including gastrointestinal disorders. People who experience frequent migraine attacks and need regular pain relief should consult their doctor to explore the most appropriate treatment options.
  3. Triptan medications  
Triptan medications should be taken at the first sign of a migraine starting. They work on the blood vessels and pain pathways that are associated with migraines. Your doctor might prescribe these if other medications haven't helped.
  4. Ergotamine medications
  5. “Good to know: 
  6. Opioid medications


## How to prevent migraine with aura?
Preventing migraines relies on a combination of lifestyle changes and medications. 
Behavioral changes that are recommended for preventing migraine attacks include: [2](https://ada.com/conditions/migraine-with-aura/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
  * Developing techniques to manage and reduce stress
  * Keeping a diary to identify migraine triggers
  * Sleeping well and establishing a consistent sleep cycle are essential. 
  * Staying hydrated
  * Establishing regular meal times and adopting a healthy, balanced diet.
  * Devising a new medication plan 
  * Following a safe weight-loss program


Where people have frequent attacks, medication may be prescribed to prevent migraine headaches. The medications that have been found most effective at migraine prevention include[2](https://ada.com/conditions/migraine-with-aura/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
  * Anticonvulsant medications (commonly used for epilepsy)
  * A couple of blood pressure medications: Beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers.
  * Antidepressants such as tricyclic antidepressants and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)
  * OnabotulinumtoxinA (Botox®) injections are approved by the FDA as a [treatment for chronic migraine](https://ada.com/conditions/chronic-migraines/#treatments)


Finding the right preventative and relieving treatment, as well as the best lifestyle changes, can positively reduce the frequency and severity of attacks and their negative effects on life, work, and sleep. Talk to your doctor about what options might be best suited for you.
## Wrapping up
Migraine with aura is a classic form of migraine accompanied by visual disturbances such as flashing lights, zigzag lines, dizziness, and difficulty speaking. As the aura usually occurs before the actual migraine episode, it can be a warning sign that a migraine episode is about to happen. Medication can help alleviate migraine aura symptoms. Lifestyle changes can also help prevent migraine episodes. 
## Find out more about your symptoms
## Migraine with aura FAQs
Q: What is an aura migraine  
A: An aura migraine is a classic form of migraine that causes severe headaches on one side of the head, combined with visual disturbances such as seeing flashing lights or zigzag lines. 
Q: How to stop migraine aura?   
A: Medication for migraine with aura can help relieve the symptoms you’re experiencing. Your healthcare provider may prescribe you with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, triptans, ergotamine,**  
Q: How common is migraine with aura?**  
A: Migraine with aura is quite a common type of migraine. About 10 to 30% of people who experience migraines also experience an aura before or during their migraine episodes.
Q: What causes an aura migraine?   
A: The cause of aura migraines is still unknown, although many triggers have been identified. Some triggers are anxiety, depression, stress, certain foods, caffeine, and changes to your sleep and eating patterns.

# Ada no identificó una enfermedad que tengo y que resulta ser seria. ¿Cómo abordarán este problema?
Si encuentras que el resultado de Ada es incorrecto te alentamos a que nos escribas a 
Estamos constantemente mejorando el conocimiento médico y la tecnología de Ada, llevando a cabo procesos de revisión del contenido médico tanto internos como externos. Cuando se plantea un problema sobre una evaluación determinada, lo revisamos de inmediato y nos aseguramos que las actualizaciones se aplican rápidamente.
Sin embargo, recuerda que Ada no está destinada a realizar diagnósticos. Ada está diseñada para ayudarte a entender mejor tu salud al ofrecerte una variedad de posibles causas para tus síntomas e información para acceder a cuidados de salud adecuados. La información provista es general y puede suceder que tu enfermedad no esté incluida en las sugerencias de Ada. Ada no está diseñada para reemplazar a un médico y siempre deberías realizar una consulta médica para buscar diagnóstico, tratamiento o consejo.

# Meningite bacteriana
Escrito pelo nosso [Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/pt/team/medical/)
Atualizado em 22 de julho de 2022 às 14:09 GMT+2
## Nesta página
  * [Visão geral](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#visao-geral)
  * [Riscos](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#riscos)
  * [Sintomas](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#sintomas)
  * [Diagnóstico](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#diagnostico)
  * [Tratamento](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#tratamento)
  * [Prevenção](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#prevencao)
  * [Prognóstico](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#prognostico)
  * [Outros nomes](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#outros-nomes)


* * *
Compartilhe esse artigo:
## Visão geral
Meningite bacteriana é uma infecção bacteriana das meninges (as membranas ao redor do cérebro). É uma condição grave e requer avaliação médica urgente. Muitas bactérias diferentes podem causar meningite bacteriana e uma das mais conhecidas é a Neisseria meningitis (a meningite meningocócica). Os sintomas típicos são dor de cabeça, rigidez do pescoço, febre e vômitos. Os sintomas podem aparecer de repente, e a pessoa afetada pode ficar muito doente em poucas horas. A meningite bacteriana é tratada com antibióticos, embora outros tratamentos de suporte possam ser necessários. A identificação e tratamento precoce aumentam a chance de uma boa recuperação.
## Riscos
Os recém-nascidos têm o mais alto risco de meningite, embora esta condição possa afetar pessoas de todas as idades. Homens podem ter um risco ligeiramente maior do que mulheres. Pessoas com outras condições (incluindo uma infecção recente de ouvido ou garganta) ou que tiveram uma fratura recente do crânio têm maior risco de contrair meningite.
## Sintomas
Os sintomas típicos da meningite bacteriana são dor de cabeça, rigidez do pescoço, náuseas, vômitos, febre e sensibilidade à luz (fotofobia). Outros sintomas podem ser sonolência e confusão. Algumas causas de meningite podem causar uma erupção cutânea profunda com manchas de cor violeta. Os sintomas podem surgir de repente, e a pessoa afetada pode ficar muito doente no espaço de algumas horas.
## Diagnóstico
O diagnóstico baseia-se nos sintomas, no exame físico e nos exames que confirmam a presença de uma infecção severa no organismo. Toma-se uma amostra do fluido cerebrospinal (o fluido nas meninges ao redor do cérebro e da coluna vertebral) permitindo o diagnóstico das bactérias específicas que estão causando a infecção.
## Tratamento
Meningite bacteriana é uma condição grave e requer atenção urgente por um médico. A infecção é tratada com antibióticos (por infusão intravenosa). As pessoas com meningite bacteriana ficam em geral muito doentes, e podem precisar de outro tratamento de suporte (como fluidos para aumentar a pressão arterial), enquanto os antibióticos trabalham para combater a infecção.
## Prevenção
Algumas causas comuns de meningite bacteriana são evitáveis por vacinação. Ater-se ao calendário de vacinação recomendado pode ajudar a evitar alguns casos de meningite. Boa higiene, como lavar as mãos, também pode ajudar a evitar alguns casos de meningite bacteriana.
## Prognóstico
O diagnóstico e tratamento precoce desta condição oferece a melhor chance de uma boa recuperação. Casos graves de meningite bacteriana têm uma alta taxa de complicações, incluindo convulsões e danos cerebrais. Em alguns casos a meningite bacteriana pode causar morte, especialmente em pessoas muito jovens e nos idosos.
## Outros nomes
  * infecção bacteriana ao redor do cérebro e medula espinhal

# White Blood Cell Count
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on May 21, 2025 at 4:59 PM GMT+3
## On this page
  * [What is a white blood cell count?](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#what-is-a-white-blood-cell-count)
  * [What are white blood cells (WBCs)?](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#what-are-white-blood-cells-wbcs)
  * [Normal white blood cell count](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#normal-white-blood-cell-count)
  * [Low WBC](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#low-wbc)
  * [High WBC](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#high-wbc)
  * [High white blood cell count during pregnancy](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#high-white-blood-cell-count-during-pregnancy)
  * [WBC Test](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#wbc-test)
  * [FAQs](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#faqs)


* * *
Share this article:
## What is a white blood cell count?
Our blood contains a certain white blood cell count (WBC, leukocytes or leucocytes) which, as part of the body’s immune system, help the body fight infection. [1](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") A white blood cell (WBC) count measures the amount of white blood cells in a sample of a person’s blood.The normal white blood cell count in a healthy adult is between 4,000 and 11,000 WBCs per microliter
To measure the number of white blood cells in a person’s body, a doctor will order a white blood cell count, often as part of a[complete blood count (CBC) test](https://ada.com/blood-test-results/#complete-blood-count-cbc). A low white blood cell count can indicate conditions including infections, inflammation, certain cancers, HIV/AIDS, and others, making it an important diagnostic test. Aside from these conditions, a person’s white blood cell count can indicate their immune system activity, response to cancer treatment and overall health.
Feeling unwell? Get a symptom assessment
## What are white blood cells (WBCs)?
There are several kinds of white blood cells (WBCs), including neutrophils, eosinophils, lymphocytes, monocytes and basophils. Each variety plays a different role in protecting the body from foreign pathogens such as viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites.[1](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
A white blood cell count checks both the overall levels of white blood cells in the blood, as well as the overall proportion of different types of white blood cells.
Feeling unwell? Get a symptom assessment with the symptom checker works before you try it for yourself.
## Normal white blood cell count
A normal white blood cell count is a reading that falls within a range established through the testing of men, women and children of all ages. Although it is possible to cite general values, exact ranges tend to differ between labs and countries.
For men, a normal white blood cell count is anywhere between 5,000 and 10,000 white blood cells per μl of blood.between 4,500 and 11,000 per μl,between 5,000 and 10,000.[2](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") Not all sources, however, differentiate between male and female values; of these sources, values for both sexes tend to lie in the range between 4,000 to 4,500 and 10,000 to 11,000 cells per μl. [3](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
Data provided by the 
Sex/Age | White Cells per microliter (µL) of blood  
---|---  
Men | 5,000 to 10,000  
Women [4](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") | 4,500 to 11,000  
Children [5](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") | 5,000 to 10,000  
## Low white blood cell count
The threshold for a low white blood cell count (leukopenia) varies between individuals and cases but is generally considered to be anything lower than 4,000 white blood cells per μl of blood in an adult.
A low white blood cell count can be caused by[6](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
  * Viral or bacterial infection
  * Diminished bone marrow function
  * Cancer
  * Autoimmune disorders including [rheumatoid arthritis](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/) and [HIV/AIDS](https://ada.com/conditions/hiv-aids/)
  * Leukemia
  * Lupus
  * [Tuberculosis](https://ada.com/conditions/tuberculosis/)
  * Cancer treatment such as radiation and chemotherapy, as well as other medications
  * Aplastic anemia


A low white blood cell count may cause symptoms such as fever, chills,[headache](https://ada.com/conditions/headache/) and bodyache.
If you are experiencing symptoms that may be related to a low white blood cell count
## High white blood cell count
Though it varies between individuals, an elevated white blood cell count (leukocytosis) is usually considered to be anything above 11,000 cells per μl of blood in an adult.[7](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
  * Infection
  * Bone marrow disease
  * Medications
  * Autoimmune disorders such as [rheumatoid arthritis](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/)
  * Leukemia
  * Allergies
  * Tuberculosis
  * Whooping cough
  * Myelofibrosis
  * Stress
  * Smoking [8](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")


In most instances, there are no specific symptoms related to an elevated white blood cell count, though symptoms associated with the underlying medical condition may occur.
If you are experiencing symptoms that may be related to a high white blood cell count
## High white blood cell count during pregnancy
Typically, white blood cell count is elevated during pregnancy,[9](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") The stress imposed on the body through pregnancy causes this rise in white blood cells. [10](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
During delivery and in the hours that follow, the white blood cell count range can be anywhere between 9,000 and 25,000 white blood cells per μl of blood. The white blood cell count will typically return to normal around four-weeks after delivery. [10](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
[Read more about Pregnancy](https://ada.com/conditions/pregnancy/)
## How to test white blood cell count?
To carry out a white blood cell count, a doctor will draw a blood sample, usually from a vein in the arm or the back of the hand. This is a common procedure, and side effects are rare, but may include lightheadedness, bleeding or infection. No special preparation is required for a white blood cell count, but a person should inform their doctor of any medications they are taking, as these can affect the results. A white blood cell count is usually taken as part of a complete blood count.
[Read more about a complete blood count »](https://ada.com/blood-test-results/#complete-blood-count-cbc/)

Q: Are there any types of cancer associated with white blood cells (WBCs)?  
A:[11](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11") There are four main types of leukemia: acute myeloid, chronic myeloid, acute lymphocytic and chronic lymphocytic. Lymphoma, the second type of cancer involving WBCs, occurs when lymphocytes (small leukocytes that are part of the immune system) behave abnormally and collect in certain areas of the body. Lymphocytes can collect anywhere in the body, most commonly in the lymph nodes in the neck, armpits and groin. [12](https://ada.com/white-blood-cell-count/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12") Treatment options are available for both types of cancer.

# Síntomas del COVID-19: Dolor de cabeza
Escrito por nuestro [Equipo de Profesionales Médicos](https://ada.com/es/team/medical/)
Actualizado el 21 de enero de 2025, 10:20 EET
## En esta página
  * [Información general](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#informacion-general)
  * [Causas](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#causas)
  * [Síntomas](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#sintomas)
  * [Duración](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#duracion)
  * [COVID-19 o dolor de cabeza normal](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#covid-19-o-dolor-de-cabeza-normal)
  * [Tratamientos](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#tratamientos)
  * [En resumen](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#en-resumen)
  * [FAQs](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#faqs)


* * *
Comparte este artículo:
## Información general
  * El dolor de cabeza puede ser uno de los primeros síntomas de una infección por el COVID-19
  * El dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19 suele durar sólo un par de días.
  * El dolor de cabeza causado por el COVID-19 se puede tratar de forma similar a cualquier otro dolor de cabeza: con reposo, hidratación, compresas frías y analgésicos.
  * El dolor de cabeza suele ser uno de los síntoma más comunes en los casos más leves de COVID-19


Aprende más acerca de tus síntomas
El dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19uno de los primeros síntomas[pérdida del olfato o el gusto](https://ada.com/es/covid/perdida-olfato-y-gusto-covid-19/). Algunos estudios sugieren que el dolor de cabeza puede indicar el pronóstico de la afección, lo que lo convierte en un factor esencial para el diagnóstico y la estrategia de tratamiento. Aunque el COVID-19 puede provocar dolor de cabeza, es importante tener en cuenta que no todos los dolores de cabeza son indicativos de una infección por COVID-19, y que no todas las personas infectadas por el coronavirus tienen dolor de cabeza.
La intensidad y duración de un dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19 puede variar entre personas, pero existen algunas formas de aliviar el dolor y evitar que se intensifique. En esta guía, te informamos sobre las causas de un dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19, la progresión habitual y las medidas que puedes tomar para sentirte mejor.
## ¿Qué causa el dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19?
El dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19 es un síntoma frecuente del coronavirus, junto con otros síntomas similares a los [de la gripe](https://ada.com/es/conditions/influenza-infection/) o [el resfriado](https://ada.com/es/conditions/common-cold/): [1](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
  * Temperatura corporal elevada
  * [Tos](https://ada.com/es/covid/tos-covid-19/)
  * Pérdida del olfato o del gusto
  * Dificultad para respirar
  * [Dolor de garganta](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-garganta-covid-19/)
  * Nariz tapada o mocosa 
  * Dolor de cuerpo
  * Diarrea
  * Sensación de cansancio y malestar


El dolor de cabeza asociado con COVID-19 puede producirse en personas de cualquier edad[3](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
La causa del dolor de cabeza[los síntomas de COVID-19](https://ada.com/es/covid/sintomas-covid-19/): [4](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") [5](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
  * El dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19 puede estar provocado por las citoquinas, que son células que regulan la respuesta del organismo a las infecciones, las inflamaciones y los traumatismos. Estas citoquinas pueden provocar más inflamación 
  * Otra posible causa podría ser la activación del sistema trigeminovascular. Este sistema se refiere a partes de un nervio craneal
  * El COVID-19 también puede afectar a los pulmones, provocando una escasez de oxígeno
  * El dolor de cabeza también puede ser consecuencia de un trombo


¿Te preocupa que tú o alguien cercano a ti puedan tener COVID-19? Comienza tu evaluación de síntomas en la app.
## ¿Cómo se siente el dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19?
Por lo general, el dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19 se presenta bastante rápido [tras la infección por el coronavirus](https://ada.com/es/covid/) y suele aparecer simultáneamente con otros síntomas. El dolor es de una intensidad de moderada a gravedolor punzantepresión[6](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
La localización del dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19 puede variar. Puedes sentir el dolor en el lado izquierdo o derecho de la cabeza, pero también es posible que el dolor de cabeza esté más localizado en la parte frontal de la cabeza. También es posible que sientas dolor en todo el cráneo. Además del dolor de cabeza generalizado, también puedes sentir dolor de cabeza detrás de los ojos. En algunos casos, el dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19 va acompañado de náuseas y vómitos. [6](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [7](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7") [8](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [9](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") [10](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
El dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19 puede estar presente durante todo el tiempo que dure la afección . El dolor puede empeorar debido a los siguientes factores: [6](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [8](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
  * Actividad física
  * Un episodio de tos
  * La presencia de sonidos fuertes o luces intensas


## ¿Cuánto tiempo dura el dolor de cabeza por el COVID?
La mayoría de veces, el dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19 sólo dura un par de días[6](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
Los dolores de cabeza asociados al COVID-19 suelen comenzar de manera repentina y empeoran gradualmente a lo largo del día
Algunos estudios sugieren que las personas que experimentan un dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19 tienen más probabilidades de verse afectadas menos tiempo, disminuyendo la duración de la infección. [4](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
## ¿Cómo saber si el dolor de cabeza es por el COVID?
El dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19 es un síntoma importante para el diagnóstico, ya que suele estar presente en el inicio de la infección. Como el coronavirus puede causar muchos síntomas, es esencial examinarlos todos juntos. Si sólo tienes dolor de cabeza, puede haber muchas otras causas posibles aparte del COVID-19. 
Sin embargo, si tu dolor de cabeza va acompañado de una pérdida del olfato o del gusto, o de cualquiera de los otros síntomas de COVID-19, es muy recomendable que te hagas una prueba y te mantengas aislado hasta que tengas los resultados. Las pruebas de diagnóstico más utilizadas[12](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
  * Pruebas PCR
  * Pruebas de antígenos


¿Te preocupa que tú o alguien cercano a ti puedan tener COVID-19? Comienza tu evaluación de síntomas en la app.
## ¿Cómo tratar el dolor de cabeza por el COVID?
El tratamiento [13](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:13 "See Footnote 13") [14](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14") [15](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/#fn:15 "See Footnote 15")
  * Descansa
  * Bebe agua
  * Utiliza una compresa fría 


Además de estos remedios caseros, también es importante saber qué analgésicos 
  * Paracetamol
  * Ibuprofeno
  * Naproxeno


En una consulta médica pueden recomendarte otros medicamentos o tratamientos en función de la gravedad de tu dolor de cabeza y otros síntomas asociados.
## En resumen
El dolor de cabeza por el COVID-19 es frecuente y puede ser uno de los primeros síntomas de una infección por el coronavirus. Aunque no todas las personas con COVID-19 experimentan dolor de cabeza, es crucial prestar atención a este síntoma, especialmente cuando se combina con otros síntomas, ya que puede indicar la gravedad de la infección.
Si experimentas dolor de cabeza junto con otros síntomas de COVID-19, se recomienda que te aisles y te hagas una prueba. Recuerda que no todos los dolores de cabeza son indicativos de COVID-19, pero siempre es mejor examinarse y estar seguro.

# Mieloma múltiple
Escrito por nuestro [Equipo de Profesionales Médicos](https://ada.com/es/team/medical/)
Actualizado el 15 de febrero de 2022, 10:00 EET
## En esta página
  * [Resumen](https://ada.com/es/conditions/multiple-myeloma/#resumen)
  * [Riesgos](https://ada.com/es/conditions/multiple-myeloma/#riesgos)
  * [Síntomas](https://ada.com/es/conditions/multiple-myeloma/#sintomas)
  * [Diagnóstico](https://ada.com/es/conditions/multiple-myeloma/#diagnostico)
  * [Tratamiento](https://ada.com/es/conditions/multiple-myeloma/#tratamiento)
  * [Pronóstico](https://ada.com/es/conditions/multiple-myeloma/#pronostico)


* * *
Comparte este artículo:
## Resumen
El mieloma múltiple es un cáncer que afecta la médula ósea (donde se fabrican y maduran los células sanguíneas). El mieloma es causado por un glóbulo blanco llamado célula plasmática que normalmente trabaja para producir las proteínas que combaten las infecciones (anticuerpos). Cuando ocurre un cáncer de células plasmáticas, estas no solo crecen en forma descontrolada en la médula ósea, sino que también interfieren con la capacidad de la médula ósea de fabricar otros glóbulos sanos. El mieloma múltiple se llama así porque el cáncer a menudo se encuentra en varios huesos diferentes. Los síntomas del mieloma múltiple pueden ser producidos por una disminución de los glóbulos sanguíneos normales, incluyendo dificultad para respirar, sentir más cansancio del habitual y encías sangrantes; o pueden ser el resultado de un rápido crecimiento de células cancerosas, tales como pérdida de peso inesperada, dolor de huesos o huesos frágiles. Actualmente no hay cura para el mieloma múltiple, pero existen alternativas de tratamiento que ayudan a controlar la enfermedad. El mieloma suele ser un cáncer de crecimiento lento y, por este motivo, el pronóstico depende de factores tales como la edad de la persona diagnosticada, la agresividad del cáncer y el desarrollo de complicaciones.
## Riesgos
El mieloma múltiple es un cáncer que afecta las células que crecen en la médula ósea. La médula ósea es el tejido esponjoso dentro de los huesos donde crecen y maduran todas las células sanguíneas (glóbulos sanguíneos). A su vez, las células plasmáticas son un tipo de glóbulo sanguíneo blanco que ayudan al cuerpo a combatir las infecciones produciendo unas proteínas llamadas anticuerpos. El mieloma es un cáncer que surge a partir de células plasmáticas anormales, haciendo que se multipliquen rápidamente. Este aumento excesivo de células plasmáticas impide el crecimiento de glóbulos sanos, lo que afecta la capacidad del cuerpo de transportar oxígeno, coagular cuando se sangra y combatir infecciones. Además, estas células plasmáticas también producen proteínas extras, que pueden dañar los riñones. La causa del mieloma múltiple se desconoce. Sin embargo, el riesgo de desarrollarlo aumenta con la edad. Raramente afecta a personas menores de 40 años y principalmente se diagnostica a los 70 años de edad. Los hombres son más propensos que las mujeres a desarrollar esta condición médica.
## Síntomas
Los síntomas más comunes incluyen palidez, dificultad para respirar, cansancio y encías sangrantes. Otros síntomas pueden incluir pérdida de peso, dolor de huesos y huesos frágiles. Algunas personas pueden presentar coágulos de sangre, infecciones recurrentes o problemas renales. Es posible que no haya síntomas en las primeras etapas de esta condición médica porque los síntomas se desarrollan a medida que la enfermedad progresa.
## Diagnóstico
El diagnóstico puede sospecharse basándose en los síntomas y un examen físico, pero solo puede confirmarse con más estudios. Los exámenes de sangre pueden mostrar si hay un problema con la producción de glóbulos blancos, y los análisis de orina pueden mostrar la presencia de mucha proteína como resultado de la mayor actividad de las células plasmáticas. Podría realizarse un examen TEP (un tipo especial de tomografía computarizada TAC) para buscar el mieloma múltiple en otras ubicaciones en el cuerpo. Se toma una pequeña muestra de médula ósea (biopsia) con una aguja para ver si hay células cancerosas.
## Tratamiento
Actualmente no hay cura para el mieloma múltiple, pero existen alternativas de tratamiento que ayudan a controlar esta condición. El tratamiento puede incluir una combinación de quimioterapia, radioterapia y trasplante de células madre. Sin embargo, la combinación exacta de terapias depende de la etapa de la enfermedad, el estado de salud general de la persona afectada y de si se han producido complicaciones. Una consulta oncológica puede brindar la mejor asesoría sobre el tratamiento en cada caso. Las complicaciones como dolor de huesos, fracturas, anemia o daño renal pueden requerir un tratamiento específico.
## Pronóstico
El mieloma múltiple no puede curarse por completo. El pronóstico varía ampliamente de una persona a otra y depende de la edad de la persona diagnosticada, la agresividad del cáncer y de si el cáncer responde bien o no a la terapia. Las personas mayores y las personas que desarrollan complicaciones, tales como infecciones y daño renal, son más propensas a morir como resultado de esta condición médica.

# Amyotrophe Lateralsklerose (ALS)
Verfasst von [Adas medizinischem Fachpersonal](https://ada.com/de/team/medical/)
Aktualisiert am 21. Juli 2025 um 09:59 OESZ
## Auf dieser Seite
  * [Was ist Amyotrophe Lateralsklerose (ALS)?](https://ada.com/de/conditions/amyotrophic-lateral-sclerosis/#was-ist-amyotrophe-lateralsklerose-als)
  * [Risiken](https://ada.com/de/conditions/amyotrophic-lateral-sclerosis/#risiken)
  * [Symptome](https://ada.com/de/conditions/amyotrophic-lateral-sclerosis/#symptome)
  * [Diagnose](https://ada.com/de/conditions/amyotrophic-lateral-sclerosis/#diagnose)

Artikel teilen:
## Was ist Amyotrophe Lateralsklerose (ALS)?
Die Amyotrophe Lateralsklerose (ALS)1 (auch als Lou-Gehrig-Krankheit oder Motoneuronerkrankung bekannt) ist eine seltene Erkrankung, bei der die Nervenzellen des Rückenmarks und Gehirns zerstört werden, die Muskelbewegungen kontrollieren.
Der Verlust dieser Nerven verursacht eine zunehmende Muskelschwäche und führt schließlich zu einer Lähmung. Die Ursache für ALS ist nicht bekannt. Frühe Symptome sind:
  * Kribbeln oder Schwäche in Armen oder Beinen,
  * Muskelkrämpfe und
  * manchmal eine Veränderung der Stimme.


Es gibt keine Heilung für ALS, jedoch einige Medikamente, die die Zerstörung der Nervenzellen verlangsamen. Die Behandlung zielt darauf ab, die Symptome von ALS zu lindern und die Person und ihre Familie zu unterstützen.
Die meisten Betroffenen mit ALS sterben schließlich an dieser Erkrankung, obwohl es bekannte Fälle von Menschen gibt, die mit ALS leben, wie zum Beispiel der Physiker Stephen Hawking.
Andere Bezeichnung für Amyotrophe Lateralsklerose: Muskeldystrophie.
Hast Du Beschwerden oder Symptome, die auf diese Erkrankung hinweisen könnten? Starte jetzt eine kostenlose Symptomanalyse mit der [Adas Symptom-Checker](https://ada.com/de/app/) funktioniert.
## Risiken für ALS
Es gibt keine bekannten Ursachen oder Risikofaktoren, die die Entwicklung von ALS begünstigen. Gene können eine kleine Rolle spielen, da 5 % der Betroffenen mit ALS ein Familienmitglied mit dieser Erkrankung haben. Menschen mit ALS vererben die Krankheit jedoch nicht unbedingt auf ihre Kinder. Die Erkrankung tritt üblicherweise im Alter zwischen 50 und 70 Jahren auf und Männer sind etwas häufiger betroffen als Frauen.
## ALS Symptome
Frühe Symptome der Amyotrophen Lateralsklerose können von Person zu Person unterschiedlich sein und umfassen Schwäche und Kribbeln in Armen und Beinen, Muskelkrämpfe und Steifheit sowie gelegentlich eine Veränderung der Stimme oder Schwierigkeiten beim Schlucken.
Betroffene mit ALS können Schwierigkeiten bei der Kontrolle ihrer Emotionen haben. Mit dem Fortschreiten der Erkrankung werden die Muskeln steif und kleiner
## Wie wird ALS diagnostiziert?
Die Diagnose kann durch die Auswertung der Symptome und durch die körperliche Untersuchung durch einen Neurologen gestellt werden. Es gibt keine alleinige Untersuchung zur Diagnosestellung von ALS.
Einige Tests können jedoch genutzt werden, um andere mögliche Ursachen für die Symptome auszuschließen. Diese schließen Bluttests, bildgebende Verfahren (gewöhnlich ein MRT), Nerventests, eine Untersuchung der Flüssigkeit, die das Rückenmark umgibt (Lumbalpunktion), und in seltenen Fällen eine Muskelbiopsie ein.
## Behandlung von ALS
Es gibt keine Heilung für ALS. Es gibt ein Medikament, welches das Fortschreiten der Krankheit verlangsamen kann. Die Wirksamkeit ist jedoch von Fall zu Fall unterschiedlich und ist mit einem Neurologen zu besprechen.
Die Behandlung von ALS erfordert Therapeuten aus verschiedenen Bereichen, um die Alltagskompetenz so lang wie möglich aufrecht zu halten und eine Person sowohl körperlich als auch sozial und emotional zu unterstützen. Atmung und Nahrungsaufnahme können schließlich durch Magensonden und Maschinen ersetzt werden, was jedoch von den Überzeugungen und Präferenzen des einzelnen Patienten abhängt.
## Prognose
Es gibt keine Heilung für ALS. Die Zerstörung der Nerven und die Muskelschwäche schreiten voran und Menschen mit ALS sterben schließlich an dieser Erkrankung.

# Resfriado común
Escrito por nuestro [Equipo de Profesionales Médicos](https://ada.com/es/team/medical/)
Actualizado el 7 de abril de 2022, 11:06 EET
## En esta página
  * [Resumen](https://ada.com/es/conditions/common-cold/#resumen)
  * [Riesgos](https://ada.com/es/conditions/common-cold/#riesgos)
  * [Síntomas](https://ada.com/es/conditions/common-cold/#sintomas)
  * [Diagnóstico](https://ada.com/es/conditions/common-cold/#diagnostico)
  * [Tratamiento](https://ada.com/es/conditions/common-cold/#tratamiento)
  * [Prevención](https://ada.com/es/conditions/common-cold/#prevencion)
  * [Pronóstico](https://ada.com/es/conditions/common-cold/#pronostico)


* * *
Comparte este artículo:
## Resumen
El resfriado común es una infección viral de la nariz y la garganta. Normalmente presenta síntomas como goteo nasal y tos. Los virus responsables de los resfriados se transmiten por las gotitas que se expulsan al aire al toser o estornudar, por eso tomar medidas como cubrirse la nariz y la boca al toser y estornudar puede ayudar a prevenir la transmisión de los virus. Las personas que tienen un resfriado suelen mejorarse dentro de una semana.
## Riesgos
Los resfriados son causados por virus que infectan la nariz y la garganta. Estos virus se propagan por las gotitas que se liberan al aire al toser o estornudar. El resfriado común se trata de una condición muy común que puede afectar a personas de todas las edades. Muchas personas se resfrían más de una vez al año, y los niños pueden resfriarse hasta 5 y 6 veces al año.
## Síntomas
Los síntomas típicos incluyen goteo nasal, nariz tapada, tos seca y dolor de garganta.
## Diagnóstico
El diagnóstico suele hacerse fácilmente basándose en los síntomas.
## Tratamiento
Si bien los resfriados no suelen requerir ningún tratamiento específico, algunas personas toman medidas para aliviar sus síntomas. Como por ejemplo beber infusiones calientes, tomar medicamentos para aliviar el dolor de garganta o utilizar descongestivos en aerosol para despejar la nariz. Además, para algunas personas el vapor de una ducha caliente ayuda a despejar su nariz y garganta.
## Prevención
Mantener buenos hábitos de higiene, como lavarse las manos y cubrirse la boca y la nariz al estornudar o toser, ayuda a prevenir la propagación de virus y a evitar resfriados.
## Pronóstico
El resfriado común suele mejorar en una semana sin un tratamiento específico.

# Graves’ Disease
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on May 15, 2025 at 11:04 AM GMT+3

## What is Graves’ disease?
Graves’ disease, also known as Basedow’s disease or diffuse toxic goiter, is an autoimmune condition in which a person’s immune system mistakenly stimulates the thyroid gland to produce excess amounts of thyroid hormone,[hyperthyroidism](https://ada.com/conditions/hyperthyroidism/) and sometimes eye problems. It is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism[1](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
[The thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland](https://ada.com/thyroid/) in the lower part of the neck, positioned below the voice box. Hormones released by the gland control the body’s metabolism, playing a key role in processes like digestion, temperature, heart rate and growth. If the levels of these hormones go [too low](https://ada.com/conditions/hypothyroidism/) or too high and are not corrected, a person can experience a range of unpleasant and potentially dangerous effects and complications. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
Symptoms of Graves’ disease may include: [1](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * Nervousness
  * Racing heart or palpitations, i.e. pronounced awareness of one’s heartbeat
  * Difficulty sleeping
  * Intolerance to heat
  * Feeling tired and/or weak
  * Swelling of the thyroid, i.e. development of a goiter
  * Irritation and bulging of the eyes, known as Graves’ ophthalmopathy or thyroid eye disease


Are you experiencing symptoms that could be associated with Graves’ disease?
Treatment for Graves’ disease depends on the particular person, but may include medication to reduce the amount of thyroid hormone being produced, radioiodine therapy and, in some cases, surgery to remove the thyroid gland. The condition may go into remission and then relapse. Treatment and monitoring is usually lifelong.
With careful management by a doctor who specializes in hormonal conditions, an endocrinologist, the outlook is good and many people with Graves’ disease are able to enjoy a full, healthy life. ref6 ref8
However, untreated or poorly treated Graves’ disease can lead to serious complications,[cardiovascular disease](https://ada.com/cardiovascular-disease-risk-factors/) and stroke, as well as thyroid storm. In the case of Graves’ eye disease, vision loss may occur. ref2 ref9 ref10
Diffuse toxic goiter can affect people of any age, though it tends to be more prevalent in adults, particularly those between the ages of 20 and 50, than children. It is more common in women
## Graves’ disease symptoms
A person with Graves’, or Basedow’s disease, may develop general signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism[1](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [3](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [4](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
  * Anxiety or nervousness
  * Irritability, agitation or restlessness
  * Rapid or irregular heartbeat or palpitations
  * Sleep disturbances, i.e. insomnia
  * Increased sweating, body warmth and heat intolerance
  * Fatigue and weakness
  * Difficulty exercising
  * Tremors, i.e. shaky hands
  * Having more bowel movements than usual
  * Unexplained weight loss or difficulty gaining weight; in some cases there may be weight gain due to increased appetite
  * Hair loss
  * [Erectile dysfunction](https://ada.com/conditions/erectile-dysfunction/) in men


Symptoms may develop gradually, and may seem to come and go. In some people, there may be swelling of the thyroid gland,[1](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [6](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [Read more about symptoms of hyperthyroidism.](https://ada.com/conditions/hyperthyroidism/#symptoms)
### Graves’ disease symptoms in females
In women, Graves’ disease may also cause menstrual irregularities including: [1](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [4](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
  * Very light periods
  * Infrequent periods
  * Absence of periods


### Bulging eyes and other eye symptoms: Graves’ ophthalmopathy (thyroid eye disease)
An estimated 25 to 50 percent of people with Graves’ disease experience eye symptoms,[7](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7") [4](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") [8](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
  * Irritation, tearing or dryness in the eyes; the eyes may feel gritty
  * Redness of the eyes and eyelids
  * Swelling of the upper eyelids
  * Sensitivity to light
  * Bulging of the eyes
  * Pain in or behind the eyes, particularly when looking up or to the side


In most cases, the eye symptoms of Graves’ disease are mild and easy to treat.[7](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7") [4](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") [8](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
  * Inability to move the eyes
  * Ulcers on the cornea (the outer layer of the eye)
  * Blurred or double vision
  * Loss of vision and blindness (rare)


If you are experiencing any eye problems and suspect that you may have thyroid eye disease, it is recommended that you see a doctor without delay.
### Graves’ dermopathy (pretibial myxedema)
A small number of people with Graves’ disease develop red, thick, swollen areas of skin, typically on the shins and the top of the feet. This is called pretibial myxedema, thyroid dermopathy or Graves’ dermopathy, and is most often seen in people who also have eye symptoms[1](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [9](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9")
Are you experiencing symptoms that could be associated with Graves’ disease?
## Causes of Graves’ disease
Graves’ disease is an autoimmune condition, which means that it is caused by the body’s immune system mistakenly targeting healthy tissue, in this case the thyroid gland. Graves’ disease occurs when immune system proteins (antibodies), which normally attack bacteria and viruses, start attacking the thyroid gland. This causes the thyroid gland to secrete more thyroid hormone than is needed by the body, leading to hyperthyroidism. [10](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
### Risk factors
It is not understood exactly what causes the immune system to target the thyroid gland, but hereditary factors are thought to be involved
It is thought that other risk factors for the development of the disease may include: [11](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11") [12](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12") [13](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:13 "See Footnote 13") [14](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14") [15](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:15 "See Footnote 15") [16](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:16 "See Footnote 16")
  * Being female
  * Having been pregnant recently
  * Having another autoimmune condition, e.g. [type 1 diabetes](https://ada.com/conditions/diabetes/), [Hashimoto’s thyroiditis](https://ada.com/conditions/hashimotos-thyroiditis-hypothyroidism/) or [rheumatoid arthritis](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/)
  * Severe stress
  * High iodine intake
  * Smoking tobacco; this is also associated with worsening of Graves’ eye symptoms
  * Certain medications, e.g. Interferon beta-1b
  * Certain infections, e.g. Yersinia enterocolitica
  * Injury to the thyroid gland, e.g. through surgery


### Causes of Graves’ ophthalmology
Graves’ ophthalmology is not the result of excess thyroid hormone in the body, but rather inflammation and swelling in the tissues behind the eyes. This swelling pushes the eyeballs forward, causing bulging and other symptoms. The same antibodies that mistakenly stimulate the thyroid gland to produce high levels of thyroid hormone mistakenly target these tissues in some people, though the exact reason for this is not clearly understood. [8](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [12](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12") [17](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:17 "See Footnote 17")
Smoking tobacco is a risk factor in the development and worsening of thyroid-associated eye disease.[8](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [17](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:17 "See Footnote 17")
## Diagnosis of Graves’ disease
The first step in the diagnosis of Graves’ disease is typically a visit to a doctor, who will take the person’s medical history and perform a physical examination. If Graves’ disease is suspected, doctors will usually order blood tests to check thyroid hormone levels, as well as levels of thyroid antibodies. An ultrasound scan of the thyroid gland and/or radioactive iodine uptake test may also be needed. These imaging tests can help the doctor to see whether any swelling or nodules, which are small lumps, are present. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
### Graves’ disease tests
#### Blood tests
These are able to measure levels of the following: [1](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [18](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:18 "See Footnote 18") [3](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [14](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14") [19](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:19 "See Footnote 19") [20](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:20 "See Footnote 20")
**[Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH)](https://ada.com/thyroid/thyroid-stimulating-hormone-tsh/):** This varies according to how much thyroid hormone is needed by the body at any given time. TSH levels are usually very low in Graves’ disease and many other conditions that cause hyperthyroidism.
Free thyroxine (FT4):
Free triiodothyronine (FT3):[FT3 levels ](https://ada.com/thyroid/triiodothyronine-t3/)are usually high when Graves’ disease is present. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [21](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:21 "See Footnote 21")
Good to know:
Thyroid antibodies:[thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPO)](https://ada.com/thyroid/tpo-antibodies/) and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (Tg) are often detected in people affected by Graves’ too.
#### Thyroid ultrasound
A non-invasive scan of the throat region, a thyroid ultrasound can help to identify nodules and swelling, thereby helping to identify the cause of the hyperthyroidism. [19](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:19 "See Footnote 19")
#### Radioactive iodine uptake test and thyroid scan
To confirm the diagnosis, a doctor may recommend a test in which the person is given a very small dose of a weakly radioactive substance and then undergoes a special imaging scan. Because the thyroid takes up iodine, this test can provide insights into how the thyroid is functioning and what the cause of the hyperthyroidism may be. It is generally safe for most people, but is not recommended for pregnant women. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [19](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:19 "See Footnote 19") [22](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:22 "See Footnote 22")
### Differential diagnosis
It is important to distinguish signs and symptoms of Graves’ disease from other conditions that can sometimes present in similar ways, such as [other thyroid problems](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/), an [anxiety disorder](https://ada.com/conditions/generalized-anxiety-disorder/) or [bipolar disorder](https://ada.com/conditions/bipolar-affective-disorder/). Blood tests and the other tests detailed above help to ensure an accurate diagnosis. [23](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:23 "See Footnote 23")
Are you experiencing symptoms that could be associated with Graves’ disease?
## Graves’ disease treatment
Treatment for Graves’ disease is generally the same as treatment for hyperthyroidismrequires lifelong monitoring and management of thyroid hormone levels,[1](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [3](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
  * Antithyroid medication; this is the term for medicine aimed at reducing thyroid function
  * Radioiodine therapy
  * Thyroid surgery


[Read more about hyperthyroidism treatment »](https://ada.com/conditions/hyperthyroidism/#treatment)
### Thyroid eye disease treatment
In many cases, Graves’ orbitopathy clears up on its own, without any specific treatment. However, in other cases treatment may be necessary. This may include: [7](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
  * In mild cases, cool compresses, lubricating eye drops and sunglasses
  * Corticosteroid medication
  * In severe cases, surgery


A person with thyroid eye disease will be referred to a doctor specializing in the eyes, called an ophthalmologist, for management of the condition. [7](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7") [17](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:17 "See Footnote 17")
Good to know:
### Pretibial myxedema treatment
The skin lesions that some people with Graves’ disease develop do not generally cause discomfort and are not usually serious. However, they can be unsightly. Treatment for thyroid dermopathy is often not necessary, but where recommended typically involves the application of corticosteroid creams. People with more severe pretibial myxedema may find that wearing compression stockings is also helpful in providing relief. [24](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:24 "See Footnote 24") [25](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:25 "See Footnote 25")
Good to know:
### Complications of Graves’ disease
If it is left untreated or medical advice is not adequately followed, Graves’ disease can cause serious complications. These include: [18](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:18 "See Footnote 18")
  * Eye damage and vision loss, in the case of thyroid eye disease [7](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7") [17](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:17 "See Footnote 17")
  * Hypothyroidism if thyroid hormone levels are not adequately monitored and managed [14](https://ada.com/conditions/graves-disease/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14")
  * Thyroid storm
  * Other complications


[Read more about thyroid storm and other complications of hyperthyroidism »](https://ada.com/conditions/hyperthyroidism/#complications)
## Other names for Graves’ disease
  * Basedow’s disease
  * Toxic diffuse goiter/Diffuse toxic goiter
