# COVID-19 Symptom: Nose
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on February 4, 2025 at 11:00 AM GMT+2
## On this page
  * [Overview](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#overview)
  * [Causes](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#causes)
  * [Symptoms](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#symptoms)
  * [Duration](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#duration)
  * [Other causes](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#other-causes)
  * [Treatments](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#treatments)
  * [Wrapping up](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#wrapping-up)
  * [FAQs](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#faqs)


* * *
Share this article:
## Overview
  * Nose symptoms COVID-19 causes include a loss or change in the sense of smell, a runny or stuffy nose, a burning sensation, and a bloody nose.
  * The nose is particularly vulnerable to inflammation caused by the virus because it has many ACE2 receptors, which the virus uses to enter cells.
  * Changes to your sense of smell are one of the most frequently reported symptoms of COVID-19, with many people experiencing a complete or partial loss of smell.
  * Nasal symptoms with COVID-19 usually go away on their own within days to a few weeks, but there’s a possibility that some symptoms, such as a reduced sense of smell, may persist long after the virus clears.


Think you might be experiencing COVID-19 symptoms
There are several nose symptoms that COVID-19 can cause
## Causes of COVID-19 nose symptoms
The nose is a primary entry point for the [coronavirus](https://ada.com/covid/) due to the high number of ACE2 receptors on its inner lining. ACE2 receptors are proteins that exist on the surface of various cells throughout the body, including the respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, kidneys, and blood vessels. These receptors play a role in regulating cellular functions through biochemical processes.
The coronavirus also has a protein on its surface that can bind to ACE2 receptors, allowing it to enter cells and disrupt normal cellular processes. Depending on where the virus binds to ACE2 receptors in the body, this can cause various problems. [1](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
Given that the coronavirus primarily enters the body through the airway, combined with the high concentration of ACE2 receptors in the nose, the nose is particularly susceptible to inflammation caused by the virus. The nose and nasopharynx, the area at the back of the nose connected to the respiratory system, typically have the highest viral load of COVID-19. [2](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
Concerned that you or a loved one may have COVID-19? Start your symptom assessment in the [app](https://ada.com/app/) first.
## Possible symptoms of the nose with COVID
There are several nose symptoms COVID-19 can cause[3](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [4](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
Changes to your sense of smell[changes in smell often go together with changes in taste](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-loss-of-taste-and-smell/) or other more general COVID-19 symptoms. [5](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
Runny and stuffy nose[runny nose is also a common symptom caused by COVID-19](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-runny-nose/), with even a [higher incidence for the Omicron variant](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-omicron-variant-symptoms/), which mainly causes symptoms in the upper respiratory tract. Once the coronavirus enters the cells of the nose and sinuses, the immune system reacts. The cells become inflamed, creating a clear mucus that traps the virus and flushes it out of the body. With COVID-19, you can have yellow mucus from the nose and a clear runny nose. [6](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [7](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
A bloody nose[COVID-19 could put you at a higher risk of having nosebleeds](https://ada.com/covid/bloody-nose-covid-19-symptom/). Further studies are required to confirm the relationship between the coronavirus and nosebleeds. [8](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [9](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9")
A dry or burning sensation in the nose[dry nose with COVID-19 is possible](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-dry-nose/), although it’s not frequently reported. These symptoms are very likely to occur together with other nasal symptoms, such as a loss or change in smell. Some people also have a nose that feels dry due to the extended use of masks or medication against other nasal symptoms of COVID-19. [10](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
## How long do nasal symptoms with COVID-19 last?
Usually, nasal symptoms are amongst the first symptomsCOVID nose symptoms go away on their own once the infection clears[most COVID-19 nose symptoms](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptoms/) go away on their own, there’s a possibility that some symptoms persist after the initial infection clears. Specifically, changes in smell may linger on for months after your COVID-19 infection. 
If you’re still experiencing symptoms after your infection has cleared, [then you might have long COVID](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-long-covid/), and you should consult your general practitioner for monitoring and treatment. [11](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
## What else can cause nasal symptoms besides COVID-19?
COVID-19 nose symptoms can be similar to other viral infections or allergies
Your sense of smell can be diminished by: [12](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12") [13](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:13 "See Footnote 13")
  * An infection with a virus, such as a virus that causes the common cold or [influenza](https://ada.com/conditions/influenza-infection/)
  * An [infection of the sinuses](https://ada.com/conditions/viral-sinusitis/)
  * [Allergies](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-vs-allergies/) (here is more info about [COVID Symptoms vs. allergies](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-vs-allergies/))
  * Nasal polyps (growths in your nose) 
  * Head injury
  * [Alzheimer’s disease](https://ada.com/conditions/alzheimers-disease/) (older adults)
  * Radiation therapy of the head and neck 


A runny or congested nose may be caused by: [14](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14") [15](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:15 "See Footnote 15")
  * [The common cold](https://ada.com/conditions/common-cold/)
  * Allergies
  * Changes in temperature or humidity
  * [Hypothyroidism](https://ada.com/conditions/hypothyroidism/)
  * Medicines such as nasal sprays, aspirin, ibuprofen, ACE inhibitors, and beta blockers
  * Hormone changes
  * Irritating substances in the air, such as smoke, perfumes, and paint fumes
  * Alcohol and spicy food


A bloody nose may be due to COVID-19, but it may also be caused by: [16](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-nose/#fn:16 "See Footnote 16")
  * Picking your nose or injury
  * Blowing your nose too hard
  * Changes in temperature and air 
  * High blood pressure
  * Conditions of the blood vessels
  * Medicines such as warfarin 


## How can symptoms of the nose due to COVID-19 be treated?
Most nasal symptoms caused by COVID do not need specific treatment
For a runny or stuffy nose
  * Nasal sprays
  * Salt water rinse 


It's vital to use only an adequate amount of nasal spray, as excess use may cause a runny or congested nose and damage to the mucous membranes of the nose. If your symptoms do not improve, you can consult your general practitioner for prescription nasal sprays. 
If you’re experiencing a nosebleed
  * Sit down
  * Lean forward with your head tilted forward
  * Press your nose right above your nostrils for about 10 to 15 minutes
  * Breathe through your mouth


When your nose has stopped bleeding, try not to pick or blow your nose, avoid extreme temperature changes, and do not do any demanding exercise for the rest of the day. 
If your nose doesn’t stop bleeding or you are losing a lot of blood, you should seek emergency medical care. 
For persistent loss of smell
  * Smell training
  * Nasal irrigation
  * Steam inhalation


If you are experiencing persistent or severe loss of smell, you should seek medical advice from your doctor. They may recommend additional treatments or therapies to help improve your symptoms. 
## Wrapping up
The nose is one of the parts of our body most prone to experiencing symptoms of an infection with the coronavirus due to its high presence of ACE2 receptors. The most frequent nasal symptom caused by the coronavirus is a loss or change in your perception of smell. Besides that, you can also experience a runny nose, a blocked nose, or, in some cases, a bloody nose. These symptoms usually go away on their own once the infection has cleared.
## Find out more about your symptoms
## Nose symptoms and COVID-19 FAQs
Q: What does COVID-19 do to your nose?  
A: COVID-19 can enter the body through the nose, mouth, or eyes, and then it binds to the ACE2 receptors on the surface of the cells lining the nasal cavity. This binding can cause inflammation in the nasal passages, leading to a range of nasal symptoms, such as a runny or stuffy nose, loss of smell, and sneezing. 
Q: What are some COVID-19 nose symptoms?   
A: The most common nasal symptoms include a runny or stuffy nose, loss of smell (anosmia) or, distorted sense of smell (parosmia), and sneezing. Other less common symptoms may include postnasal drip, itchy or watery eyes, and sore throat.
Q: How do you reset your nose after COVID-19?  
A: You can try smell training, nasal irrigation, and steam inhalation to reset your nose after COVID-19. Smell training involves exposing yourself to different smells to retrain the brain. Nasal irrigation and steam inhalation can help clear blockages and improve the sense of smell. Seek medical advice if you are experiencing persistent or severe loss of smell.
Q: When does COVID-19 nose go away?  
A: The duration of COVID-19 nose symptoms can vary depending on the individual and the severity of the illness. In some cases, the symptoms can last for several weeks or even months after the initial infection. However, in most cases, the symptoms improve within a few days to a week as the body's immune system fights off the virus. 
Q: Can COVID-19 cause nasal congestion?  
A: Yes, COVID-19 can cause nasal congestion, a common symptom of the illness. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), around 5% of people with COVID-19 experience nasal congestion. However, other studies have reported higher rates of nasal congestion, with some suggesting that it may be present in up to 20-30% of cases.

# COVID-19-Symptom: Übelkeit und Erbrechen
Verfasst von [Adas medizinischem Fachpersonal](https://ada.com/de/team/medical/)
Aktualisiert am 1. Juli 2025 um 13:00 OESZ

## Überblick
Gerade am Beginn einer Coronavirus-Infektion kann es zu Übelkeit, Erbrechen und anderen Magen-/Darm-Beschwerden kommen. In den meisten Fällen handelt es sich dabei um leichte bis mittelschwere Symptome. Hier erfährst Du, wie häufig Verdauungsbeschwerden wie Übelkeit und Erbrechen bei COVID-19 auftreten, wie lange sie meistens dauern und ab wann Du ärztliche Hilfe suchen solltest. Außerdem findest Du unter anderem Tipps, was Du tun kannst, damit Dir weniger übel ist.
  * Übelkeit und Erbrechen sind mögliche Symptome einer Coronavirus-Infektion.
  * COVID-19-bedingtes Erbrechen klingt normalerweise innerhalb eines Tages ab.
  * Ein Übelkeitsgefühl kann in manchen Fällen auch nach der akuten Coronavirus-Infektion bestehen bleiben.


Finde mehr über Deine Symptome heraus.
## Was sind Verdauungsbeschwerden aufgrund einer Coronavirus-Infektion?
Eine Infektion mit Coronaviren kann zu Verdauungsbeschwerden führen – am häufigsten zu Übelkeit und Erbrechen[1](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-uebelkeit-und-erbrechen/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * Bauchschmerzen oder Magenschmerzen
  * [Durchfall](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-durchfall/) (Diarrhöe)
  * [Appetitlosigkeit](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-appetitlosigkeit/)


Diese Verdauungsbeschwerden bei COVID-19 können entweder jeweils allein oder zusammen mit anderen Symptomen der Coronavirus-Infektion auftreten wie zum Beispiel Fieber. [1](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-uebelkeit-und-erbrechen/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
Wichtig zu wissen[ersten Symptomen einer Coronavirus-Infektion](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-symptome/) und können gerade bei Kindern
## Was sind die Ursachen von Übelkeit und Erbrechen aufgrund einer Coronavirus-Infektion?
Derzeit ist noch nicht vollständig geklärt, warum eine Coronavirus-Infektion zu Übelkeit und Erbrechen führen kann. Es gibt allerdings verschiedene Hypothesen, zum Beispiel: [1](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-uebelkeit-und-erbrechen/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * Das Coronavirus heftet sich an Bindestellen für das Angiotensin-konvertierendes Enzym 2 (ACE2) – auch auf Zellen im Verdauungstrakt. Dieser Angriff des Coronavirus auf Zellen im Magen-/Darmbereich kann Übelkeit und Erbrechen verursachen.
  * Coronaviren können eine Entzündungsreaktion im Körper auslösen, die das Verdauungssystem verletzen kann.
  * Eine Coronavirus-Infektion kann bei einigen Menschen mit Stress- und Angstreaktionen einhergehen, die wiederum zu Übelkeit, Erbrechen, [Bauchschmerzen](https://ada.com/de/conditions/abdominal-pain/) und anderen Verdauungssymptomen führen können.


## Wie machen sich Übelkeit und Erbrechen aufgrund einer Coronavirus-Infektion bemerkbar?
Erbrechen und Übelkeit treten häufig zu Beginn einer Coronavirus-Infektion auf. Bei Übelkeit hast Du das Gefühl, Dich gleich übergeben zu müssen. Bei manchen Menschen kann es auch zu einer Appetitlosigkeit kommen. Das heißt, Du hast weniger Lust etwas zu essen. Dieses Symptom ist häufig, wenn Du auch an einem [Geschmacks- oder Geruchsverlust](https://ada.com/de/covid/geruchs-und-geschmacksverlust-corona/) leidest, wodurch das Essen unangenehm schmecken kann. [1](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-uebelkeit-und-erbrechen/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
## Wie lange dauern Übelkeit und Erbrechen aufgrund einer Coronavirus-Infektion?
Normalerweise klingt das Erbrechen aufgrund von COVID-19 innerhalb von 12 bis 24 Stunden ab. Das Gefühl der Übelkeit kann noch eine Weile anhalten und verschwindet in den meisten Fällen nach ein paar Tagen. Bei manchen Menschen können Verdauungssymptome wie Übelkeit über Wochen bis Monate anhalten, [was ein Hinweis auf Long-COVID sein kann](https://ada.com/de/covid/long-covid-symptome/). [2](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-uebelkeit-und-erbrechen/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [3](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-uebelkeit-und-erbrechen/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [4](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-uebelkeit-und-erbrechen/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
## Welche anderen Ursachen für Übelkeit und Erbrechen gibt es neben einer Coronavirus-Infektion?
Übelkeit und Erbrechen können viele unterschiedliche Ursachen haben. Beispiele sind: [5](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-uebelkeit-und-erbrechen/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
  * Infektionen mit anderen Viren oder Bakterien (Magen-Darm-[Grippe](https://ada.com/de/conditions/influenza-infection/))
  * Allergien
  * Lebensmittelvergiftungen
  * Entzündliche Darmerkrankungen
  * [Migräne](https://ada.com/de/conditions/migraine/)
  * Erkrankungen der Leber oder Bauchspeicheldrüse
  * Krebserkrankungen
  * Chemotherapien


Zur Abklärung der Ursache ist es wichtig, dass Du Dich auf eine Coronavirus-Infektion testen 
Mit der [Ada-App](https://ada.com/de/app/) kannst Du Deine Symptome ganz einfach checken. 
## Wie lassen sich Übelkeit und Erbrechen bei einer Coronavirus-Infektion behandeln?
[Die Behandlung hängt davon ab, ob Du ein erhöhtes Risiko für einen schweren COVID-19-Verlauf hast](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-medikament-und-behandlung/). Wenn Du aufgrund einer Coronavirus-Infektion erbrechen musst, verlierst Du viel Flüssigkeit. Es ist wichtig, dass Du… [6](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-uebelkeit-und-erbrechen/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [7](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-uebelkeit-und-erbrechen/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
  * ausreichend trinkst.
  * Dich ausruhst.
  * versuchst, keine Mahlzeit auszulassen, denn ein leerer Magen kann das Übelkeitsgefühl noch verstärken. Am besten, Du isst kleinere Mengen und vermeidest fettige, scharfe oder sehr süße Speisen, da diese die Übelkeit verschlimmern können.


Falls Essensgerüche Deine Übelkeit verstärken, kannst Du auch versuchen, nur kalt zu essen. Denn warmes Essen riecht meistens stärker.
Es ist wichtig, dass Du Deine Symptome im Blick behältst und so schnell wie möglich ärztliche Hilfe suchst, wenn Du… [6](https://ada.com/de/covid/corona-uebelkeit-und-erbrechen/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
  * mehrmals täglich erbrichst.
  * besonders stark oder schmerzhaft erbrichst.
  * im Erbrochenen Blut bemerkst.
  * Dich immer schlechter fühlst.
  * Schwierigkeiten beim Atmen hast, auch wenn Du aufrecht stehst.
  * Dich sehr schwach fühlst und Dir einfache Tätigkeiten schwerfallen.
  * zitterst oder es Dich schüttelt.
  * Dich nach einem Monat noch unwohl fühlst.


## Das Wichtigste auf einen Blick
Übelkeit und Erbrechen sowie weitere Verdauungsbeschwerden wie Bauchschmerzen können Symptome einer Coronavirus-Infektion sein. Sie treten meistens am Anfang einer Coronavirus-Infektion auf und klingen innerhalb weniger Tage ab. Bei Erbrechen ist es wichtig, viel zu trinken und Dich auszuruhen.

## What is bacterial meningitis?
Bacterial meningitis is a bacterial infection of the meninges, the membranes around the brain and spinal cord. It is a serious condition and requires urgent medical treatment.
Many different bacteria can cause bacterial meningitis. Typical symptoms are headache, neck stiffness, fever, and vomiting. Symptoms can come on very suddenly, and the affected person can become very sick within a few hours.
Think you might be experiencing bacterial meningitis
Bacterial meningitis is treated with antibiotics, though other treatments might be needed to support the person through the illness. Meningitis can occasionally lead to death, but early recognition and treatment give the best chance of a good recovery. If you become concerned that you or someone you know may have meningitis, you can do a free symptom assessment using the 
## Signs and symptoms of bacterial meningitis
Typical symptoms of bacterial meningitis include:
  * Headache
  * Neck stiffness
  * Nausea
  * Vomiting
  * Fever
  * Sensitivity to light (photophobia)


Other symptoms include drowsiness and confusion. Some types of meningitis can cause a deep purple, blotching rash.
Symptoms can come on very suddenly, and the affected person can become very sick within a few hours.
### Symptoms of bacterial meningitis in infants and young children
In children[1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") It is important to remember that infants and very young children often cannot tell caregivers how they feel, so vigilance is important.
In babies and young children[1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
  * Fast breathing
  * Difficulty breathing
  * Excessive, high-pitched crying or moaning, or crying that is noticeably different from the baby’s usual cry
  * Irritability
  * Lethargy or less activity than usual
  * Drowsiness, sleepiness, or being difficult to wake up
  * Refusal to eat and/or vomiting
  * Jerky movements and stiffness, or floppiness
  * High fever, above 38 °C / 100.4 °F, or changing body temperature, i.e., being hot and then cold
  * Seizures
  * Bulging fontanelle, the soft spot on top of a baby’s head


If seizures occur or if the baby’s fontanelle is bulging, seek emergency medical help immediately.[2](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") Children younger than one year of age do not usually have a stiff neck. [3](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
In young children, early symptoms indicating that meningitis is developing can include: [2](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
  * Leg pains
  * Cold hands or feet
  * Rash (see below)
  * Blueness, pallor, or duskiness around the lips.


### Symptoms of bacterial meningitis in older children, teens, and adults
The classic triad of symptoms of meningitis are a stiff neck, headache and fever, but these are not all present in all cases[1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * Fever
  * Headache
  * A stiff neck
  * Altered mental status, for example confusion, disorientation or unusual sleepiness.


Other symptoms include: [1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [4](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
  * Pale, blotchy or bluish skin
  * Rash
  * Nausea
  * Vomiting
  * Photophobia or discomfort around bright light
  * Muscle pain or joint pain
  * [Abdominal pain](https://ada.com/conditions/abdominal-pain/) or diarrhea
  * Irritability
  * Seizures
  * Cranial nerve problems, such as nonreactive pupils
  * Shock, the symptoms of which include low blood pressure, rapid heartbeat, difficulty breathing, and low urine output


To check whether someone’s pupils are reactive, shine a small light, for example from a penlight, directly into the eye. If the pupil shrinks and then enlarges again when the light is removed, the pupillary reaction is normal. If this does not happen, the pupils may be nonreactive.
If seizures occur or the affected person is showing signs of altered consciousness, seek emergency medical help immediately.
If the person affected has recently been taking antibiotics, some symptoms may be different or absent. People with suppressed or damaged immune systems may also not show clear signs of meningitis. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
If it is not certain that the ill person has meningitis, but it is suspected, seek medical care immediately. It is better to err on the side of caution.
### Identifying the rash associated with bacterial meningitis
A rash is one of the most distinctive symptoms of bacterial meningitis in children and adultsred or purple in color, and can occur anywhere on the body,[2](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
The rash develops as small spots, which can occur in groups. [5](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") It is another important feature of the rash associated with bacterial meningitis that it does not go away/fade when pressed. [2](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
Good to know:
## What causes bacterial meningitis?
Newborn children are the population group at the highest risk of meningitis, although this condition can affect people of all ages. Males may be slightly more at risk than females. People with other medical conditions, including a recent [ear infection](https://ada.com/conditions/middle-ear-infection/) or [throat infection](https://ada.com/conditions/acute-pharyngitis/), or who have had a recent skull fracture, are at increased risk of meningitis.
### How bacterial meningitis affects the brain and body
Meningitis occurs when bacteria invade the bloodstream, cross the blood-brain barrier, and infect the meninges, membranes that cover the brain and the spinal cord. The meninges are filled with a fluid called cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF. Usually, the blood and brain systems are separate. Healthy CSF is sterile, meaning it is free from bacteria or other microorganisms.
The bacteria that infect the meninges in bacterial meningitis can come from anywhere in the body, [1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1"), and once they are in the CSF, they multiply, releasing toxins. This causes inflammation of the meninges and the brain, which increases intracranial pressure (ICP), i.e., pressure inside the skull. This increase in pressure causes many of the distinctive symptoms of meningitis,
Because of the blood-brain barrier, the body’s immune system battles to fight the infection, which causes great stress on the body. White blood cells and other elements of the immune system enter the CSF. The flow of blood components into the CSF means that the amount of blood flowing in the body is reduced, which affects the amount of oxygen available to the muscles and organs. The body tries to maintain its oxygen supply to the vital organs by reducing blood flow to the extremities, resulting in cold hands and feet.
The spread of blood components into the CSF, along with the bacterial infection, can cause the brain to swell, a condition known as cerebral edema. Intracranial pressure increases, causing complications and, in some cases, death. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
Bacterial meningitis can result in complications that affect cognitive functioning if not treated in time, and it is often fatal if not treated.
### Conditions that increase the risk of developing bacterial meningitis
Some medical conditions can increase the vulnerability of certain people to bacterial meningitis. These include some chronic conditions, recent bacterial infections, and some surgical procedures of the skull and head.
Chronic conditions which increase the risk of catching bacterial meningitis include: [1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * [Diabetes mellitus](https://ada.com/conditions/diabetes/)
  * [Chronic kidney problems](https://ada.com/conditions/chronic-renal-failure/)
  * [Cystic fibrosis](https://ada.com/conditions/cystic-fibrosis/)
  * [Sickle cell disease](https://ada.com/conditions/sickle-cell-disease/)
  * [Thalassemia major](https://ada.com/conditions/thalassemia/)
  * Congenital malformations of the brain membranes, spinal cord or skull
  * Hypoparathyroidism, or an underactive parathyroid gland
  * Having an underactive spleen or no spleen
  * [HIV infection or Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS)](https://ada.com/conditions/hiv-aids/)
  * [Cirrhosis of the liver](https://ada.com/conditions/liver-cirrhosis/)


Other factors which increase a person’s risk of developing bacterial meningitis include:
  * Being very young or very old
  * Alcoholism
  * IV drug use
  * An infection elsewhere in the body, such as [otitis media](https://ada.com/conditions/acute-otitis-media/), mastoiditis, [bacterial sinusitis](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-sinusitis/), [bacterial endocarditis](https://ada.com/conditions/infective-endocarditis/), or [pneumonia](https://ada.com/conditions/pneumonia/)
  * Recent cranial surgery
  * Cranial shunts or stents
  * Head injuries that penetrate the scalp, meningeal membranes, and/or skull
  * Crowding, for example, in a military barracks or student dormitory
  * Exposure to someone with bacterial meningitis


Various bacteria can cause meningitis. The ones most often encountered include: [1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * Haemophilus influenzae
  * Staphylococcus aureus or Staphylococcus epidermidis
  * Pneumococcus, also known as Streptococcus pneumoniae
  * Meningococcus, also known as Neisseria meningitidis
  * Mycobacterium [tuberculosis](https://ada.com/conditions/tuberculosis/), although this is rare


Other bacteria which can cause meningitis include: [1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * Escherichia coli
  * Klebsiella
  * Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  * Salmonella
  * Listeria monocytogenes (see [FAQs](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#faqs))


### Meningococcal meningitis
Meningococcal meningitis is caused by a bacteria known as Neisseria meningitidis. Rates of meningococcal meningitis are dropping in the developed world, largely due to the availability of a vaccine against Meningococcus C. [4](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") Meningococcal infection can cause septicemia or meningitis, or both (see [FAQs](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#faqs)).
Many people carry meningococcal bacteria in their nose and throat, where they are quite harmless. These bacteria have to breach the immune system in order to cause an infection, and they tend to cause only isolated cases or small outbreaks. [2](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") These bacteria can be passed on by contact such as kissing, sneezing or coughing.
However, meningococcus is endemic to certain developing countries in Asia and Africa. It is a common cause of meningitis associated with overseas travel. Muslim pilgrims on the Hajj are particularly at risk. [3](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") Travellers to these regions should ask their physicians about the possibility of getting the meningococcus C vaccine; vaccinations against meningococcus A, W135 and Y may also be useful.
### Pneumococcal meningitis
Severe pneumococcal infections are more common in developing countries. [4](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") Like meningococcus, pneumococcus can cause meningitis and septicemia, but many people carry it harmlessly in their noses and throats, and infections can only happen if the bacteria breach the immune system. [2](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
Meningitis caused by pneumococcus can be more severe than that caused by meningococcus, and is associated with somewhat higher mortality. [3](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") However, vaccines against pneumococcal meningitis are available.
## Bacterial meningitis diagnosis
Diagnosis is based on the symptoms, the physical examination, and tests that confirm the presence of a severe infection in the body. A sample of cerebrospinal fluid, the fluid in the meninges around the brain and spinal cord, is taken and tested for the specific bacteria causing the infection. When bacterial meningitis is suspected, antibiotic therapy should be started right away.[1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
### Lumbar puncture
Also known as a spinal tap,
A lumbar puncture is done under local anesthetic, and a needle is inserted into a gap between two lumbar vertebrae in the lower back. A needle is used to draw off a small amount of fluid from around the spinal cord. The spinal cord itself is not touched.
Good to know:[FAQs](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#faqs)). These people will require a CT scan first. The attending physicians will determine who may need a CT scan.
### Blood and CSF tests
The CSF sample taken during the lumbar puncture will be analysed to confirm the presence of bacteria, determine what kind of bacteria are causing the infection, and determine how far along the infection is.
Blood tests may also be carried out to check organ function and dehydration. These results will guide the treatment.
Think you might be experiencing bacterial meningitis
## Treating bacterial meningitis
Bacterial meningitis is a serious condition and requires urgent medical care.
### Antibiotic treatment of bacterial meningitis
Most cases of bacterial meningitis are treated with intravenous antibiotics administered as soon as possible. Because the treatment often begins before the exact bacteria responsible are[1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [3](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
  * Cefotaxime
  * Vancomycin
  * Ampicillin
  * Ceftriaxone
  * Penicillin
  * Benzylpenicillin


Good to know
### Supportive treatment for bacterial meningitis
People with meningitis will be treated as inpatients in hospital, and most will need to be in intensive care for a short time.[2](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") coughing or straining (which can increase intracranial pressure), pain, fever and hypotension (low blood pressure). [1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") There is some evidence that administering corticosteroids reduces inflammation, which decreases the risk of some complications. [3](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
## Complications of bacterial meningitis
Because meningitis involves a severe infection of the brain and the spinal cord, and also affects the body as a whole, complications are common. Even with prompt treatment, almost three in ten survivors of meningitis have neurological complications of some kind, with one in seven experiencing serious long-term problems. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
### Short-term complications
The severity of the bacterial infection in meningitis can cause short-term complications such as: [1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * Sepsis
  * Coma
  * Seizures
  * Cerebral edema
  * [Pericardial effusion](https://ada.com/conditions/pericardial-effusion/)
  * Hemolytic [anemia](https://ada.com/conditions/anemia/)
  * [Septic arthritis](https://ada.com/conditions/septic-arthritis/)
  * Peripheral gangrene
  * Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome


#### Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome
Severe bacterial infections, such as bacterial meningitis, can cause a rare complication called Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome, a condition in which the adrenal glands fail due to bleeding. The syndrome causes bleeding throughout the body and, because of the damage to the adrenal glands, adrenal insufficiency. Symptoms include: [6](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [7](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
  * A rash, which begins as small, pink patches or pimple-like swellings, which expand into larger, purple patches
  * Malaise and weakness
  * Dizziness
  * Cough
  * Joint and muscle pain
  * Fever
  * Rigors
  * Nausea and vomiting
  * Headache
  * Low blood pressure
  * Fast heart rate
  * Sepsis


Good to know:
Most cases are caused by severe infection with meningococcal bacteria, Group B streptococcus, Streptococcus aeruginosa, Staphylococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome is a medical emergency and anyone who shows symptoms of the syndrome should receive medical care immediately.[6](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
### Long-term complications
In the long term, some people who have had meningitis, experience some degree of: [2](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [4](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
  * Hearing loss
  * Sight loss or blindness
  * Ataxia, loss of coordinated muscle movements
  * Seizures or epilepsy
  * Learning and motor difficulties
  * Cranial nerve dysfunction, which can affect the facial muscles, smell, sight and taste
  * Hydrocephalus, or fluid buildup in the brain
  * Organ damage, for example, kidney damage
  * In children, damage to the growth plates of the bones leads to impaired growth


Think you might be experiencing bacterial meningitis
## What are the bacterial meningitis precautions?
Some common causes of bacterial meningitis are preventable by vaccine. Keeping to the recommended vaccination schedule can help prevent some cases of meningitis. Good hygiene, such as washing hands, can also help to avoid some cases of bacterial meningitis.
### Vaccinations
In many countries, children are routinely vaccinated against Haemophilus influenzae, meningococcus and pneumococcus. It is possible to be vaccinated as an adult.
### Post-exposure prophylactic antibiotics
People who have been in contact with someone with bacterial meningitis, especially meningococcal meningitis and pneumococcal meningitis should be offered a short course of preventative antibiotics. [3](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") Rifampin or ceftriaxone in prophylactic doses is offered to: [1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * Housemates and family members living with the affected person
  * Coworkers
  * Caregivers
  * Classmates or people in the same school dormitory
  * People living in the same student accommodation or military barracks
  * Paramedics who were in contact with the affected person


## Find out more about your symptoms
## Bacterial meningitis FAQs
Q: How is bacterial meningitis related to septicemia?  
A:[8](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") especially for young children and babies. [9](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") Meningococcal meningitis and meningococcal septicemia are both types of meningococcal disease; meningococcal septicemia is also sometimes called meningococcemia. [10](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10") Meningitis and septicemia are both medical emergencies, and if you suspect that you or a loved one has meningitis or septicemia, you should seek medical care as soon as possible.
Q: What are the symptoms of septicaemia?  
A:[8](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") The symptoms of meningococcal septicemia include: [10](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10") [4](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
  * Fever
  * Fatigue
  * Cold hands and feet
  * Pale, mottled, or blue skin
  * Rapid heartbeat
  * Chills
  * Vomiting and nausea, sometimes with diarrhea
  * Abdominal pain, muscle pain, joint pain, and/or chest pain
  * Low urine output
  * Thirstiness
  * Rapid breathing, labored breathing, or grunting while breathing
  * Low blood pressure
  * A purple rash on the skin that does not fade when pressed


Not all affected people will have all of these symptoms. If the rash is present or if the affected person has lowered blood pressure, the infection is serious ,and an ambulance should be called.[All cases of septicemia](https://ada.com/conditions/sepsis/) will require urgent medical care, and it is essential that medical care is sought as soon as possible. The chances of a good outcome are improved if the disease is spotted early. Parents of small children or the caregivers of people who are at risk of septicemia should be on the lookout for: [4](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
  * Fever
  * Vomiting and nausea
  * Lethargy
  * Pain in the legs
  * Cold hands and/or feet
  * Pale, mottled, or bluish skin


These are the earliest symptoms; others may appear as the infection continues. It is possible to have meningococcal septicemia and meningococcal meningitis at the same time. For the symptoms of meningococcal septicemia, see above. If you are concerned that you or a loved one may have meningococcal meningitis or septicemia, start a free 
Q: What is the difference between viral and bacterial meningitis?  
A:[aseptic meningitis](https://ada.com/conditions/viral-meningitis/). Viral meningitis is a serious medical problem in itself, and anyone who might have it should seek medical help as soon as they can, but it is usually less serious than bacterial meningitis.
Most cases of viral meningitis in people with healthy immune systems clear up on their own within a week or so, and complications are not common. However, everyone who presents with the symptoms of meningitis should seek urgent medical care, as it is not possible to tell whether meningitis is caused by bacteria or viruses just by looking at the symptoms.
Viruses that can cause aseptic meningitis include the [flu](https://ada.com/conditions/influenza-infection/) virus, the [common cold](https://ada.com/conditions/common-cold/) virus, the [measles](https://ada.com/conditions/measles/) virus, [HIV](https://ada.com/conditions/acute-hiv-infection/), AND the [mumps](https://ada.com/conditions/mumps/) virus, as well as enteroviruses such as the [polio](https://ada.com/conditions/poliovirus-infection/) virus. [11](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
Q: What is the treatment for viral meningitis?  
A:However, everyone who presents with the symptoms of meningitis should seek urgent medical care, as it is not possible to tell whether meningitis is caused by bacteria or viruses just by looking at the symptoms.[12](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
Some kinds of viral meningitis can be prevented by vaccines which prevent the diseases that can lead to viral meningitis. Diseases associated with viral meningitis, which a person can be vaccinated against, include the chickenpox, measles, mumps, and influenza vaccines.
Q: Can meningitis be caused by fungi, parasites, or amoebas?  
A:
Fungal meningitis is rare in the developed world, but can be caused by Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, Blastomyces, or Coccidioides. Most of these fungal organisms are found in soil contaminated by bird or bat droppings. Candida, another fungus that can cause meningitis, is usually found in hospital settings. Fungal meningitis cannot be passed from person to person. [13](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:13 "See Footnote 13")
Parasitic meningitis can be caused by parasitic nematodes (worms) and roundworms. [14](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14") Most cases are found in people who have traveled to Southeast Asia and eaten contaminated meat or fish, seafood, eggs, snails, or fresh produce washed in contaminated water. However, a roundworm called Baylisascaris procyonis is found in raccoon droppings in North America. [15](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:15 "See Footnote 15") Parasitic meningitis is quite rare.
Amebic meningitis is very rare, but very serious.[16](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:16 "See Footnote 16")
Q: Does Haemophilus influenzae cause the flu?  
A:[17](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:17 "See Footnote 17") Influenza is a viral disease caused by a type of orthomyxovirus. Haemophilus influenzae was named by its discoverer during an influenza epidemic in the late 1800s; at that time, it was not known that viruses caused influenza, and the disease was thought to be caused by bacteria.
Q: Who is at risk from Listeria monocytogenes infection?  
A:
  * Pregnant women
  * Infants and young children
  * People over 60 years of age
  * Alcoholics
  * Immunosuppressed individuals
  * People with [diabetes](https://ada.com/conditions/diabetes/)
  * People with [chronic kidney](https://ada.com/conditions/chronic-renal-failure/) or liver disease.


Q: What is a brain herniation?  
A:Brain herniation is a serious medical condition, and treatment is essential.
Q: How is the risk of brain herniation minimized during the diagnosis of bacterial meningitis?  
A:[1](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [3](https://ada.com/conditions/bacterial-meningitis/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
  * A history of stroke or other central nervous system problems
  * Seizures within the previous seven days
  * Altered or reduced consciousness
  * A very severe [headache](https://ada.com/conditions/headache/)
  * A possible neurological deficit, such as nonreactive pupils or gaze palsy, a condition that affects the ability of the eyes to move in the same direction simultaneously.

# HDL Cholesterol
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on July 21, 2025 at 11:29 AM GMT+3
## On this page
  * [What is HDL cholesterol?](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#what-is-hdl-cholesterol)
  * [HDL vs. LDL](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#hdl-vs-ldl)
  * [Normal HDL](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#normal-hdl)
  * [Increase HDL](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#increase-hdl)
  * [Wrapping up](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#wrapping-up)
  * [FAqs](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#faqs)


* * *
Share this article:
You probably know that cholesterol levels are an important measure of your health[lowering cholesterol](https://ada.com/editorial/how-to-lower-cholesterol/) can keep your heart and blood vessels healthy. So it might surprise you to hear that there's a "good" kind of cholesterol.
High-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol is often nicknamed “good cholesterol”.
So what is HDL cholesterol, and why is it named "good?” And what do you need to do to increase your HDL cholesterol levels?
Let's find out.
Are you worried about your HDL cholesterol levelssymptom checker works before you try it for yourself.
## What is HDL cholesterol?
Your body needs a certain amount of cholesterol to function normally. To transport that cholesterol to where it's needed, your liver produces molecules called lipoproteins. [1](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") These particles are made up of fats and proteins that bind to cholesterol so your blood can transport it around your body. [1](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
Your liver produces 2 main types of lipoprotein: [2](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
  * High-density lipoproteins (HDLs), or "good cholesterol"
  * Low-density lipoproteins (LDLs), or "bad cholesterol"


HDL is the densest and smallest type of lipoprotein, and it contains the highest amount of protein. [3](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") But what makes HDL cholesterol "good"?
## Why is HDL cholesterol better than LDL cholesterol?
Let's start with a quick cholesterol recap.
When your cholesterol levels get too high, fatty buildups can start to form in the walls of your arteries. [4](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") Over time, these buildups turn to plaques, which can narrow your arteries and make it difficult for blood to flow through. [5](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
This can increase your chances of developing [cardiovascular disease](https://ada.com/cardiovascular/) and other conditions including: [6](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
  * Heart attack
  * [Stroke](https://ada.com/signs-of-stroke/)
  * Chronic kidney disease


Now, on to HDL cholesterol. This "good cholesterol" gets its name because: [7](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7") [8](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
  * It transports LDL cholesterol, the primary driver of fatty buildups, back to the liver, where it's removed from your body.
  * It can have an anti-inflammatory effect, protecting blood vessels from LDL cholesterol.
  * It can remove existing plaques from artery walls.
  * It has antioxidant effects, which protect chemical messengers and cells in the body.


Your HDL cholesterol level provides an important indicator for the health of your cardiovascular system. [9](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9")
## What is the normal HDL cholesterol range?
A healthy HDL cholesterol range is 40 mg per deciliter of blood and higher for men and more than or equal to 50 mg/dL for women.[10](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
If HDL cholesterol levels go below 50 mg per deciliter of blood for women and 40 mg per deciliter for men, you are 'at risk'.
You can determine your HDL cholesterol levels by getting a lipid profile test at your GP[11](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
  * Total cholesterol
  * LDL cholesterol
  * HDL cholesterol
  * [Triglycerides](https://ada.com/biomarkers/triglycerides/)


After taking a lipid profile test, your GP can use the information to carry out a 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk assessment. [10](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10") This will allow them to calculate the risk of you developing heart problems within the next 10 years.
Are you worried about your HDL cholesterol levelssymptom checker works before you try it for yourself.
## How to increase HDL cholesterol?
You can increase your HDL cholesterol levels[12](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
These can include: [12](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
  * Eating a balanced diet
  * Losing weight
  * Exercising regularly
  * Avoiding or quitting smoking
  * Reducing alcohol consumption


There are also medications your doctor can prescribe if your HDL cholesterol is low. [12](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
## Wrapping up
Not all cholesterol is bad. Having healthy, high HDL cholesterol levels is extremely important for your health.
So remember to stay active, eat healthy foods, and make sure you regularly check your blood cholesterol levels.
## Find out more about your symptoms
## FAqs
Q: When should I test my HDL cholesterol?  
A: You should check your HDL levels as part of your lipid profile with a cholesterol level test every 4 to 6 years.
Q: How can I naturally increase my HDL cholesterol levels?  
A: Lifestyle changes are the main way to naturally increase HDL cholesterol levels. If lifestyle changes aren't enough, your doctor may prescribe medications to help.
Q: What impact does my diet have on HDL cholesterol?  
A: Having a balanced diet is one of the main ways to maintain stable HDL levels. It also contributes to lowering LDL cholesterol, the "bad" kind.
Q: Can a high HDL cholesterol level make up for high LDL cholesterol?  
A: Unfortunately, we do not have the answer to this. More research is necessary to tell for sure. Either way, it's essential to maintain healthy, low LDL levels.

# Research and Publications 
Objective and peer-reviewed research can raise the industry bar for quality, safety, and performance. Here's some research that looks at the performance and efficacy of Ada's technology.
Scroll through or navigate to a topic of interest below. 
[ Safety and accuracy ](https://about.ada.com/studies/#safety-and-accuracy) [ Patient experience ](https://about.ada.com/studies/#patient-experience) [ Global health and universal coverage ](https://about.ada.com/studies/#global-health-and-universal-coverage) [ Rare diseases ](https://about.ada.com/studies/#rare-diseases) [ Public health and surveillance ](https://about.ada.com/studies/#public-health-and-surveillance) [ Commentary and industry ](https://about.ada.com/studies/#commentary-and-industry)
## Safety and accuracy
  * China’s 8 most popular symptom checkers showed a range of coverage, safety, and accuracy, factors relevant to user and physician choice.
  * Ada offered the highest coverage (99.5%) and advice safety (99.5%) compared with the average (69.6% and 90.3%, respectively).
  * Ada’s accuracy was significantly higher, and more than twice the average (61.5% vs 28.7%).


Chinese Journal of General Practitioners, 2023
  * Ada was significantly more accurate in the recognition of inflammatory rheumatic diseases (IRD) than physicians (70% vs physicians' 54%), which included experienced rheumatology physicians.
  * Ada was more accurate than physicians in suggesting the correct final diagnosis (54% of cases vs physicians' 32%).
  * Highlights the potential of using symptom checkers early in the patient journey and the advantages of considering complete patient information to establish a correct diagnosis.
  * Shows the potential of symptom checkers to make accurate triage and diagnostic decisions in rheumatology.


Rheumatology International, 2022
  * Ada outperformed all other symptom checkers in suggesting the correct diagnosis for skin rashes.
  * Ada's top condition suggestion matched the correct diagnosis in 73.3% of cases, vs an average of 30.8%.
  * The correct diagnosis was provided within Ada's top three condition suggestions in 93.3% of instances vs an average of 43.3%.


Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology, 2022
  * Real-world hospital ED study of 378 patients, comparing the safety of Ada’s urgency advice to that of the Manchester Triage System (MTS).
  * Ada demonstrated a high rate of safety (94.7%) over all medical specialties of the Emergency Department, with a focus on Internal Medicine, Orthopedics and Trauma, and Neurology.
  * From the 3 lowest MTS categories, 43.4% could have safely accessed lower urgency care such as seeing a GP or managing their symptoms at home.
  * Ada has the potential to relieve pressure on Emergency Departments by guiding patients to lower urgency care if used at home.


JMIR mHealth and uHealth, 2022
  * One of Ada's top 5 condition suggestions matched therapist's formal diagnoses in 69% of cases, and Ada's top suggestion matched in 51% of cases.
  * Symptom checkers have potential to complement the mental health diagnostic process, but further investigation is recommended.
  * The usability of Ada was rated as high in the System Usability Scale.


JMIR Mental Health, 2022
  * When used in combination with ER physicians assessments, Ada significantly increased diagnostic accuracy (87.3%) compared with an ER physician alone (80.9%).
  * Patients with early diagnosis and rapid treatment allocation exhibited significantly reduced complications and length of hospital stay.
  * AI tools have the potential to benefit the diagnostic efficacy of clinicians and improve quality of care.


Annals of Surgery, 2022
  * One of Ada’s top 5 condition suggestions matched the correct diagnosis in 70% of cases, close to physicians' top 3 average of 68.9%.
  * 90% of patients found Ada easy to use, and 83% considered Ada to be an efficient way to document their medical problems quickly.
  * Ada’s correct ‘diagnoses’ were nearly identical to one of the board-certified emergency physicians'.


JMIR Mhealth Uhealth, 2022
  * Ada’s DDSS prototype could support doctors’ decision-making by showing them new pathways and potential diagnoses.
  * Ada provided accurate decision support in the clinical inpatient setting for people presenting with dyspnea.


JMIR Formative Research, 2022
  * Using a dataset from 464,547 patients, Ada's CVD risk prediction tool achieved superior performance to several established general CVD risk prediction models.
  * Ada could be used to direct individuals to app-based behavior change recommendations for risk reduction and guidance.


PLOS ONE, 2021
  * Ada identified the correct condition in the top 3 suggestions in 83% of cases, compared to the next best of 77%, including Australia-specific scenarios.
  * 63% of Ada’s urgency advice matched the gold standard, compared to the next highest app’s score of 52%


Australian Journal of Primary Health, 2021
  * Ada had 73% accuracy compared to a 38% all-app average.
  * Ada's exhibited 97% disposition safety compared to an 83% all-app average.


PLOS ONE, 2021
  * The utility of symptom checkers relies on safety, coverage, and accuracy.
  * Ada’s advice was safe in 97% of cases, on par with GPs and with 99% condition coverage for the clinical scenarios.
  * Ada showed 70% accuracy for top 3 suggestion fit vs competitor average of 38%.


BMJ Open, 2020
  * 46.4% of 26,646 Ada assessments were completed outside primary care clinic hours.
  * Ada’s recommendations were comparable to triage nurses’.


Journal of Medical Internet Research, 2020
  * Ada could help identify mental health disorders in adults.


JMIR Formative Research, 2019
  * Ada ranked highly on precision out of the 24 tested in the ear, nose, and throat (ENT) discipline.


HNO, 2019
  * Ada was the most accurate of the 4 apps tested.
  * Ada was found to be fast and easy to use.


Pulse Today, 2019
  * Ada was "by far the best" app out of the 4 tested, asking clear questions and providing the best condition suggestions.


Wired UK, 2017
## Patient experience
  * 93% of Ada’s assessments provided useful information prior to consultation with 83% of Ada’s top condition suggestions matching the physician’s primary diagnosis.
  * In 52% of appointments, Ada saved more than 1 minute of primary care consultation time.
  * Most physicians agreed that Ada is safe and effective, guiding patients to the correct care, providing useful information, and saving time in consultations.


Healthcare Information and Management Systems Society (HIMSS), 2023
  * Ada supported conversation and improved rapport for 90% of patients, 73% of physicians, and 100% of nurses.
  * Patients reported high usability and understood the tool’s questions.


JMIR Formative Research, 2022
  * Ada could decrease the average triage nurse waiting times by 54%.


JMIR Formative Research, 2021
  * 97.8% of patients rated Ada very or quite easy to use.
  * 12.8% or patients would have delayed their appointment or used lower-intensity care.


JMIR Human Factors, 2020
## Global health and universal coverage
  * The readability of Ada's consumer-facing medical text was reduced from grade 11, to grade 7 without compromising on medical quality.
  * AI companies can reduce the burden on vulnerable healthcare systems, but should be designed and adapted to the needs of the local population.
  * Efforts should be made to reduce bias in AI by using white-box systems.


Pending publication, The Lancet, 2022
  * Protocol for a clinical study set in a Tanzanian district hospital outpatient clinic to investigate the usefulness of a prototype diagnosis decision support system (DDSS) in the hands of a mid-level healthcare worker.
  * The diagnostic accuracy and qualitative data on the usability, usefulness, and acceptance of the prototype DDSS will provide insights on the appropriateness of the prototype DDSS interface.


JMIR Research Protocols, 2022
  * Protocol for first-of-type clinical study set in a Tanzanian district hospital outpatient clinic to investigate the usefulness of symptom assessment applications in LMICs.
  * Evaluation of Ada's compared to gold-standard differential diagnoses and triage advice for participants with various conditions and age groups, including children.


BMJ Open, 2022
  * Ada’s knowledge base was adapted to account for differences in incidence and disease presentation in South Africa, including optimizing 25 maternal and 25 pediatric conditions.
  * Ada’s readability was lowered from grade 11 level to below grade 8 level (7.4) while still maintaining medical accuracy to improve accessibility and uptake.
  * White-box AI like Ada, based on interpretable models that can be explained and easily understood by a human, can control and reduce data bias.


2022
  * AI solutions can only improve health outcomes in LMICs if they are designed and adapted with the needs of the local population in mind.
  * To account for regional differences in incidence and disease presentation, 51 maternal and pediatric health conditions were optimized in Ada for South Africa.
  * Ada’s content readability score has been reduced from grade 11 to below grade 8 (7.4±0.8) while still maintaining medical accuracy.
  * White-box AI-approach like Ada’s makes it possible to capture the differences in underrepresented populations and low-income countriea.


European Journal of Public Health, 2021
## Rare diseases
  * The rare Cold Agglutinin Disease model was created and incorporated into Ada’s medical knowledge and reasoning engine.
  * In the first 30 days, CAD was suggested among the top 3 conditions in 48 assessments.
  * Integrating CAD in a symptom assessment can help speed up disease detection, potentially providing quicker access to healthcare systems.


Gesellschaft für Thrombose- und Hämostaseforschung (GTH), 2023
  * A new approach of conducting expert interviews to create 11 clinical vignettes on lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs) which were then used to update Ada’s condition models. 
  * 15 LSD patients and 9 LSD experts will rate both new and old disease models in Ada to compare efficacy. 
  * This novel approach can potentially shorten the ‘time to diagnosis’ for rare diseases.


European Conference on Rare Disease (ECRD), 2022
  * Ada could help detect genetic auto-inflammatory disorders, including the important group of Periodic Fever Syndromes.


The Internist (Der Internist), 2021
  * Retrospective analysis of the diagnostic costs of rare inflammatory systemic diseases and the impact of a prototype Ada as a diagnostic decision support system (DDSS).
  * If this Ada DDSS prototype were released, it has the potential to lead to earlier diagnosis and could save between 50% and 70% of diagnostic costs.


BMC Health Services Research, 2021
  * Rare diseases were suggested as the most likely condition in 4% of Ada symptom assessments and among the top five suggestions in 17% of assessments.
  * This is in line with epidemiological studies suggesting that ~2–4% of the population is living with a rare disease.
  * Ada shows the potential to shorten the diagnostic odyssey of people living with rare diseases.


RE(ACT) Congress - International Rare Diseases Research Consortium, Berlin, 2020
  * 89.25% of Ada’s top suggestions matched the confirmed diagnosis.
  * 33.3% of participants could have received their rare disease diagnosis in the first documented clinical visit with Ada.


Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 2019
## Public health and surveillance
  * Ada has the potential to help surface users who should seek care, including possible early cases and users who do not participate in screening programs.
  * Correlations between Ada’s cancer frequency in Germany and the German cancer registry incidence data were statistically significant.
  * Between 23% and 94% of Ada assessments where cancer was suggested reported no advanced signs, and between 19% and 41% reported first signs and no advanced signs.


AI in Cancer Diagnostics: from research to clinical practice, European Association for Cancer Research (EACR), 2021
  * Ada uncovered similar ILI trends to an official German surveillance system and could help identify health trends in countries without population-based monitoring systems.


JMIR Public Health Surveillance, 2021
  * Digital symptom-based screening tools can substantially reduce the transmission of COVID-19.
  * Applications like Ada (combined with testing and self-isolation) could prevent an additional 8% of the population being infected.


Pending publication, JMIR, 2021
  * A review of data from 950,000 users found that Ada could help uncover the impact of public health policies like COVID-19 lockdown measures.


JMIR mHealth and uHealth, 2020
## Commentary and industry
BMC Arthritis Research & Therapy, 2022
Medical Journal of Australia (MJA), 2021
  * Proposals by the EU and FDA have set the regulatory groundwork for algorithm change protocols. The FDA proposals are detailed and actionable but are yet to be finalized. The EU has not yet detailed its plan. The authors recommended the EU set out an approach that is coordinated, actionable, and consultative.
  * The public, manufacturers, and medical community should be engaged to inform requirements of algorithm change, with a focus on post market surveillance, RWP measurement, clinical evaluation, and labeling.


JMIR Formative Research, 2021
Clinical Psychological Science, 2021
Journal of Medical Internet Research, 2021
  * Ada could help detect genetic autoinflammatory disorders, including familial Mediterranean fever.


Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases, 2020
  * Ada Health successfully demonstrates the feasibility of a pathophysiology-based DDSS with Medical Deep Reasoning (MDR).
  * MDR extends current DDSS capabilities by utilizing pathophysiology to describe the dynamic components of disease pathogenesis to create an individualized, high-resolution model for personal healthcare. 
  * Facilitating the integration of this kind of health-related data will significantly advance personalized medicine.


MedInfo, World Congress of Medical and Health Informatics, 2019

# Our work in rare diseases
The average person living with a rare disease endures a 5-year diagnostic odyssey. That often means unnecessary care visits, delayed treatments, and poor outcomes. 
Many people living with a rare disease will never get an accurate diagnosis in their lifetime.
We’re working to shorten the time to diagnosis and improve outcomes for people living with rare diseases.
## The rare disease diagnostic challenge
There are over 7,000 known rare diseases. Most have a genetic basis and many share symptoms with more common disorders. This makes it almost impossible for any human to detect all rare diseases without help. 
Specialist referral is often delayed because GPs don’t suspect a rare disease. In many parts of the world, lack of access means people may never receive the rare disease diagnosis they desperately need for adequate care.
Rare but widespread:
## Helping rare starts with finding rare
At Ada, we envision a world where every person with a rare disease has timely access to the healthcare they need. 
Our AI and commitment to modeling rare diseases can turn everyday devices in homes and clinics across the world into powerful tools for improving disease recognition, time to diagnosis, and access to care.
“By using AI to raise the suspicion of a rare disease early, we could speed up referral to specialist clinics for diagnosis. That could mean simplified rare disease journeys and a reduced burden on people living with a rare disease, doctors, and health systems.”
####  Vanessa Lemarié 
Chief Client Officer
## Together, we can:
Empower patients and raise awareness.
  * Educate people with accurate information about possible diseases.
  * Provide immediate access to holistic guidance, resources, and care.
  * Connect and educate stakeholders to build advocacy.


Reduce the time and burden of detection.
  * Increase diagnostic accuracy and referral efficiency.
  * Accelerate identification and decrease time to diagnosis.
  * Avoid costs from unnecessary tests and treatment.


Facilitate collaboration and support clinical research.
  * Build a consolidated view of health by collating symptoms, observations, and risk factors.
  * Allow specialists to compare evidence with Ada’s suggestions using our intelligent assessment technology.
  * Share anonymous cases for peer collaboration and modeling.


We’ve modeled hundreds of rare diseases, from Amyloid neuropathy to Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
We work in rare diseases with

# Síntomas del COVID-19
Escrito por nuestro [Equipo de Profesionales Médicos](https://ada.com/es/team/medical/)
Actualizado el 21 de enero de 2025, 10:30 EET
## En esta página
  * [Información general](https://ada.com/es/covid/sintomas-covid-19/#informacion-general)
  * [Síntomas](https://ada.com/es/covid/sintomas-covid-19/#sintomas)
  * [Nuevos síntomas](https://ada.com/es/covid/sintomas-covid-19/#nuevos-sintomas)
  * [Síntomas graves](https://ada.com/es/covid/sintomas-covid-19/#sintomas-graves)
  * [Síntomas COVID-19 prolongado](https://ada.com/es/covid/sintomas-covid-19/#sintomas-covid-19-prolongado)
  * [Síntomas en personas vacunadas](https://ada.com/es/covid/sintomas-covid-19/#sintomas-en-personas-vacunadas)
  * [En resumen](https://ada.com/es/covid/sintomas-covid-19/#en-resumen)

Comparte este artículo:
## Información general
  * Hay una ámplia variedad de síntomas del COVID que pueden ser leves o graves.
  * Las nuevas variantes del COVID-19 causan la aparición de nuevos síntomas.
  * En algunos casos, los nuevos síntomas del COVID pueden aparecer o continuar 3 meses después de la infección inicial y pueden durar al menos 2 meses más. Esto se conoce como COVID de larga duración.
  * Las personas con ciertas enfermedades subyacentes o preexistentes pueden correr el riesgo de presentar graves síntomas del COVID.


Aprende más acerca de tus síntomas
Cuando se trata de los síntomas del COVID-19
Mientras que algunas personas presentan pocos síntomas, otras pueden tener muchos a la vez. Lo que es aún más extraño, es que algunas personas que dieron positivo en las pruebas del COVID no han presentado ningún síntoma, siendo estas asintomáticas.
Así como lavariedad de síntomas del COVID-19 es muy amplia, también lo es la gravedad. Puede ser que sólo tengas un caso leve, o que tus síntomas sean intensos e incluso potencialmente mortales, lo que se conoce como COVID-19 graveduración de los síntomasCOVID de larga duración
Independientemente de lo leves o graves que sean tus síntomas del COVID, es importante recordar que si das positivo en la prueba del COVID, puedes transmitirle el virus a otras personas.
## ¿Cuáles son los síntomas del COVID-19?
Los primeros síntomas del COVID se pueden parecer a los de otras infecciones respiratorias agudas. Los Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades (CDC) de EE.UU. reconocen que éstos son los síntomas más comunes relacionados con COVID-19[1](https://ada.com/es/covid/sintomas-covid-19/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * Fiebre o escalofríos:
  * Tos[Una tos seca es común en individuos con COVID-19](https://ada.com/es/covid/tos-covid-19/). Puede causar irritación y dificultad para respirar.
  * Dificultad para respirar o falta de aliento
  * Fatiga
  * Dolores musculares o corporales
  * Dolor de cabeza:[Los dolores de cabeza](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-cabeza-covid/) pueden ir de moderados a intensos. Pueden ir acompañados de otros síntomas como fatiga, fiebre o malestar general.
  * [Pérdida del gusto o del olfato](https://ada.com/es/covid/perdida-olfato-y-gusto-covid-19/): Este es uno de los síntomas más comunes del COVID-19 y puede durar varias semanas después de la infección inicial.
  * Dolor de garganta:[El dolor de garganta](https://ada.com/es/covid/dolor-de-garganta-covid-19/) puede indicar que tienes COVID-19. Puede variar de leve a grave y causar molestias al tragar.
  * Congestión o secreción nasal:
  * Náuseas o vómitos:
  * Diarrea


¿Te preocupa que tú o alguien cercano a ti puedan tener COVID-19? Comienza tu evaluación de síntomas en la app.
## ¿Cuáles son los nuevos síntomas del COVID-19?
Los síntomas de las nuevas variantes de coronavirus pueden variar un poco en comparación con las anteriores, produciendo algunos síntomas menos comunes. De hecho, lo que sabemos sobre los síntomas [del COVID-19](https://ada.com/es/covid/) ha ido evolucionando a medida que avanzaba la pandemia, ya que las nuevas variantes trajeron consigo nuevos síntomas.
Algunos de los síntomas del COVID-19 menos comunes o nuevos
  * Pérdida de apetito: Puede variar de leve a grave.
  * Erupciones cutáneas: Aparecen como sarpullidos o manchas descoloridas en la piel y pueden ir acompañadas de picazón o sensación de quemadura.
  * Confusión, desorientación o dificultad para concentrarse: Pueden producirse debido a la fiebre, otros síntomas o, potencialmente, por el propio virus.
  * Irregularidades menstruales: Las mujeres pueden presentar ausencia de la menstruación o cambios en el flujo y la duración del período. Esto puede ser debido a una respuesta inflamatoria subyacente causada por el virus.
  * Irritación o enrojecimiento de los ojos: Esto puede empeorar con el tiempo, por lo que es importante buscar atención médica si este síntoma persiste durante más de unos días.
  * Problemas para respirar: Puede incluir dificultad para respirar, falta de aliento o respiración entrecortada.
  * Decoloración de la lengua: Puede ir acompañada de manchas blancas en la lengua, lo que puede indicar una respuesta inflamatoria subyacente.
  * Sudores nocturnos: Pueden producirse como una señal de que tu organismo está combatiendo la infección. También puedes presentar otros síntomas como escalofríos, fiebre y dolores corporales.
  * Fatiga extrema: También puedes presentar otros síntomas al mismo tiempo, como mareos, confusión y dificultad para concentrarte.
  * Dolor de estómago o retorcijones: Esto puede ser un signo del virus y puede empeorar con el tiempo. Es importante buscar atención médica si el dolor persiste durante más de unos días.
  * Rigidez articular o muscular: Esto también puede empeorar con el tiempo. También puedes sentir dolor, sensibilidad o hinchazón en la zona afectada.
  * Mareos: Pueden ir de leves a intensos, e ir acompañados de otros síntomas como fatiga, confusión o dificultad para concentrarse.


Por lo general, los síntomas del COVID aparecen entre 2 y 14 días después de la exposición al virus. El transcurso de la afección es de leve a moderado en la mayoría de las personas y, en la mayoría de los casos, los síntomas mejoran al cabo de 1 o 2 semanas.
## ¿Cuáles son los síntomas graves del COVID-19?
En casos poco frecuentes, es posible presentar síntomas graves debido al COVID-19. El riesgo de sufrir COVID-19 grave puede aumentar en los pacientes de edad avanzada y en personas que tienen afecciones subyacentes o preexistentes. Algunas afecciones relacionadas con un mayor riesgo incluyen afecciones cardíacas o pulmonares, afecciones del sistema inmunitario, obesidad o diabetes. [2](https://ada.com/es/covid/sintomas-covid-19/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
Cualquier persona que presente estos síntomas del COVID-19 grave
  * Dificultad para respirar
  * Dolor persistente o presión en el pecho
  * Confusión
  * Incapacidad para mantenerse despierto
  * Piel pálida, gris o azulada


## ¿Cuáles son los síntomas del COVID-19 prolongado?
En algunos casos, tus síntomas del COVID-19 pueden prolongarse más allá del periodo de la infección. Esto se conoce como síntomas post COVID-19 o síntomas del COVID-19 de larga duración
  * COVID-19 prolongado
  * COVID-19 crónico
  * COVID-19 persistente
  * COVID-19 de largo recorrido
  * COVID-19 a largo plazo


Según el Centro para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades (CDC), alrededor del 7,5% de los adultos estadounidenses infectados por el virus presentan síntomas del COVID-19 de larga duración, es decir, síntomas que duran 3 meses o más. Los síntomas del COVID-19 a largo plazo son más comunes en personas que han sufrido una enfermedad grave por COVID-19, pero cualquier persona infectada por el virus puede desarrollar COVID-19 de larga duración. [3](https://ada.com/es/covid/sintomas-covid-19/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
Los síntomas del COVID de larga duración más comunes
  * Cansancio extremo
  * Dificultad para respirar o falta de aliento
  * Dolor en el pecho
  * Problemas de memoria y concentración
  * Dificultad para dormir
  * Palpitaciones
  * Mareos o vértigo
  * Depresión y ansiedad
  * Sensación de malestar
  * Cambios en el olfato o el gusto
  * Erupciones cutáneas (tanto en adultos como en niños)
  * Tos
  * Dolor de cabeza
  * Dolores o ruidos en el oído
  * Diarrea o dolor de estómago
  * Cambios en el ciclo menstrual


Si crees que puedes estar sufriendo COVID prolongado, realiza una consulta médica para obtener más información sobre las posibles opciones de tratamiento.
¿Te preocupa que tú o alguien cercano a ti puedan tener COVID-19? Comienza tu evaluación de síntomas en la app.
## Síntomas del COVID-19 en personas vacunadas
Los síntomas del COVID-19 en personas vacunadas pueden ser los mismos que en personas que no se vacunaron. La gran diferencia es que los síntomas suelen ser mucho menos graves
## En resumen
A pesar de que los síntomas del COVID pueden variar mucho, la comunidad médica sigue aprendiendo cada vez más con cada nueva variante. Los síntomas que eran comunes en la primera oleada del COVID-19 pueden ser menos frecuentes en [las nuevas variantes](https://ada.com/es/covid/nueva-variante-covid-19/).
En cualquier caso, es importante conocer los síntomas del COVID-19 para poder someterse a pruebas si aparece algún signo o síntoma del virus e iniciar el tratamiento correcto en casa o con la ayuda de profesionales de la salud.
## Aprende más acerca de tus síntomas
## Preguntas más frecuentes
P: ¿Cuáles son los síntomas de la variante Ómicron del COVID-19? [Los síntomas de la variante Ómicron](https://ada.com/es/covid/omicron-sintomas/) del COVID-19 suelen parecerse a los de otras variantes, y pueden incluir dolor de garganta, fiebre, tos, dolores de cabeza, dolores musculares y fatiga.

# Hypothyroidism
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on September 16, 2024 at 10:00 AM GMT+3

## What is hypothyroidism?
Hypothyroidism refers to a condition in which the thyroid gland produces less hormone than normal.[congenital hypothyroidism](https://ada.com/conditions/congenital-hypothyroidism/).
Symptoms depend on the age of the person, but include tiredness, dry hair and skin, slowed thinking and weight gain. The treatment of this condition is replacement of the [thyroid hormone with medication](https://ada.com/thyroid/).

Diagnosis is based on the symptoms
## Treatment
Treatment consists of replacing thyroid hormone with medication
## Prevention
Avoiding radiation to the thyroid, and taking plenty of iodine in the diet can help to prevent some cases of hypothyroidism. In many countries, pregnant women and newborns are screened (tested without symptoms) for hypothyroidism. This allows early treatment and helps to prevent the consequences of undiagnosed hypothyroidism before birth and in childhood.

## Other names for hypothyroidism
