Comparte este artículo:
## Resumen
La infección por sífilis es una enfermedad de transmisión sexual (ETS) causada por una infección bacteriana. El término médico para la sífilis que se diagnostica en sus primeras etapas es sífilis primaria. Los adultos jóvenes suelen ser los más afectados. Los síntomas tempranos son pequeñas llagas indoloras en los genitales y el agrandamiento de los ganglios linfáticos. Esta infección puede atacar muchas partes distintas del cuerpo, por lo que los síntomas tardíos pueden variar de persona en persona. Mantener relaciones sexuales con protección ayuda a reducir el riesgo de contraer sífilis. Se emplean antibióticos para tratar la infección. Cuando se hace un tratamiento temprano y efectivo, la mayoría de las personas se recupera bien.
## Riesgos
La infección por sífilis es una enfermedad de transmisión sexual causada por una bacteria llamada Treponema pallidum. Si la infección no se diagnostica y se trata, las infecciones por sífilis tienden a causar etapas (oleadas) de síntomas que se conocen como etapas primaria, secundaria y terciaria (o tardía). La sífilis puede tardar años en avanzar de la primera etapa a la tardía. Es más común que se diagnostique en adultos jóvenes entre los 15 y 24 años.
## Síntomas
Los síntomas tempranos de sífilis son una llaga indolora en la zona genital, en la boca o en las nalgas y el agrandamiento de los ganglios linfáticos de la ingle. Estos síntomas suelen desaparecer en cuestión de semanas y a veces no se notan. A medida que la la sífilis avanza, la persona afectada puede presentar sarpullido, fiebre, dolor articular, pérdida de cabello, bultos pequeños en la zona genital y dolores musculares. La sífilis avanza a sus etapas tardías lentamente a través de los años y afecta el corazón, el cerebro y otras partes del cuerpo. Esto causa una variedad de síntomas, que incluyen dificultad para respirar, confusión, problemas de memoria, pérdida de la coordinación y daño nervioso, entre muchos otros.
## Diagnóstico
El diagnóstico suele hacerse sobre la base de los síntomas, un examen físico y un análisis de sangre para detectar anticuerpos (proteínas que combaten las infecciones) de sífilis. Muchas personas reciben el diagnóstico después de una prueba de detección (realizando el test a personas que están en riesgo pero no presentan síntomas), porque es posible que la sífilis no cause síntomas o que cause síntomas muy poco comunes. Si existe una úlcera, se puede tomar una muestra para analizarla con el fin de detectar signos de la bacteria.
## Tratamiento
La sífilis se trata con antibióticos. Generalmente se hace análisis de seguimiento para verificar si la infección quedó totalmente tratada.
## Prevención
Mantener prácticas sexuales seguras, como utilizar condón (preservativo), puede evitar nuevas infecciones con sífilis. Las mujeres embarazadas usualmente son examinadas para detectar sífilis (cuando no hay síntomas) con el fin de evitar que la bacteria pase al bebé.
## Pronóstico
Con diagnóstico y tratamiento tempranos la mayoría de las personas se recuperan bien y no quedan con problemas a largo plazo. Si la sífilis no se trata, puede diseminarse lentamente a otras partes del cuerpo y dañar los vasos sanguíneos, el cerebro y los nervios.

# Dermatite atópica
Escrito pelo nosso [Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/pt/team/medical/)
Atualizado em 15 de fevereiro de 2022 às 10:00 GMT+2
## Nesta página
  * [Visão geral](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/atopic-dermatitis/#visao-geral)
  * [Riscos](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/atopic-dermatitis/#riscos)
  * [Sintomas](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/atopic-dermatitis/#sintomas)

  * [Tratamento](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/atopic-dermatitis/#tratamento)
  * [Prevenção](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/atopic-dermatitis/#prevencao)
  * [Prognóstico](https://ada.com/pt/conditions/atopic-dermatitis/#prognostico)


* * *
Compartilhe esse artigo:
## Visão geral
A dermatite atópica, muitas vezes chamado de eczema atópico, é uma condição de pele muito comum, especialmente em crianças. As pessoas com esta condição sofrem dermatite (inflamação da pele) devido a alergias ou por ter a pele sensível a certas substâncias. Em geral afeta crianças menores de cinco anos, e pode persistir até mais tarde. Os sintomas típicos são uma erupção pruriginosa (com coceira) e pele escamosa e seca. Esses sintomas tendem a piorar em resposta a certos gatilhos. O tratamento consiste em manter a pele úmida e usar cremes ou medicamentos para abrandar a pele e tratar a inflamação. Muitas crianças com dermatite atópica descobrem que sua condição melhora com o tempo, e podem não apresentar nenhum sintoma ao chegar à adolescência. Algumas pessoas têm eczema atópico que continua até a idade adulta.
Você se preocupa que você ou um familiar seu possam ter essa condição? Comece sua [o aplicativo](https://ada.com/pt/app/) primeiro.
## Riscos
A dermatite atópica é uma condição comum. É mais comum em crianças menores de cinco anos, e é raro que o primeiro episódio de eczema atópico surja na idade adulta. Pessoas com alergias (incluindo febre do feno e asma alérgica) têm mais chances de ter eczema atópico. Os fatores que desencadeiam o eczema atópico podem ser secura, calor e suor, substâncias irritantes (como certas roupas ou produtos químicos), estresse emocional ou físico, infecções de pele e alérgenos, e com frequência, alimentos.
## Sintomas
Os sintomas típicos do eczema são uma erupção cutânea vermelha com coceira e pele seca e escamosa. A erupção pode exsudar e a pele pode ficar vermelha de tanto coçar. A erupção muitas vezes afeta a face, couro cabeludo, cotovelos e joelhos. As pessoas que sofrem de eczema por longo tempo podem desenvolver pele espessa ou cicatrizes de tanto coçar ou esfregar. Se a erupção infeccionar, pode haver um exsudado amarelo espesso, bem como vermelhidão e crostas nas áreas do eczema.
## Diagnóstico
O diagnóstico geralmente é baseado nos sintomas e na aparência física da erupção cutânea. Manter um diário dos sintomas e dos testes para alérgenos específicos pode ser útil para identificar os fatores desencadeadores do eczema.
## Tratamento
Manter a pele úmida ajuda a aliviar os sintomas do eczema atópico. Algumas pessoas usam panos úmidos ou bandagens nas áreas de pele seca e irritada. Usar sabonetes ou produtos para banho que contenham hidratantes ou óleos pode ser útil para acalmar a pele e proteger contra substâncias irritantes. Cremes esteróides são muito utilizados para tratar as erupções do eczema. Comprimidos anti-histamínicos também podem ser úteis para reduzir a coceira.
## Prevenção
Identificar e evitar gatilhos que pioram os sintomas pode ajudar na prevenção de episódios de dermatite atópica.
## Prognóstico
A maioria das pessoas aprende a administrar suas reações e evitar os gatilhos da sua dermatite atópica; isso ajuda a manter os sintomas em um nível aceitável. As crianças com dermatite atópica vão constatar que a sua condição melhora com o crescimento e pode desaparecer ao chegar a adolescência. No entanto, podem ter sempre uma tendência para a pele sensível ou seca. Algumas pessoas continuam a ter eczemas na idade adulta.
## Saiba mais sobre seus sintomas

# Cushing-Syndrom
Verfasst von [Adas medizinischem Fachpersonal](https://ada.com/de/team/medical/)
Aktualisiert am 15. Februar 2022 um 10:01 OEZ
## Auf dieser Seite
  * [Was ist Cushing-Syndrom?](https://ada.com/de/conditions/cushings-syndrome/#was-ist-cushing-syndrom)
  * [Risiken](https://ada.com/de/conditions/cushings-syndrome/#risiken)
  * [Symptome](https://ada.com/de/conditions/cushings-syndrome/#symptome)
  * [Diagnose](https://ada.com/de/conditions/cushings-syndrome/#diagnose)
  * [Behandlung](https://ada.com/de/conditions/cushings-syndrome/#behandlung)
  * [Prognose](https://ada.com/de/conditions/cushings-syndrome/#prognose)
  * [Vorsorge](https://ada.com/de/conditions/cushings-syndrome/#vorsorge)

Artikel teilen:
## Was ist Cushing-Syndrom?
Das Cushing-Syndrom ist eine Erkrankung, die durch einen Überschuss am Steroidhormon Cortisol verursacht wird. Mögliche Ursachen sind die Einnahme einer zu großen Menge von Medikamenten, die Cortisol (Steroide) enthalten, oder die Überproduktion von Cortisol durch den Körper.
Menschen mit dem Cushing-Syndrom nehmen am Bauch und im Gesicht zu und entwickeln eine dünne, gedehnte Haut. Diese Erkrankung betrifft meist Erwachsene im Alter zwischen 20 und 50 Jahren. Die Behandlung des Cushing-Syndroms hängt seiner Ursache ab. Wurde die zugrunde liegende Ursache ermittelt und beseitigt, erholen sich die meisten Betroffenen gut. Ein unbehandeltes Cushing-Syndrom kann Osteoporose, Diabetes, Bluthochdruck und Schlaganfälle verursachen.
## Risiken
Die Entwicklung des Cushing-Syndroms wird durch zu viel Cortisol im Körper
## Symptome des Cushing-Syndroms
Die typischen Symptome
  * ein rotes, volles Gesicht (Mondgesicht),
  * eine Gewichtszunahme am Bauch,
  * ein Buckel zwischen den Schultern,
  * Veränderungen der Haut (dünne Haut, Dehnungsstreifen, schnelle Blutergussbildung, verstärktes Haarwachstum) und
  * Muskelschwäche.


Frauen können behaarter werden. Kinder wachsen möglicherweise nicht so schnell wie Gleichaltrige. Cortisol kann die Sexualfunktion beeinträchtigen. Manche Männer leiden dabei unter Erektionsstörungen und einem verringerten sexuellen Verlangen.
Wenn Du Dir unsicher bist, ob diese Beschwerden auf Dich zutreffen, starte eine 
## Diagnose
Eine Diagnose wird durch die Auswertung der medizinischen Vorgeschichte
Eine häufige Ursache ist die Einnahme kortisonhaltiger Medikamente.
## Behandlung
Die Behandlung hängt von der Ursache des hohen Cortisolspiegels ab. Wird dieser durch die Einnahme von Cortisol verursacht, sollte die Dosierung der Medikamente langsam verringert werden.
Kann die Ursache des hohen Cortisolspiegels nicht sicher beseitigt werden, kann das Cortisol durch andere Medikamente blockiert werden.
## Prognose
Die Prognose hängt von den zugrunde liegenden Ursachen ab. Durch die Beendigung der Einnahme von cortisolhaltigen Medikamenten oder die Entfernung des cortisolproduzierenden Wuchses ist eine vollständige Genesung möglich. Wird das Cushing-Syndrom nicht behandelt, kann es zu Komplikationen wie:
  * [Diabetes](https://ada.com/de/conditions/diabetes-mellitus-type-2/),
  * [Osteoporose](https://ada.com/de/conditions/osteoporosis/),
  * [Bluthochdruck](https://ada.com/de/conditions/essential-hypertension/),
  * [Herzinfarkten](https://ada.com/de/conditions/myocardial-infarction/) oder
  * Schlaganfällen führen.


## Vorsorge
Wenn die langfristige Einnahme von cortisolhaltigen Medikamenten vermieden wird, kann einigen Fällen des Cushing-Syndroms vorgebeugt werden.

# Depressive Episode
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on April 7, 2025 at 2:00 PM GMT+2
## On this page
  * [What is a depressive episode?](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#what-is-a-depressive-episode)
  * [Symptoms](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#symptoms)
  * [Causes](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#causes)
  * [Diagnosis](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#diagnosis)
    * [Minor depressive episode](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#minor-depressive-episode)
  * [Treatment](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#treatment)
    * [Psychotherapy](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#psychotherapy)
    * [Medication](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#medication)
    * [Other remedies](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#other-remedies)
  * [Prevention](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#prevention)
  * [Associated terms used for depressive episodes](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#associated-terms-used-for-depressive-episodes)
  * [FAQs](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#faqs)

Share this article:
## What is a depressive episode?
The definition of a depressive episode is a period of depression that persists for at least two weeks[1](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") During a depressive episode, a person will typically experience low or depressed mood and/or loss of interest in most activities, as well as a number of other symptoms of depression, such as tiredness, changes in appetite, feelings of worthlessness, and recurrent thoughts of death. The length of a depressive episode varies, but the average duration is thought to be six to eight months. [2](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
Think you might be experiencing a depressive episode
Depression is a common illness, and many people will experience one or more episodes of depression in their lifetime[3](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [4](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") People who have a history of depression, other mental health conditions such as [bipolar disorder](https://ada.com/conditions/bipolar-affective-disorder/) or [anxiety](https://ada.com/conditions/generalized-anxiety-disorder/), or chronic physical conditions such as [diabetes](https://ada.com/conditions/diabetes/), chronic pain or [multiple sclerosis](https://ada.com/conditions/multiple-sclerosis/) [5](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5"), also have a higher risk of experiencing a depressive episode. [2](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
The severity of a depressive episode varies; it may be classified as major or minor, depending on the number of symptoms and degree of impairment (social, domestic, and work) experienced. Regardless of the severity, all depressive episodes should be taken seriously and treatedEffective treatment, which typically involves medication and/or therapy, for depression is available.[4](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
Without appropriate treatment, the risk of experiencing further episodes of depression is thought to be higher. The risk of another depressive episode occurring seems to increase with every new episode, with each one likely to last longer and be more severe than the previous one. Timely treatment can alleviate the symptoms of depression[6](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
## Depressive episode symptoms
The symptoms of a depressive episode typically include a depressed mood, i.e. feeling sad, empty, or hopeless, and/or loss of interest or enjoyment in most activities, together with any number of the following: [1](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [7](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
  * Feeling worthless or excessively guilty
  * Fatigue or lethargy
  * Difficulty with concentration, memory, and decision-making
  * Insomnia is not being able to sleep through the night, waking up early, or sleeping too much
  * Appetite changes
  * Unexplained weight loss or gain
  * Unexplained physical ailments that do not respond to treatment, such as headaches, digestive problems, or pain
  * Sluggishness, restlessness, agitation, or irritability
  * Thoughts of death or suicide, sometimes with suicide plans or suicide attempts


These symptoms are usually present every day or almost every day, for at least two weeks.[1](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
[Signs of depression](https://ada.com/signs-of-depression/) may differ according to sex and age. There are also various types of depression and depressive disorders, including major depression, [bipolar disorder](https://ada.com/conditions/bipolar-affective-disorder/) (previously known as manic depression), [postpartum depression](https://ada.com/signs-of-postpartum-depression/) and dysthymia, among others. [8](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
If a person seems to be in imminent danger of harming themselves, an emergency support provider should be contacted immediately.
If you are worried that you or someone you know may have this condition, use the [symptom checker](https://ada.com/app/) works.
## Causes of a depressive episode
The causes of depressive episodes are complex and varied, involving social, psychological and biological factors. Depression may occur as an isolated episode or as part of a chronic depressive condition. [4](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") While the exact causes are not yet fully understood, the following may increase a person’s likelihood of experiencing a depressive episode: [2](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [3](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") ref7 [9](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") [10](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
  * History of depressive episodes
  * [Bipolar disorder](https://ada.com/conditions/bipolar-affective-disorder/)
  * [Anxiety](https://ada.com/conditions/generalized-anxiety-disorder/)
  * [Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder](https://ada.com/conditions/attention-deficit-hyperactivity-disorder/) (ADHD)
  * Other mental health conditions
  * Family history of depression
  * Changes in the functioning of the brain
  * History of sleep problems
  * Chronic pain
  * Heart disease, cancer and other chronic health conditions
  * Stressful life events such as losing one’s job, losing a loved one (bereavement) or psychological trauma
  * Lack of personal support structures
  * Drug and alcohol abuse
  * Childhood trauma


People who have recently had a baby may experience [postpartum depression](https://ada.com/signs-of-postpartum-depression/). [11](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
Sometimes, there is no obvious cause for the occurence of a depressive episode. [10](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
Some health conditions, such as [hypothyroidism](https://ada.com/conditions/hypothyroidism/), can cause symptoms of depression. [3](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") While uncommon, adverse reactions to certain medications can also cause depressed mood. [2](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") However, treating these underlying causes and disorders should alleviate the symptoms.
## Diagnosis of a depressive episode
After taking the affected person’s medical history and performing a physical examination, a doctor or the mental health specialist to which the person is referred to, can diagnose a depressive episode based on the criteria set out in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition
A major depressive episode (MDE) is characterized by five or more[1](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * Depressed mood for most of the day
  * Loss of interest or enjoyment in all or most activities
  * Significant unexplained weight loss or gain, or appetite changes
  * Sleep disturbances, including insomnia or sleeping too much (hypersomnia)
  * Restlessness or sluggishness
  * Tiredness or lack of energy
  * Feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt
  * Difficulty thinking, concentrating or making decisions
  * Thoughts of death or suicide – there may be suicide plans or suicide attempts


These symptoms should indicate a marked difference from the affected person’s previous functioning. For the diagnosis to be made, at least one of the symptoms needs to be depressed mood or loss of interest in most activities.[1](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
If the symptoms are attributed to another mental health condition, the diagnosis and treatment may be different to that detailed here for a depressive episode. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
To rule out any other health conditions that could be causing symptoms of a depressive state, such as a [thyroid disorder](https://ada.com/thyroid/), a doctor may order [blood tests](https://ada.com/blood-test-results/) or scans. If a person is considered to be at risk of dementia, the doctor will also check for this condition, as some of the symptoms can be similar to depression. [2](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
### Minor depressive episode
If only two to four of the above symptoms are present, instead of a major depressive episode, a diagnosis of a minor depressive episode may be made. At least one of the symptoms needs to be a depressed mood or loss of interest in most activities. This may occur as part of a minor depressive disorder.
Think you might be experiencing a depressive episode
## Depressive episode treatment
Depression is considered to be a treatable condition, with treatment often involving a combination of medication and therapy.[2](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [3](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [11](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
### Psychotherapy
Psychotherapy is talk therapy, and there are several different types that may be effective for people experiencing a mild or moderate depressive episode. These include counseling, problem-solving therapy, interpersonal therapy, group therapy, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) – which can help a person develop more helpful ways of thinking and acting. [10](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10") [12](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
For some people, a combination of psychotherapy and medication may be more effective than psychotherapy alone for depression. [12](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
### Medication
Medication may be prescribed in cases of moderate or severe depression, often in combination with a course of psychotherapy. [2](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") While the way it works is not yet fully understood, antidepressant medication may alter the levels of neurotransmitters in the brain with a positive impact on mood. [10](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10") [12](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
Several different types of antidepressants are available. The main categories include: [12](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12") [13](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:13 "See Footnote 13")
  * Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs):[2](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") SSRIs tend to cause fewer side-effects than other antidepressants. Examples of SSRIs include fluoxetine, paroxetine, and sertraline.
  * Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs):
  * Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs):
  * Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs):[14](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14")


There are also a few other types of antidepressants, such as bupropion and mirtazapine.
It may take a few weeks for an antidepressant to take effect and alleviate the symptoms of a depressive episode. A doctor will advise on how long the medication should be taken and what to do if a person wishes to stop taking it. While antidepressants are not considered to be addictive, stopping them suddenly may cause discontinuation symptoms,[12](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
Some people may experience side effects while taking antidepressants, including: [12](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
  * Nausea and vomiting
  * Weight gain
  * Diarrhea or constipation
  * Feeling sleepy
  * Sexual problems


While less common, other side-effects may include serotonin syndrome, a potentially life-threatening condition where high levels of serotonin cause mental and physical symptoms like anxiety, rapid heartbeat, high temperature and vomiting, [15](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:15 "See Footnote 15") and suicidal thoughts. [12](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
It may be necessary for a person to try several different medications before finding one that they feel works for them. [12](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12") The type of antidepressants prescribed will depend on the affected person’s age, health, and medical history. A doctor will arrange check-ups a couple of weeks after treatment is started and regularly thereafter to monitor progress. [2](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
### Other remedies
Exercise:[2](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [3](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
St John’s Wort:[10](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10") [12](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT):[10](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
Light therapy:[seasonal affective disorder (SAD)](https://ada.com/conditions/seasonal-affective-disorder/) and non-seasonal major depressive disorder. Light therapy may be helpful on its own or in combination with psychotherapy or antidepressant medication. [16](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:16 "See Footnote 16")
Acupuncture, spiritual practice, and nutritional changes may also be suggested as complementary therapies to help in the treatment of depressive episodes, though there is insufficient scientific evidence to support their efficacy. [3](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
If the depressive episode is mild, a doctor may suggest waiting for two weeks to see if it clears on its own. In addition, they may recommend self-help resources, relaxation therapies, and a small number of psychotherapy sessions. Antidepressants are not usually prescribed for mild depression unless they persist or cause complications.[2](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [11](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
In severe cases of depression, where a person is at risk of harming themselves or others or is experiencing psychotic symptoms, they may be referred to a specialist care facility. [2](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
If a person seems in imminent danger of harming themselves, an emergency support provider should be contacted immediately.
## Prevention of depressive episodes
Speaking to a healthcare professional and following the treatment program they recommend is very important
While there is no known way to prevent a depressive episode, certain positive behaviors may be helpful. These include: [10](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
  * Talking about feelings when upset
  * Staying active, e.g. exercising and getting outdoors
  * Eating a balanced diet
  * Avoiding alcohol and drugs
  * Writing down factors that may be causing the depression and trying to find solutions


## Associated terms used for depressive episodes
  * Major Depression
  * Depression
  * Mild Depression
  * Dysthymia
  * Chronic depression
  * Dysthymic Disorder
  * Neurotic depression
  * Persistent depressive disorder
  * Affective disorder
  * Mood disorder

Q: I feel a depressive episode coming on. What can I do to stop it?  
A:speak to a psychotherapist or other qualified healthcare professional.
Q: How long does a depressive episode last?  
A:[2](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
Q: What should I do during a depressive episode?  
A:
Q: If a loved one is experiencing a depressive episode, what is the best thing to do?  
A:[10](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
  * Listening without judgment
  * Spending time with the person
  * Reassuring them that they can get better
  * Helping them to eat a balanced diet
  * Helping them get outside and moving, e.g. by taking them on regular walks or supporting them in exercising
  * Helping them to avoid alcohol
  * Encouraging them to speak to a healthcare professional
  * Encouraging them to adhere to their treatment program


It is important to understand that it may take a person experiencing depression a long time to get better. The support of family, friends and broader social networks is an important part of recovery.

# Rheumatic Fever
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on October 4, 2022 at 8:05 AM GMT+2
## On this page
  * [What is rheumatic fever?](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#what-is-rheumatic-fever)
  * [What causes rheumatic fever?](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#what-causes-rheumatic-fever)
  * [Scarlet fever vs rheumatic fever](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#scarlet-fever-vs-rheumatic-fever)
  * [What are the symptoms of rheumatic fever?](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#what-are-the-symptoms-of-rheumatic-fever)
  * [How is rheumatic fever diagnosed?](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#how-is-rheumatic-fever-diagnosed)
  * [How is rheumatic fever treated?](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#how-is-rheumatic-fever-treated)
  * [Complications of rheumatic fever](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#complications-of-rheumatic-fever)
  * [Rheumatic heart disease](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#rheumatic-heart-disease)
  * [Who is at risk of getting rheumatic fever and how can it be prevented?](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#who-is-at-risk-of-getting-rheumatic-fever-and-how-can-it-be-prevented)
  * [Rheumatic fever FAQs](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#rheumatic-fever-faqs)


* * *
Share this article:
Rheumatic fever is an inflammatory disease which can affect the brain, skin, joints and heart. It is an uncommon complication of untreated group A streptococci bacterial infections of the throat or skin.[1](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
A high fever, sore joints, chest pain and tiredness can all be symptoms of rheumatic fever. Usually, these symptoms will resolve spontaneously, however, there is a risk of long-term damage to the heart, a condition known as rheumatic heart disease. [3](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
The best way to prevent rheumatic fever is to prevent certain bacterial infections or by treating them promptly with antibiotics.
Feeling unwell? Get a symptom assessment with the [symptom checker](https://ada.com/app/) works before you try it for yourself.
## What is rheumatic fever?
Rheumatic fever is the result of a faulty reaction of the body’s immune system to certain types of bacteria. This causes it to attack healthy tissues along with the infection, causing damage to the body. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
The symptoms experienced by someone with rheumatic fever are the result of inflammation caused by the immune system. Most commonly affected parts of the body include the skin, joints and heart. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [3](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
## What causes rheumatic fever?
Rheumatic fever may develop from untreated throat or skin infections, specifically those caused by a type of bacteria called group A Streptococcus[1](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
Infections which can develop into rheumatic fever include:
  * [strep throat](https://ada.com/covid/strep-vs-covid-19-symptoms/)
  * scarlet fever
  * [impetigo](https://ada.com/conditions/impetigo/)


Not everyone with these conditions will get rheumatic fever, but it is still important to treat them with antibiotics in order to reduce the risk.
## Scarlet fever vs rheumatic fever
Scarlet fever is a pink, bumpy rash which may develop as a result of a group A streptococci infection in the throat or on the skin. Doctors will treat scarlet fever with antibiotics and it rarely causes any complications. Scarlet fever which has not been successfully treated may develop into rheumatic fever, which can be more serious. [4](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
## What are the symptoms of rheumatic fever?
Symptoms usually appear 1 to 5 weeks after a bacterial throat infection. The most common rheumatic fever symptoms are:
  * fever
  * joint pain
  * chest pain
  * uncontrollable movements, such as jerking, in the hands, feet and face
  * feeling short of breath
  * fatigue
  * small lumps under the skin


Rarely, people with rheumatic fever may get a rash, which appears as pale pink rings. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [3](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
If you are worried that you or someone you know may have this condition, use the [symptom checker](https://ada.com/app/) works.
## How is rheumatic fever diagnosed?
There is no single test for rheumatic fever. A doctor may ask you questions about your health and perform an examination to reach a rheumatic fever diagnosis. Often, a throat swab will be taken to check what bacteria is causing the infection. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
After that, further investigations may be done to see what organs are affected. Common investigations include an echocardiogram or electrocardiogram (ECG) to look for any damage to the heart. It may be necessary to have blood tests done, to confirm if there are signs of infection or inflammation in the body. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
## How is rheumatic fever treated?
Rheumatic fever treatment focuses on treating the underlying bacterial infection with a course of antibiotics. It is important that these are taken correctly to reduce the chance of the infection returning. [6](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") It may be necessary to take antibiotics for several years to prevent rheumatic fever coming back. Most people recover within about 3 months, but this can vary depending on the severity. [2](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
Rheumatic fever symptoms are treated with a variety of medicines. These may include:
  * painkillers to ease chest or joint pain
  * steroid injections
  * medication to prevent uncontrolled movements
  * anti-inflammatory medications


If rheumatic fever leads to long term effects, life-long medication may be needed to support heart function. [2](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
## Complications of rheumatic fever
Rheumatic fever is known as an autoimmune disease. This means that the body’s immune system damages its own tissues and cells when fighting unwanted pathogens. Long term effects of rheumatic fever include damage to organs, especially the heart. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
## Rheumatic heart disease
Rheumatic fever can cause permanent damage to heart valves and muscle, which can cause heart failure. Symptoms may not be noticed for several years and commonly include irregular heartbeats, chest pain and breathlessness. [7](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
There is no cure for rheumatic heart disease, but medications can help the symptoms. In some cases, surgery to replace heart valves may be recommended. [7](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
## Who is at risk of getting rheumatic fever and how can it be prevented?
Rheumatic fever mostly affects children and young adults under the age of 30.[^8] It is becoming increasingly less common in countries with developed health care systems, due to the availability of antibiotics to treat throat and skin infections. 
Higher risk groups include those living in areas of poverty, overcrowding or where access to healthcare is limited. [7](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
The best way to prevent rheumatic fever is to avoid getting group A streptococci[7](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatic-fever/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
## Find out more about your symptoms
## Rheumatic fever FAQs
Q: How does rheumatic fever affect the heart?
A: Rheumatic fever causes an autoimmune response, which means the body’s immune system attacks its own organs, including heart valves. This can cause long-term damage to the heart, a condition known as rheumatic heart disease.
Q: How common is rheumatic fever?
A: Rheumatic fever has become rare in countries where streptococcal
Q: How is rheumatic fever diagnosed?
A: In order to diagnose Rheumatic fever, your doctor may ask you about your past medical history and your symptoms. Often, further investigations are done to confirm a diagnosis or to see how the disease is affecting your body, especially the heart. 
Q: How long does rheumatic fever last?
A: With treatment, most people go on to make a full recovery after 1-3 months. If complications arise, you may need follow-up treatments and check-ups for a number of years to spot the long-term effects of rheumatic fever.

## What is rheumatoid arthritis?
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a long-term, inflammatory arthritis, which develops gradually and is caused by an autoimmune reaction. This means that the immune system mistakenly forms proteins which are meant to fight infections, known as antibodies, that attack the body tissue instead.
The symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis occur in episodes or flare ups of pain and swelling in the joints, with periods of remission in between. Usually the joints are affected symmetrically, especially the hands, wrists and feet, and many joints may be inflamed. It can also affect other parts of a person’s body, including the lungs, heart and eyes. Onset may include symptoms such as fever and fatigue.
The prevalence of RA varies between populations around the world, from 0.1 percent in rural Africans to 5 percent in some Native American groups. Women are affected two to three times more often than men. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
The age of onset for rheumatoid arthritis is usually over 35, and the likelihood of developing the condition increases as a person gets older. Onset is highest among adults in their 60s.[2](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") Rheumatoid arthritis is normally a lifelong condition that worsens with age.
If RA is not treated early, it can cause irreversible damage to joints, leading to disability. However, it can normally be well-managed with medications to slow down the immune system, thereby slowing the progression of the disease, as well as pain medications for relief of symptoms. There is currently no specific cure for rheumatoid arthritis.
By definition, rheumatoid arthritis appears in adults and not in children. However, a related condition may sometimes appear in children,[juvenile idiopathic arthritis](https://ada.com/conditions/juvenile-idiopathic-arthritis/), previously known as [juvenile rheumatoid arthritis](https://ada.com/conditions/juvenile-rheumatoid-arthritis/). Juvenile idiopathic arthritis may clear up by the time adulthood is reached. Many children with this condition also experience regular fevers.
If you think you might have rheumatoid arthritis, try using 
## Rheumatoid arthritis symptoms
In most people, rheumatoid arthritis (RA) symptoms begin very subtly,
Early signs and symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis may include: [1](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
  * Joint stiffness, often in the hands and feet, usually worse in the morning
  * Joint pain and swelling
  * Fatigue
  * Muscle pain
  * Low-grade fever
  * Numbness and tingling in the hands


Good to know:
## Causes of rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease, which means that it is caused by abnormal functioning of the immune system.In rheumatoid arthritis, the body attacks its own joint tissue.
People with RA produce an excess of white blood cells in the synovial membrane, also known as the synovium, the tissue that lines the cavities of joints, causing inflammation. This can lead to joint erosion, loss of motion and occasionally damage to other associated parts of the body, such as the lungs, heart, blood vessels and eyes.
If RA is left untreated, pannus tissue may form, in which there is excess, uneven tissue growth in a joint, which can further erode and damage cartilage and bone.
## Risk factors
It is not certain what causes rheumatoid arthritis (RA), but some possible contributing factors have been identified, including:
### Genetics
Specific variants in the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) genes are associated with a higher risk of developing RA. These variations make the white blood cells attempt to correct abnormalities in the joints more quickly than usual, which may be what leads to the inflammation and associated tissue damage that results from rheumatoid arthritis.
However, rheumatoid arthritis is not an inherited condition;[3](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") Other non-HLA genes have also been linked to RA. [4](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
### Bacteria and viruses
Certain microbial infections are believed to play an important role in triggering and worsening RA. These may include: [5](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
  * A gum infection,
  * A urine infection,
  * The Epstein-Barr virus, best known as the cause of mononucleosis


### Smoking
Research has shown that exposure to certain irritants in the air may play a role in a person’s risk of developing rheumatoid arthritis, including: [6](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [7](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
  * Tobacco smoke
  * Silica dust, mainly affecting people in the mining industry
  * Certain mineral oils, such as found in hydraulic oil


Good to know:
### Being female
Rheumatoid arthritis is far more common in women,[8](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") It has been suggested that this may be due to production of [prolactin](https://ada.com/hormones/prolactin/), the milk production hormone, having an inflammatory effect. [7](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
### Physical trauma
Physical trauma has been linked to rheumatoid arthritis onset, such as with sports injuries. Physical trauma can trigger inflammation, which it is thought may contribute to the development of rheumatoid arthritis, possibly at a much later date. However, it is not known why this might be. Some people may have a predisposition to such inflammation. [9](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9")
### Obesity
Research has found that obesity may have an impact on the development of the condition. [10](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10") [11](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11") It is not known why this is, but one reason postulated is that fat cells release proteins called cytokines, which create inflammation throughout the body. [12](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12")
Good to know:[13](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:13 "See Footnote 13") It can also lead to earlier deterioration of the main joints, such as the knees, due to increased pressure.
## Rheumatoid arthritis and COVID-19
People with rheumatoid arthritis are more susceptible to infections, including an infection with the coronavirus. If you have rheumatoid arthritis and [COVID-19](https://ada.com/covid/), you may be at risk for severe complications
## Diagnosing rheumatoid arthritis
Diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is generally confirmed after referral to a rheumatologist, a type of doctor specializing in inflammation and pain in the joints, muscles, or fibrous tissues.
RA can take a long time to diagnose as its early onset can be subtle and present similarly to other, less long-term conditions, such as flu, also known as [influenza](https://ada.com/conditions/influenza-infection/). It also often presents similarly to other types of arthritis, such as [reactive arthritis](https://ada.com/conditions/reactive-arthritis/).
Unlike other types of arthritis, there is no specific test for rheumatoid arthritis. Instead, a rheumatologist relies on gathering information to rule out other conditions and identify the cause of a person’s symptoms. Diagnosis may be made from a combination of reported medical history and symptoms, a physical examination, laboratory tests and medical imaging. Try the 
### Interview and physical exam
It is important that a person describe any joint pain and other symptoms, as well as how long they have been going on for.
A doctor will look for signs of rheumatoid arthritis, such as swollen, tender, warm joints with painful or limited movement, and rheumatoid nodules (see [complications](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#complications)). They may also ask for family medical history; if another member of their family has the disease, then a person has a higher risk of having the condition themselves.
### Laboratory tests
If a doctor suspects rheumatoid arthritis, one or more blood tests may be done to help make a diagnosis. These include: [14](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14")
Testing for rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibodies:
Measuring inflammatory markers:
  * Tumor necrosis factor-alpha
  * Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR or sed rate)
  * C-reactive protein (CRP)


Good to know:
[Read more about Blood Test Results »](https://ada.com/blood-test-results/)
### Medical imaging
A doctor may also recommend an X-ray, ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the affected joint. This can help to rule out other conditions that present with similar symptoms, such as gout. However, at an early stage of rheumatoid arthritis, any characteristic damage caused by the condition may not be apparent. [14](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14")
## Treating rheumatoid arthritis
It is very important to start treatment as soon as possible to prevent any permanent joint damage. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) can usually be effectively managed with early, appropriate treatment. There is currently no rheumatoid arthritis cure, and it is usually a chronic condition requiring lifelong treatment.
The main aims of treatment for RA are: [15](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:15 "See Footnote 15") [16](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:16 "See Footnote 16")
  * To prevent joint damage
  * To minimize pain and other symptoms, and maintain quality of life
  * To prevent the development of associated conditions such as [osteoporosis](https://ada.com/conditions/osteoporosis/) and [cardiovascular disease](https://ada.com/cardiovascular-disease-risk-factors/)


There are three main aspects of rheumatoid arthritis treatment:
  * Medication
  * Physical therapy
  * In some cases, surgery


### Medications
Rheumatoid arthritis is usually treated with a combination of medications. The five main types of drugs used for rheumatoid arthritis are: [16](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:16 "See Footnote 16")
Disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs),
Biologic agents:
Steroids:
Painkillers.
### Physical therapy
People with rheumatoid arthritis often become inactive due to joint pain and stiffness. However, inactivity can lead to inflexibility, muscle and tendon shortening, and muscle weakness. In turn, weakness further increases fatigue and decreases stability of the joints.
A physiotherapist can recommend safe exercises
An occupational therapist may recommend ways to approach day-to-day activities
A podiatrist may work with a person on ways to ease problems with the feet and ankles,
Some people find that yoga helps to relieve symptoms, although currently there is not strong medical evidence to support this. People with RA must do yoga with proper supervision to ensure that it is safe.
### Surgery
Occasionally, surgery is needed to treat joints affected by rheumatoid arthritis. These can be minor surgeries, such as to release a nerve or tendon or more major surgeries such as hip, knee, shoulder and elbow replacements.
### Diet
There are no clear-cut answers as to what diet to follow with rheumatoid arthritis, as there is a lot of conflicting evidence, and different diets may affect people in different ways. However, it is generally recommended that a person eat: [17](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:17 "See Footnote 17") [18](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:18 "See Footnote 18")
  * A balanced and varied diet
  * Omega-3 fatty acid-rich food
  * Calcium-rich food,
  * Vitamin-D-rich food,
  * Iron-rich food,


Weight loss may be recommended
### Natural treatment
Natural treatments have not conclusively been shown to stop or slow rheumatoid arthritis progression, but certain treatments may help with pain relief when used in conjunction with prescribed rheumatoid arthritis medications, including:
Supplements for rheumatoid arthritis containing gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) have been shown to modestly improve joint pain, stiffness and grip strength. [19](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:19 "See Footnote 19") This includes evening primrose oil or borage oil, especially when combined with fish oil, which reduces the synthesis of inflammatory by-products of GLA. [20](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:20 "See Footnote 20")
Calcium and vitamin D supplements may be recommended if not enough is consumed through diet. These can help to minimize [bone loss](https://ada.com/conditions/osteoporosis/), which is associated with steroid therapy. [16](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:16 "See Footnote 16")
Some people find that home remedies, such as essential oils and turmeric help to relieve symptoms, although there is currently no strong medical evidence to support these.
Good to know:
### Support groups
Some people find it helpful to discuss their condition and treatment in support groups. There are many local support groups which meet up in person, as well as online forums, such as on 
## Complications
As the condition progresses, further signs and symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis may develop, such as: [1](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [21](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:21 "See Footnote 21")
Rheumatoid arthritis in hands:[carpal tunnel syndrome](https://ada.com/conditions/carpal-tunnel-syndrome/). This is the compression of a nerve running through the wrist, characterized by tingling, numbness and weakness in the hand. Certain permanent bone alterations can also occur with long-term rheumatoid arthritis, such as swan neck deformities, boutonniere deformities, ulnar deviation and the bowstring sign.
Rheumatoid arthritis in knee:
Rheumatoid arthritis in feet:
Rheumatoid arthritis nodules:
Rheumatoid arthritis can cause inflammation of tissues other than the joints, for example: [1](https://ada.com/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
Rheumatoid arthritis in the lungs:
Rheumatoid arthritis in the cervical spine, the bones of the neck:
Inflammation of the blood vessels,
Inflammation of the skin,
Inflammation of the tissue surrounding the heart,[Pericarditis](https://ada.com/conditions/pericarditis/): may cause chest pain and shortness of breath.
## Prevention
While there is no known way to prevent the onset of rheumatoid arthritis, there are a few known ways in which a person can reduce the risk. These include:
  * Quitting tobacco smoking
  * Being physically active and eating a healthy diet
  * Taking steps to maintain a healthy weight


It is also important to see a doctor as soon as symptoms develop, as early treatment can greatly minimize the rheumatoid arthritis progression, as well as any permanent damage caused by flare ups.

# Hemorragia gastrointestinal inferior
Escrito por nuestro [Equipo de Profesionales Médicos](https://ada.com/es/team/medical/)
Actualizado el 15 de febrero de 2022, 10:01 EET
## En esta página
  * [Resumen](https://ada.com/es/conditions/lower-gastrointestinal-hemorrhage/#resumen)
  * [Riesgos](https://ada.com/es/conditions/lower-gastrointestinal-hemorrhage/#riesgos)

  * [Diagnóstico](https://ada.com/es/conditions/lower-gastrointestinal-hemorrhage/#diagnostico)
  * [Tratamiento](https://ada.com/es/conditions/lower-gastrointestinal-hemorrhage/#tratamiento)
  * [Prevención](https://ada.com/es/conditions/lower-gastrointestinal-hemorrhage/#prevencion)
  * [Pronóstico](https://ada.com/es/conditions/lower-gastrointestinal-hemorrhage/#pronostico)

Comparte este artículo:
## Resumen
El sangrado del tracto gastrointestinal inferior es una condición médica en donde se presenta una hemorragia desde la parte inferior del sistema digestivo, específicamente del intestino grueso, el recto o el ano. Los síntomas principales son sangre roja y fresca que sale del ano o movimientos intestinales color granate. Una hemorragia significativa del tracto gastrointestinal inferior es una emergencia médica. Los adultos mayores y las personas con antecedentes de enfermedad diverticular, enfermedad inflamatoria intestinal y cáncer de colon o recto desarrollan más comúnmente esta condición médica. El tratamiento depende de la causa de la hemorragia, pero casi siempre incluye reemplazo de fluidos y sangre, y de ser posible encontrar el origen y detener el sangrado.
¿Te sientes mal? Revisa tus síntomas con la app verificador de síntomas antes de probar nuestra app.
## Riesgos
Existen muchas causas posibles para una hemorragia del tracto gastrointestinal inferior. Los problemas de salud que causan sangrado en pequeña cantidad son las hemorroides, las fisuras anales y algunas enfermedades de transmisión sexual. Los problemas de salud que pueden provocar hemorragias mayores son los distintos tipos de cáncer de intestino (cáncer de colon, recto o ano), algunas infecciones intestinales (como intoxicación alimentaria), un trastorno diverticular, malformaciones de los vasos sanguíneos dentro del intestino y enfermedades inflamatorias del intestino (colitis ulcerativa y enfermedad de Crohn). Las personas que toman medicamentos para diluir la sangre tienen mayor riesgo de una hemorragia importante del intestino. Generalmente afecta más a los adultos mayores que a las personas más jóvenes.
## Síntomas
El síntoma más común es un sangrado rojo brillante desde el ano o en las heces (materia fecal). Otros síntomas pueden incluir dolor abdominal, mareos, palpitaciones, debilidad, confusión y desmayo, dependiendo de cuánta sangre se pierda.
## Diagnóstico
El diagnóstico de la causa de la hemorragia se basa en la historia clínica de la persona, hallazgos de laboratorio y examinando el interior del intestino por medio de una endoscopia (una cámara larga y flexible que se pasa por la boca o el ano para mirar el intestino). En casos graves de pérdida de sangre y emergencia, la evaluación diagnóstica sólo se hace después de haber reanimado a la persona y detenido la hemorragia.
## Tratamiento
El tratamiento depende de la cantidad de sangre perdida y de la causa de la hemorragia. La causa debe investigarse y tratarse para evitar futuros sangrados. En caso de una hemorragia menor, puede controlarse con una terapia médica o endoscópica. En caso de una pérdida importante de sangre, el tratamiento envuelve hospitalización y reanimación de la persona afectada. Esto puede requerir fluidos por goteo o transfusiones de sangre, además de vigilar la presión arterial, el pulso cardíaco, etc. Las personas con una hemorragia grande pueden necesitar una cirugía de emergencia para encontrar y tratar la causa del sangrado.
## Prevención
Las personas que toman medicamentos para diluir la sangre y que tienen riesgo de sangrar por el intestino deben vigilar de cerca el tiempo de coagulación de su sangre. Recibir un diagnóstico y tratamiento tempranos de las condiciones médicas que pueden causar hemorragia del intestino puede ayudar a prevenir algunos casos de hemorragia del tracto gastrointestinal inferior.
## Pronóstico
El pronóstico después de una hemorragia del tracto gastrointestinal inferior depende de la causa de fondo. El pronóstico de recuperación a menudo es bueno si se encuentra y se trata la fuente de la hemorragia. Los adultos mayores y las personas con otros problemas de salud corren mayor riesgo de tener una hemorragia importante y desarrollar complicaciones.
## Aprende más acerca de tus síntomas

# Harnblasenkarzinom
Verfasst von [Adas medizinischem Fachpersonal](https://ada.com/de/team/medical/)
Aktualisiert am 15. Februar 2022 um 10:01 OEZ
## Auf dieser Seite
  * [Was ist Harnblasenkarzinom?](https://ada.com/de/conditions/bladder-cancer/#was-ist-harnblasenkarzinom)
  * [Risiken](https://ada.com/de/conditions/bladder-cancer/#risiken)
  * [Symptome](https://ada.com/de/conditions/bladder-cancer/#symptome)
  * [Diagnose](https://ada.com/de/conditions/bladder-cancer/#diagnose)
  * [Behandlung](https://ada.com/de/conditions/bladder-cancer/#behandlung)
  * [Prognose](https://ada.com/de/conditions/bladder-cancer/#prognose)

Artikel teilen:
## Was ist Harnblasenkarzinom?
Blasenkrebs ist die Entwicklung eines Krebses in der Harnblase. Diese Erkrankung ist bei Männern häufiger verbreitet als bei Frauen und tritt im Alter häufiger auf. Die häufigsten Symptome sind Blut im Urin (Hämaturie) und Probleme beim Wasserlassen. Die Behandlung und die Prognose nach einer Blasenkrebs-Erkrankung hängen von der Größe und der Art des Krebses ab.
## Risiken
Blasenkrebs ist unter Männern häufiger verbreitet als unter Frauen und tritt im Alter mit höherer Wahrscheinlichkeit auf. Bei Rauchern oder Menschen, die Zigarettenrauch ausgesetzt sind, besteht ein höheres Risiko für Blasenkrebs.
Die Belastung durch einige industrielle Chemikalien und Dämpfe, darunter Arsen, Benzol und Dieselabgase
## Symptome
Typische Symptome sind Blut im Urin (Hämaturie) und Probleme beim Wasserlassen[Bei einigen Menschen kann es zu wiederkehrenden Infektionen der Harnwege](https://ada.com/de/conditions/urinary-tract-infection/) (Blasen- oder Nierenentzündungen). Weitere Symptome können Schmerzen im unteren Bauch oder im Rücken
Mit der Ada-[App](https://ada.com/de/app/) kannst Du Deine Symptome ganz einfach checken. 
## Diagnose
Die Diagnose erfolgt basierend auf den Symptomen und, gelegentlich, auf einer körperlichen Untersuchung. Eine Urinuntersuchung kann durchgeführt werden, um im Urin nach Blut- und Krebszellen zu suchen.
Eine Zystoskopie (der Blick in das Innere der Blase mittels einer Kamera) wird durchgeführt, um die Diagnose zu bestätigen und eine Probe des Krebses für weitere Untersuchungen zu entnehmen. Eine Computertomographie (CT) ist ebenfalls hilfreich, um zu untersuchen, ob der Krebs an andere Stellen gestreut hat.
## Behandlung
Die Behandlung des Blasenkrebs hängt von der Größe und der genauen Art des Krebses sowie davon ab, ob der Krebs bereits gestreut hat. Die Kombination dieser Faktoren bestimmt das Krebsstadium. Abhängig vom Stadium kann Blasenkrebs durch einen chirurgischen Eingriff, eine Strahlentherapie oder Chemotherapie oder durch eine Kombination behandelt werden.
## Prognose
Die Prognose bei Blasenkrebs hängt von einer Reihe von Faktoren ab:
  * das Stadium, in dem der Krebs diagnostiziert wird,
  * das Alter der betroffenen Person
  * und wie diese auf die Therapie anspricht.


Bei jüngeren Menschen wird der Krebs tendenziell in einem früheren Stadium diagnostiziert und sie sprechen besser auf die Behandlung an als ältere Menschen.
## Vorsorge
Die Wahrscheinlichkeit von Blasenkrebs kann verringert werden, indem man mit dem Rauchen aufhört.

# COVID Arm: What To Know
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on January 29, 2025 at 11:33 AM GMT+2
## On this page
  * [Overview](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-arm/#overview)
  * [What is COVID arm?](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-arm/#what-is-covid-arm)
  * [Other causes](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-arm/#other-causes)
  * [Duration](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-arm/#duration)
  * [Treatments](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-arm/#treatments)
  * [Wrapping up](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-arm/#wrapping-up)
  * [FAQs](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-arm/#faqs)


* * *
Share this article:
## Overview
  * COVID arm is a rare side effect of the COVID-19 vaccine that produces redness, soreness and/or itchiness near the injection point
  * The onset of symptoms is unique in COVID arm, appearing 5-9 days after the injection
  * COVID arm is harmless, and most cases resolve themselves in less than a week
  * Pain medications, antihistamines, and cool compresses can provide relief for COVID arm symptoms


Think you might be experiencing COVID-19 symptoms
Over 13 billion doses of the COVID-19 vaccine have been administered worldwide as of May 2023. Shortly after receiving the vaccine, it’s common to experience some mild side effects. One of the talked about effects is what has been called “COVID arm[soreness](https://ada.com/conditions/muscle-soreness/) that appears 5-9 days after the injection.
## What is COVID arm?
“COVID arm" is a term used to refer to soreness, redness, and itchinessappears 5-9 days after[1](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-arm/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") They’re also less likely to occur with a second dose in a person who didn’t have a reaction to the first dose of the vaccine.
Health researchers believe that COVID arm is part of the body’s natural response to the vaccine. When a vaccine is injected into a muscle, your body responds by producing antibodies and fighter cells to fend it off. However, in some individuals, this reaction can become hyperactive and cause the muscle cells to act as if they’re fighting an actual infection. 
This overreaction can result in the following symptoms
  * Redness
  * Swelling
  * Warmth
  * Hardness
  * Itchiness
  * Discomfort
  * Welt
  * Rash


It’s important to note that "COVID arm" is different from a rapid onset allergic reaction to a vaccine that occurs mere hours after a vaccine is received and can be life-threatening, affecting breathing and [heart rate](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-heart-palpitations/). Individuals with severe allergic reactions
Concerned that you or a loved one may have COVID-19? Start your symptom assessment in the [app](https://ada.com/app/) first.
## What else can cause arm redness or soreness?
In some cases, COVID arm has been confused with other skin conditions[2](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-arm/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
Other causes[3](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-arm/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
  * Abscesses
  * Insect bites
  * Drug reactions
  * Hives
  * Sweet syndrome 


## How long does COVID arm last?
The duration of COVID arm that arises from the COVID vaccine varies from person to person. [Most symptoms associated with COVID](https://ada.com/covid/) arm clear within 24 hours to a week – with 3 to 4 days being the most common time it takes to subside. In some cases, COVID arm has persisted up to 21 days. [4](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-arm/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
## How do you treat COVID arm?
There are several ways to treat the discomfort[5](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-arm/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
  * Over-the-counter pain medications: Pain relievers, such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen, can be effective in reducing arm soreness after a vaccine shot.
  * Antihistamines: Medications like Benadryl can help relieve any itchiness at the injection point.
  * Cold compresses: Applying a cold compress or ice pack to the area can help reduce swelling and discomfort.
  * Gentle arm movements: Moving the arm gently and regularly can help to reduce stiffness and soreness.
  * Rest: Taking a break and resting the arm can also help to reduce discomfort.
  * Heat therapy: Using a warm compress, such as a heating pad, can also help to relieve arm soreness after a vaccine shot.


If you experience COVID arm after your shot, tell your vaccination provider. Your vaccination provider may recommend that you receive your next COVID-19 vaccine in the opposite arm if possible.
## Wrapping up
COVID arm is a common side-effect after a COVID-19 vaccine caused by your body's immune response to the shot. The onset of the symptoms is typically 5-7 days after the shot was administered, and symptoms typically clear in less than a week on their own. 
Although these delayed injection site reactions may be a nuisance, they’re harmless. However, if the soreness persists or becomes severe, seek medical advice.

Q: How long does COVID arm last?
Q: Will COVID arm go away by itself?
Q: Should you move your arm after COVID vaccine?
Q: Is COVID arm contagious?
Q: Is COVID arm an allergic reaction?

# Small Cell Lung Cancer
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on February 15, 2022 at 10:01 AM GMT+2
## On this page
  * [What is small cell lung cancer?](https://ada.com/conditions/small-cell-lung-cancer/#what-is-small-cell-lung-cancer)
  * [Risks for small cell lung cancer](https://ada.com/conditions/small-cell-lung-cancer/#risks-for-small-cell-lung-cancer)
  * [Symptoms of small cell lung](https://ada.com/conditions/small-cell-lung-cancer/#symptoms-of-small-cell-lung)
  * [Diagnosing small cell luing cancer](https://ada.com/conditions/small-cell-lung-cancer/#diagnosing-small-cell-luing-cancer)
  * [Treatment](https://ada.com/conditions/small-cell-lung-cancer/#treatment)
  * [Preventing small cell lung cancer](https://ada.com/conditions/small-cell-lung-cancer/#preventing-small-cell-lung-cancer)


* * *
Share this article:
## What is small cell lung cancer?
Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a type of lung cancer. Almost all cases of SCLC are caused by smoking. It is mostly centrally located in lungs and grows very rapidly and aggressively, which means it can spread quickly to distant sites.
Typical symptoms of small cell lung cancer include coughing, chest pain, shortness of breath and weight loss. SCLC can be diagnosed after carrying out blood tests and scans of the lungs and testing a small sample of lung tissue. Treatment depends on the stage of the cancer. Not all cases can be cured, as the cancer has often already spread by the time of diagnosis.
## Risks for small cell lung cancer
Cancer occurs when abnormal cells grow uncontrollably. These cells destroy the normal cells around them, and can spread into other areas of the body. There are two broad types of lung cancer, small cell and [non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)](https://ada.com/conditions/non-small-cell-lung-cancer/). Small cell lung cancer is the less common type.
SCLC mostly affects smokers. Non-smokers are rarely affected. This tumor is slightly more common in men than women and is usually diagnosed in people between the ages of 60 and 80.
## Symptoms of small cell lung
The typical symptoms are:
  * a cough with bloody phlegm
  * chest pain
  * shortness of breath
  * and weight loss.


Wheezing and a loss of appetite are also common. If the tumor has spread, symptoms may include [headache](https://ada.com/conditions/headache/) which is at its most acute in the morning, blurred vision, light sensitivity, nausea, vomiting, confusion, bone pain and difficulty swallowing.
## Diagnosing small cell luing cancer
For people who smoke and display the symptoms of SCLC, a suspected diagnosis is commonly made. A physical examination is then carried out involving blood tests, a chest x-ray, a phlegm test and lung function tests.
A small piece of the lung tissue is taken (a biopsy) and investigated to confirm the diagnosis. Further biopsies and scans may be done to see if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. This process is called staging
## Treatment
The treatment of small cell lung cancer depends on the size of the cancer and whether the cancer has spread. These combination of these factors decides the stage of the cancer. Depending on the stage, SCLC can be treated by radiotherapy, chemotherapy and surgery, or a combination of these. The treating doctor can give the best advice about appropriate treatment. People who have SCLC may benefit from taking part in a support group or counseling program, especially whilst undergoing their treatment.
## Preventing small cell lung cancer
Quitting or totally avoiding smoking is the best way to prevent SCLC.

# Transitorische ischämische Attacke
Verfasst von [Adas medizinischem Fachpersonal](https://ada.com/de/team/medical/)
Aktualisiert am 3. Juli 2025 um 14:40 OESZ
## Auf dieser Seite
  * [Was ist transitorische ischämische Attacke?](https://ada.com/de/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#was-ist-transitorische-ischaemische-attacke)
  * [Risiken](https://ada.com/de/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#risiken)
  * [Symptome](https://ada.com/de/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#symptome)
  * [Diagnose](https://ada.com/de/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#diagnose)
  * [Behandlung](https://ada.com/de/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#behandlung)
  * [Prognose](https://ada.com/de/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#prognose)
  * [Vorsorge](https://ada.com/de/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#vorsorge)


* * *
Artikel teilen:
## Was ist transitorische ischämische Attacke?
Eine transitorische ischämische Attacke (TIA), manchmal auch Mini-Schlaganfall genannt, ist eine plötzliche, kurz andauernde neurologische Erkrankung.
Sie wird durch eine kleine, vorübergehende Blockade in einem Blutgefäß im Gehirn verursacht. Die Symptome dauern in den meisten Fällen weniger als eine Stunde an, doch sie können bis zu 24 Stunden anhalten. Typische Symptome sind der Verlust des Sehvermögens, eine undeutliche Sprache und eine Schwäche des Gesichts, der Arme oder Beine.
Die Behandlung zielt darauf ab, eine weitere TIA und einen Schlaganfall zu verhindern, indem das Blut verdünnt wird und Erkrankungen, die das Risiko eines Schlaganfalls erhöhen, behandelt werden. Obwohl eine TIA selbst keinen dauerhaften Schaden im Gehirn verursacht, ist sie ein Warnsignal dafür, dass sich in naher Zukunft ein Schlaganfall ereignen kann. Betroffene, die eine TIA hatten, sollten mit einem Arzt Maßnahmen besprechen, um Schlaganfälle zu vermeiden. [1](https://ada.com/de/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
Finde mehr über Deine Symptome heraus.
## Risiken
Eine transitorische ischämische Attacke (TIA) wird durch eine kleine, vorübergehende Blockade in einem Blutgefäß im Gehirn verursacht. Dies führt zu einer vorübergehenden Sauerstoffunterversorgung des Gehirns, wodurch die Symptome der TIA ausgelöst werden. Diese Erkrankung kann jeden betreffen, doch sie tritt am häufigsten bei Personen über 60 Jahren auf.
Einige medizinische Erkrankungen, z. B.:
  * [hoher Blutdruck](https://ada.com/de/conditions/essential-hypertension/),
  * [Diabetes](https://ada.com/de/conditions/diabetes-mellitus-type-2/),
  * Vorhofflimmern (ein abnormer Herzrhythmus) oder ein
  * hoher Cholesterinspiegel,


stellen ein erhöhtes Risiko
## Symptome eines Mini-Schlaganfalls
Die Symptome einer transitorischen ischämischen Attacke können sich von Person zu Person leicht unterscheiden, doch sie sind immer von kurzer Dauer. Die Symptome dauern in den meisten Fällen weniger als eine Stunde, doch sie können bis zu 24 Stunden anhalten.
Sie können:
  * den Verlust des Sehvermögens,
  * eine undeutliche Sprache und
  * eine Schwäche des Gesichts, der Arme oder der Bein umfassen. 


Vorübergehende Veränderungen des Verhaltens, des Gedächtnisses und der Bewegung sind ebenfalls möglich.[2](https://ada.com/de/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
## Transitorische ischämische Attacke Diagnose
Die Diagnose kann basierend auf einer Beschreibung der Symptome und einer Untersuchung des Nervensystems[1](https://ada.com/de/conditions/transient-ischemic-attack/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
Finde mehr über Deine Symptome heraus.
## Transitorische ischämische Attacke Behandlung
Die Behandlung nach einer transitorischen ischämischen Attacke (TIA) kann die Einnahme von blutverdünnenden Medikamenten
## Prognose
Eine transitorische ischämische Attacke (TIA) verursacht keinen dauerhaften Schaden im Gehirn.
## Vorsorge
Veränderungen des Lebensstils, wie z. B. eine gesunde Ernährung, regelmäßiges Training, das Einstellen des Rauchens und ein verringerter Alkoholkonsum, können das Risiko einer transitorischen ischämischen Attacke und eines Schlaganfalls verringern.
Eine gute Kontrolle bei hohem Blutdruck, hohem Cholesterinspiegel und Diabetes kann eine TIA verhindern. Personen, die an Erkrankungen leiden, welche das Risiko einer Bildung von Blutgerinnseln im Herzen erhöhen, wie etwa Vorhofflimmern, sollten in Erwägung ziehen, blutverdünnende Medikamente einzunehmen.
