  * [Staging](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#staging)
  * [Other names](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#other-names)
  * [FAQ](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#faq)


* * *
Share this article:
## What is gallbladder cancer?
Gallbladder cancer, also known as a malignant neoplasm of the gallbladder, is a rare cancer with just over 12,000 new cases expected to be confirmed in the U.S. in 2018. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
The gallbladder is a small, pear-shaped organ which sits under the liver on the right side of the body.
Treatment of gallbladder cancer depends on the size of the cancer and whether it has already spread at the time of diagnosis. If it is diagnosed early enough, it can be cured by removing the gallbladder, part of the liver and associated lymph nodes. A person does not need a gallbladder to live a normal life.
There are normally no early symptoms of gallbladder cancer, or they may go unnoticed,
This condition most commonly affects people older than 65. Women are affected over two times more often than men. Gallstones and persistent inflammation of the gallbladder, known as [cholecystitis](https://ada.com/conditions/cholecystitis/), are known to increase the risk of gallbladder cancer, though most people with these conditions never develop gallbladder cancer.[2](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
If you are worried that you or someone you know may have this condition, use the [symptom checker](https://ada.com/app/) works
## Types of gallbladder cancer
There are different types of gallbladder cancer, with different treatments and outcomes, depending on which cells the cancer develops in. For example:
### Adenocarcinomas
About 85 percent of gallbladder cancers are adenocarcinomas developing from the gland cells in the lining of the gallbladder, which normally produce mucus.
There are two main types of gallbladder adenocarcinoma: [3](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [4](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
  * Non-papillary adenocarcinoma:
  * Papillary adenocarcinoma:


Other types of gallbladder cancer are extremely rare. These include: [3](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [4](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
### Squamous cell cancers
This develops from the skin-like cells that line the gallbladder. Squamous cell cancers are treated similarly to adenocarcinomas, with removal of the gallbladder as the best treatment, if still possible at the time of diagnosis.
### Adenosquamous carcinomas
These have both squamous cancer cells and glandular cancer cells. Adenosquamous cancers are treated similarly to adenocarcinomas, with removal of the gallbladder as the best treatment if still possible at the time of diagnosis.
## Symptoms of gallbladder cancer
Gallbladder cancer does not normally have early symptoms. Signs of gallbladder cancer tend to appear when the tumor is fairly large and may have spread.
The most common gallbladder cancer symptoms include: [5](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [6](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
Stomach pain:
Nausea and/or vomiting:
Yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes, known as jaundice:[bilirubin](https://ada.com/biomarkers/bilirubin/), building up in the blood and settling in different areas of the body.
Lumps on the right side of the stomach:
Less common signs of gallbladder cancer may include: [5](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [6](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
  * Loss of appetite and/or weight
  * Indigestion, such as bloating and burping
  * Swollen stomach
  * Fever
  * Itchiness
  * Dark urine
  * Greasy or light-colored feces


Good to know:
If you are worried that you or someone you know may have this condition, use the [symptom checker](https://ada.com/app/) works
## Causes and risk factors
It is not known what causes most gallbladder cancers. However, there are factors that can increase the risk of developing it.
Risk factors for gallbladder cancer may include: [7](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
  * History of gallbladder disease:[cholelithiasis](https://ada.com/conditions/symptomatic-cholelithiasis/), [cholecystitis](https://ada.com/conditions/cholecystitis/), gallbladder polyps, porcelain gallbladder, and bile duct abnormalities increase risk for gallbladder cancer.
  * Being female:
  * Being over the age of about 65
  * Family history
  * Being obese:
  * Chronic typhoid:
  * Ethnicity and geography:
  * Being of particular ethnic groups:


Good to know:
## Gallbladder cancer and COVID-19
COVID-19 can cause severe symptoms in patients being treated for anal cancer. This is because cancer therapy weakens the immune system, which puts you at a higher risk of contracting the coronavirus. Taking the necessary precautions and getting tested as soon as possible if you start experiencing symptoms is essential. Talk to your doctor to determine whether you're eligible for [antiviral medication](https://ada.com/covid/antiviral-medication/). 
## Diagnosis of gallbladder cancer
Gallbladder cancer can be difficult to detect and diagnose for several reasons:
  * There are normally no noticeable signs or symptoms in its early stages
  * The typical symptoms are similar to the symptoms of many other conditions


For this reason, gallbladder cancer is sometimes found when the gallbladder is removed to treat another condition.
Otherwise, as the first step, a doctor will typically take the person’s medical history and perform a physical examination. In addition, a doctor may perform the following diagnostic tests: [8](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
### Blood tests
Blood tests may be done to test for: [8](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
Liver and gallbladder function:
Tumor markers:
### Imaging tests
There are many possible imaging tests that may be used to test for gallbladder cancer: [8](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
Ultrasound:
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP):[keyhole surgery](https://ada.com/keyhole-surgery/).
Computed tomography (CT) scan:
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP):
These imaging methods may be used to create a picture of the structures inside the body. These may help:
  * To look for areas that may contain cancer
  * To help a doctor guide a biopsy needle to take a tissue sample from a suspicious area
  * To see how far cancer has spread
  * To help check if the treatment is working
  * To see if there are signs that the cancer has returned after treatment


### Biopsy
A biopsy is often the only way to be certain of a gallbladder cancer diagnosis. This involves removal of a small amount of tissue or sometimes fluid
## Treatment
The treatment of gallbladder cancer depends on the size of the cancer, the exact type of cancer and whether the cancer has spread. The combination of these factors decides the stage of the cancer.
The three main treatments used are: [9](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9")
  * Surgery
  * Radiation therapy
  * Chemotherapy


Alternative treatments are also being developed in clinical trials.
### Surgery
If the gallbladder cancer is found early enough and has not yet spread, then the gallbladder and surrounding tissues will be removed in a surgery known as cholecystectomy.[10](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
However, most gallbladder cancers are found when they have spread too far to be removed by surgery, when they are known as unresectable. Doctors may then focus on treatments to relieve symptoms and help an affected person to live longer.
Certain types of surgery are sometimes used to relieve symptoms caused by the tumor blocking the bile duct and bile building up in the gallbladder: [9](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") [11](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
#### Biliary bypass
This involves a doctor cutting the gallbladder or bile duct in an area before the blockage and sewing it to the small intestine to create a pathway around the blocked area.
#### Endoscopic stent
A thin tube called a stent is fed in from the mouth and through the digestive system to drain bile that has built up in the area, either into the small intestine or into a bag outside of the body.
#### Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
If endoscopic stent surgery is not possible, then the stent is placed by cutting the skin. This procedure may be done to relieve jaundice before other surgical procedures are carried out
### Gallbladder cancer radiotherapy and chemotherapy
Also known as radiation therapy, radiotherapy uses X-rays to destroy cancer cells.
Chemotherapy is the use of medication to destroy cancer cells. Most of the chemotherapy medications for gallbladder cancer are administered into the bloodstream, though some may be given in tablet form.
Radiotherapy and chemotherapy may be used to treat gallbladder cancer, but, used alone, they are unlikely to cure this type of cancer. Radiotherapy and chemotherapy are not usually used to treat early gallbladder cancer[12](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12") often in combination with each other.
Radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy may be used to treat gallbladder cancer in the following cases: [13](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:13 "See Footnote 13") [14](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14")
Palliative care:[chemotherapy](https://ada.com/chemotherapy-side-effects/), cause side effects, and may themselves require palliative care.
After surgery to remove tumors:
As part of treatment for advanced gallbladder cancer:
Good to know:[chemotherapy side effects](https://ada.com/chemotherapy-side-effects/)).
## Gallbladder cancer staging
Once gallbladder cancer is diagnosed, doctors will try to find out whether it has spread and if so, how far, in a process known as staging.
Gallbladder cancers usually undergo pathologic staging, which is determined during surgery to remove the cancerous tissue.. [15](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:15 "See Footnote 15")
The cancer maybe given a number stage from 1 to 4. The lower the number, the less the cancer has spread. 0 is the earliest stage gallbladder cancer, also known as carcinoma in situ.
Gallbladder cancer is considered to be stage 3 or stage 4 gallbladder cancer once the tumor has grown through all of the outer layers of the gallbladder.
The staging system most often used to determine the stage for gallbladder cancer is the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM system.
#### Subtype
Adenocarcinomas and papillary carcinomas may have a better prognosis than rarer cancers, such as squamous and adenosquamous carcinomas.
#### Lymphovascular invasion
Gallbladder cancers, which are seen under the microscope in small blood vessels or lymph vessels, tend to have a poor prognosis, as there’s a greater chance they have spread outside of the gallbladder.
#### Resection extent
Resectable cancers – those that are thought to be completely removable by surgery – have a better outlook. Most gallbladder cancers are unresectable by the time they’re found, as they have already spread too far or are in too difficult a place to be entirely removed by surgery.
## Other names for gallbladder cancer
  * Malignant neoplasm of gallbladder

[17](https://ada.com/conditions/gallbladder-cancer/#fn:17 "See Footnote 17")

## What is premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD)?
Premenstrual dysphoric disorder, abbreviated to PMDD, is a severe type of [premenstrual syndrome (PMS)](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-syndrome/). The majority of people who menstruate experience cyclical physical and emotional changes in the days leading up to their period, such as tender breasts and mood changes. The type and extent of premenstrual symptoms experienced varies from person to person; PMS may be very mild or more serious. In a small number of women, monthly PMS symptoms may be severe, possibly leading to a diagnosis of PMDD. [1](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
Symptoms of PMDD are generally similar to symptoms of PMS, but are significantly more intense.[2](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") Common symptoms of PMDD include: [3](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") ref4
  * Irritability
  * Anger
  * Anxiety
  * [Depression](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/)
  * Tiredness
  * Tension
  * Bloating


PMDD symptoms typically develop roughly 5-14 days before menstruation and generally interfere with a person’s wellbeing and daily life, for example by making interpersonal conflict more likely. Symptoms of premenstrual dysphoric disorder should go away within a few days of menstruating.[4](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
Concerned that you or a loved one may have this condition? Start your symptom assessment in the 
The exact causes of PMDD are not clearly understood, though there is a clear link to the hormonal changes that a woman experiences as part of her monthly menstrual cycle. Some research suggests that women who have PMS or PMDD may be sensitive to rising levels of the [hormone progesterone](https://ada.com/biomarkers/progesterone/), the level of which increases after the release of an egg from the ovaries (ovulation) each month. It has been suggested that fluctuating hormone levels, that occur during the menstrual cycle, may affect levels of the neurotransmitter serotonin in the brain and thus impact a person’s mood. [6](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
Treatment for PMDD is available.[2](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
  * Lifestyle changes
  * Supplements and natural remedies
  * Psychotherapy
  * Antidepressant medication
  * Hormone therapy, e.g. birth control pills
  * Surgery


With treatment strategies, most women are able to effectively manage the symptoms of PMDD. The condition may seem to come and go, and some months may be worse than others. PMDD will not be present after menopause.[6](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [7](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
PMDD is thought to affect an estimated 5-8 percent of women of all races and backgrounds. [4](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [8](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") Because many of the symptoms can be caused by – or mistaken for – other conditions, e.g. [depression](https://ada.com/signs-of-depression/) or [thyroiditis](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/), it is necessary to undergo a thorough health check before a diagnosis of premenstrual dysphoric disorder can be made. [6](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
Feeling unwell? Get a symptom assessment with the symptom checker works before you try it for yourself.
## PMDD symptoms
Symptoms of premenstrual dysphoric disorder may vary from person to person and from one menstrual cycle to the next, but commonly include the following: [3](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [4](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") [2](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [6](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [7](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7") [8](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [9](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9")
### Psychological symptoms
  * Severe irritability; this is often the most prevalent symptom [8](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
  * Extreme anger or aggression, rage
  * Severe anxiety and/or tension
  * Low self-esteem
  * Lasting sadness
  * Feelings of hopelessness
  * Feeling overwhelmed or out of control
  * Low mood or depression
  * Mood swings
  * Loss of interest in activities that are usually enjoyable
  * Forgetfulness and difficulty concentrating
  * Sleep disturbances, e.g. sleeping more or less than usual
  * Appetite changes and/or food cravings


### Physical symptoms
  * Tiredness
  * Lethargy, lack of energy
  * Breast swelling and tenderness or pain
  * Bloating
  * Nausea
  * Diarrhea
  * Weight gain
  * [Headaches](https://ada.com/conditions/headache/)
  * Muscle and/or joint aches
  * Swelling of the hands and/or feet


While mild forms of these psychological and physical symptoms may be experienced in regular PMS, many of them are more extreme in PMDD. Symptoms are typically so severe that they interfere with the person’s ability to go about their daily life,[10](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10")
PMDD symptoms typically develop between a few days and two weeks before menstruation, worsening in the build-up to and peaking about two days before, the period. The symptoms tend to disappear within a few days after the beginning of menstruation and are absent until ovulation has once again occurred.
## PMDD causes
While it is not yet completely understood what causes symptoms of premenstrual dysphoric disorder or premenstrual syndrome to develop in certain women, it is known that changing hormone levels play a key role. [6](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
It is thought that fluctuations in hormones following the release of an egg (ovulation) as part of the monthly menstrual cycle may affect the levels of serotonin and other neurotransmitters in the brain, causing many of the psychological symptoms that characterize PMDD. Some women may be more sensitive than others to the effects of an increased level of progesterone in the body, which naturally occurs after ovulation, in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. [8](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
Today, it is generally agreed that PMDD is not caused by an “imbalance” in a person’s hormones,[6](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
### Risk factors for PMDD
A number of factors may make a person more likely to develop premenstrual syndrome or premenstrual dysphoric disorder. It is thought that these may include: [6](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [8](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [11](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11") [9](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") [12](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:12 "See Footnote 12") [13](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:13 "See Footnote 13")
  * Family history of PMS or PMDD
  * Personal or family history of mental health conditions, e.g. [depression](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/) or [anxiety](https://ada.com/conditions/generalized-anxiety-disorder/)
  * Stress
  * Being overweight
  * Being in one’s mid-20s or one’s 30s, which seems to be the average age range of onset; PMDD may worsen with age [14](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14") [15](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:15 "See Footnote 15") [16](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:16 "See Footnote 16")
  * History of early-life abuse


## Diagnosis of PMDD
Diagnosis of premenstrual dysphoric disorder can only be made by a medical professional,[blood tests](https://ada.com/blood-test-results/) may be ordered to rule out other conditions that may be causing symptoms, such as [anemia](https://ada.com/conditions/anemia/) or an underlying [thyroid disorder](https://ada.com/conditions/thyroiditis/). [3](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [8](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
The doctor will ask questions about the symptoms being experienced. To provide detailed information on when they occur and how often, it is recommended that anyone who is concerned that they may have PMDD, keep a daily symptom diary or chart for 2-3 months, including severity ratings of symptoms and dates of menstruation.[3](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [9](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") Details can be recorded in a notebook or by using a specialized app designed for people affected by PMDD, several of which exist. The free Ada app can also help track symptoms. [how it works](https://ada.com/app/).
### Criteria for a diagnosis of premenstrual dysphoric disorder
According to the criteria set out in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5), for a PMDD diagnosis to be made, at least five of the following symptoms must be present cyclically during most menstrual cycles[8](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
  * Depressed mood, feeling hopeless, negative thoughts about oneself
  * Anxiety, tension, feeling “on edge”
  * Unstable emotions, e.g. suddenly becoming sad or a heightened sensitivity to rejection
  * Lasting anger or irritability, or an increase in fighting with loved ones
  * Loss of interest in activities that are normally enjoyed
  * Difficulty concentrating
  * Lethargy, becoming tired easily or lack of energy
  * Appetite changes, eating too much or food cravings
  * Sleep disturbances, including sleeping too much or insomnia
  * Feeling overwhelmed or out of control
  * Physical symptoms, e.g. tender breasts, headaches, body pain, bloating


For a diagnosis of PMDD to be made, the symptoms need to be present most of the time during the week before menstruation and go away within a few days after menstruation begins, being absent in the week after the period.
Additional criteria require that: [8](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
  * Symptoms must be so severe that they significantly interfere with the person’s daily functioning
  * Symptoms must not be caused by another disorder, e.g. [depression](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/) or [bipolar disorder](https://ada.com/conditions/bipolar-affective-disorder/)
  * Symptoms must be documented and rated on a daily basis by the person, for a minimum of two menstrual cycles


### Differentiating PMDD from bipolar disorder and other conditions
In many cases, a person’s symptoms may be related to a different condition. Symptoms of [major depression](https://ada.com/conditions/depressive-episode/), [anxiety](https://ada.com/conditions/generalized-anxiety-disorder/), [bipolar disorder](https://ada.com/conditions/bipolar-affective-disorder/) and other mental health conditions may become worse in the build-up to menstruation, which may lead to them being mistaken for PMS or PMDD. This is called premenstrual exacerbation (PME) of symptoms. [9](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") [17](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:17 "See Footnote 17")
It is generally possible to tell the difference between PMDD and another disorder by tracking symptoms over a few months.[pregnancy](https://ada.com/conditions/pregnancy/) or after [menopause](https://ada.com/conditions/menopause/), PMDD symptoms will not be present. Differentiating PMDD from other mental health conditions is important, as treatment approaches differ.[9](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") [17](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:17 "See Footnote 17")
It is possible to have both PMDD and another condition,[17](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:17 "See Footnote 17")
## PMDD treatment
There are a number of possible treatments for premenstrual dysphoric disorder. These include antidepressant medications, hormone therapies, lifestyle changes and other remedies.
### Medication
Medication recommended for the treatment of PMDD includes antidepressants, hormone therapy and painkillers.
#### Antidepressant medication
In many cases, a doctor will recommend a low dose of an antidepressant for the treatment of PMDD. This will usually take the form of a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) or selective serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI), which may increase the levels of serotonin in the brain and provide relief from symptoms of PMDD, particularly mood symptoms. This type of medication does not suppress ovulation. While considered effective for many people, SSRIs may cause unpleasant side-effects in some women and might not be suitable for everyone. [6](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [8](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [11](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11") [9](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9") [14](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14")
#### Hormone therapy
Birth control:[estrogen](https://ada.com/hormones/estradiol/) and progesterone, the hormones involved in the menstrual cycle. By preventing ovulation from occurring each month, these hormonal contraceptive pills may help to reduce premenstrual symptoms. However, they may cause unpleasant side-effects and may not provide relief for everyone, even worsening cyclical symptoms in some cases. [3](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") [4](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") [6](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [8](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [14](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14")
Estrogen patch:[6](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [8](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [11](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
Good to know:[5](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [11](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists:[osteoporosis](https://ada.com/conditions/osteoporosis/) that may occur with long-term use. [6](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [8](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [11](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:11 "See Footnote 11")
#### Other medication
Benzodiazepines:highly addictive and should be used with extreme caution,[9](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9")
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs):[4](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") [8](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
### Psychotherapy
Some women may find talk therapy in the form of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) helpful in the management of PMDD symptoms. [6](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [14](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14") CBT may be recommended as part of a combined treatment approach or, in some cases, on its own.
### Lifestyle and dietary changes
Reducing stress:[2](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2") [6](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [14](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14")

### Supplements and natural remedies
Before taking any supplement or natural remedy for PMDD, it is important to consult a doctor. Some supplements and natural remedies may cause side-effects, or interact or interfere with medications, and may not be suitable for everyone.
Calcium:[8](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8") [14](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:14 "See Footnote 14") [18](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:18 "See Footnote 18") [19](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:19 "See Footnote 19")
**[Magnesium](https://ada.com/micronutrients/magnesium/):** Though the results of studies have been mixed, and further research is needed, it is thought that taking a magnesium supplement may help to relieve some premenstrual symptoms in some women, such as water retention. ### Surgery
In severe cases of PMDD where other treatments have not been effective or suitable, surgery may be considered.[menopause](https://ada.com/conditions/menopause/), PMDD symptoms can be expected to disappear permanently.
To prevent complications that can arise from early menopause, it is typically necessary to take estrogen in the form of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) after the surgery. Having a hysterectomy prevents a woman from being able to fall pregnant, so it is not considered an option for someone who may want to have children. Before recommending surgery, a doctor will typically suggest inducing a temporary menopause with (GnRH) agonists to see how well the person responds. [10](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:10 "See Footnote 10") [6](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6") [5](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5") [18](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:18 "See Footnote 18") [19](https://ada.com/conditions/premenstrual-dysphoric-disorder-pmdd/#fn:19 "See Footnote 19")

Q: Are PMDD and PCOS linked?

PCOS is characterized by cysts on the ovaries and can cause irregular or absent menstruation, as well as other symptoms like excess hair growth and weight gain. It may also be associated with an increased risk of depression, anxiety and/or sleep disorders. # Vitamin E
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on September 11, 2024 at 2:00 PM GMT+3
## On this page
  * [What is vitamin E?](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#what-is-vitamin-e)
  * [What is vitamin E good for?](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#what-is-vitamin-e-good-for)
  * [What are vitamin E deficiency symptoms?](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#what-are-vitamin-e-deficiency-symptoms)
  * [What is the recommended intake of vitamin E?](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#what-is-the-recommended-intake-of-vitamin-e)
  * [What foods have vitamin E?](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#what-foods-have-vitamin-e)
  * [What are side effects of vitamin E?](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#what-are-side-effects-of-vitamin-e)
  * [When is a vitamin E test useful?](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#when-is-a-vitamin-e-test-useful)
  * [Vitamin E FAQ](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#vitamin-e-faq)


* * *
Share this article:
Our body needs vitamin E to maintain healthy skin, vision, and immune system
Vitamin E is an antioxidant which is believed to have strong beneficial health effects. Vitamin E is one of the most commonly consumed dietary supplements in the United States. [1](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
What are the exact benefits of vitamin E? Should everyone take vitamin E? Let’s resolve these questions.
Do you think that your Vitamin E levels might be too low or too high?
## What is vitamin E?
Vitamin E is a fat-soluble vitamin which means the body can only absorb it from food if eaten with fat. Like other [micronutrients](https://ada.com/micronutrients/) and vitamins, our body cannot produce vitamin EVitamin E is naturally contained in a variety of plant-based foods such as nuts, seeds, vegetables, and plant oils[2](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
As an antioxidant, vitamin E protects the body from damage caused by free radicals. Free radicals are aggressive oxygen compounds which form during normal metabolic reactions but also as a result of UV light or cigarette smoke. These substances can damage tissues or cells, if not deactivated by antioxidants.
Scientific research is still exploring other possible functions and health-promoting effects of vitamin E.
## What is vitamin E good for?
Vitamin E protects the blood vessels and prevents clots from forming. Vitamin E is also one of the most effective nutrients for regulating immune function. This makes it a significant contributor to combating bacterial and viral infections. [3](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
There are many benefits of vitamin E for the skin. It protects us from the harmful effects of sun exposure, and so it’s a common ingredient in sunscreen and skincare products.
But aside from our skin, what else is vitamin E good for? Researchers are currently exploring if high doses of vitamin E can help prevent chronic diseases
  * Heart disease:[4](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") Several controlled trials could not find any preventive effects. [4](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4") [5](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
  * Cancer[6](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
  * Neurodegenerative diseases:[Alzheimer’s](https://ada.com/conditions/alzheimers-disease/), [Parkinson’s](https://ada.com/conditions/parkinsons-disease/), or ALS. [6](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")


More research is needed to fully understand the effects and health benefits of vitamin E. However, it’s important to know that there is no benefit to our bodies if we consume more vitamin E than we need.
## What are vitamin E deficiency symptoms?
Vitamin E is found in many foods and supplements. Therefore, most people consume enough vitamin E through their diet and deficiency is rare. Usually, only people with certain medical conditions lack vitamin E[pancreatitis](https://ada.com/conditions/chronic-pancreatitis/), [cystic fibrosis](https://ada.com/conditions/cystic-fibrosis/), or digestive disorders sometimes develop a deficiency.
Symptoms of vitamin E deficiency include[7](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
  * Poor immune function
  * [Retinopathy](https://ada.com/conditions/hypertensive-retinopathy/), a damaged retina which leads to impaired vision
  * Ataxia, a condition which affects movement and coordination
  * Muscular weakness
  * Cardiac arrhythmia.


Read more about [vitamin deficiency tests](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-deficiency-test/) if you believe you might not get enough vitamins.
Do you think that your Vitamin E levels might be too low?
## What is the recommended intake of vitamin E?
For healthy adults, the daily “Recommended Dietary Allowance” (RDA) for vitamin E is 15 mg. The RDA for pregnant women remains at 15 mg, whereas lactating women are advised to get 19 mg per day. [7](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
## What foods have vitamin E?
As only plants can produce vitamin E, they are very good sources of vitamin E[8](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#fn:8 "See Footnote 8")
  * Vegetable oils: wheat germ oil, rapeseed oil, sunflower oil, soybean oil
  * Nuts: almonds, hazelnuts, peanuts, pine nuts
  * Green leafy vegetables: spinach, broccoli
  * Sunflower seeds
  * Avocado
  * Tomato
  * Mango
  * Kiwi


## What are side effects of vitamin E?
Vitamin E obtained from food is not harmful. However, there have been some reports of negative effects from vitamin E supplements. Among these are muscle weakness, nausea, diarrhea and fatigue. Taking higher doses may increase the risk of side effects. [9](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#fn:9 "See Footnote 9")
If you take vitamin E supplements, you should avoid taking too much. A daily dose of up to 540 mg is considered safe and unlikely to be harmful. [2](https://ada.com/micronutrients/vitamin-e/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
## When is a vitamin E test useful?
A vitamin E test is useful for people who belong to one of the risk groups and experience typical vitamin E deficiency symptoms. If you have an intestinal disease or cystic fibrosis you belong to the risk group.
If you also experience neurological symptoms such as ataxia and muscle weakness, this may indicate a vitamin E deficiency. In this case, a vitamin E test will help to find the cause of your symptoms.
## Find out more about your symptoms
## Vitamin E FAQ
Q: What is vitamin E for?  
A: Vitamin E is a fat-soluble vitamin and an antioxidant. It protects our organs, tissues, and cells from harmful substances called free radicals.
Q: What is vitamin E oil?  
A: Vitamin E oil is a common ingredient in
Q: What side effects can vitamin E cause?  
A: When consumed from food, vitamin E is unlikely to cause side effects. Supplementing higher doses of vitamin E may cause muscle weakness, diarrhea, and nausea. The most significant risk is bleeding, with doses >1000 mg per day.
Q: When do I need to seek medical help?  
A: Neurological symptoms coupled with certain medical conditions may indicate a vitamin E deficiency. The risk group includes people with CF or intestinal diseases. If you experience these conditions, think about seeking medical help.

# COVID-19: can COVID affect your period?
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on April 29, 2024 at 10:30 AM GMT+3

## Overview
  * COVID-19 can affect your period. 
  * Stress and anxiety due to the pandemic can affect your menstrual cycle.
  * The COVID vaccine can cause changes to your menstrual cycle. 
  * Changes in your period due to COVID-19 often resolve themselves quite quickly.


Think you might be experiencing COVID-19 symptoms
COVID has often been related to menstrual changes such as a late period, a missed period, and various changes in the length and volume of menstruation. This article will discuss in detail how COVID-19 affects your period and in what way COVID vaccination is related to changes in your menstrual cycle. 
## Can COVID-19 affect your period?
Getting [COVID ](https://ada.com/covid/)may affect your period. Scientists studied the link between COVID and the menstrual cycle and concluded that getting infected with the coronavirus may result in temporary changes in the menstrual cycle.[1](https://ada.com/covid/can-covid-affect-your-period/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * The coronavirus infection has been shown to cause stress, which leads to disruptions in the production of ovulatory hormones and results in menstrual irregularities. 
  * The coronavirus has an affinity to bind to ACE-2 receptors ovaries and the endometrium[pregnancy](https://ada.com/conditions/pregnancy/), this inner lining sheds and exits the body via the vaginal canal. If the coronavirus binds to the ACE-2 receptors in the ovaries and the endometrium, the virus may affect these structures directly and cause menstrual irregularities. 


Besides an infection with COVID-19, other factors may affect your period[1](https://ada.com/covid/can-covid-affect-your-period/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * Extreme emotions
  * Hormonal changes
  * Gynecological changes
  * Autoimmune disorders
  * Nutrition 
  * Genetics
  * Infection with other viruses or bacteria
  * Lifestyle changes 


This means that besides the actual infection with the coronavirus, COVID and menstrual cycle changes may also be explained by the stress, anxiety, and depression
Studies also concluded that the link between COVID and menstrual cycle changes depends on the severity of your infection. Women who reported more severe symptoms of COVID-19 were also more likely to experience changes in their menstrual cycle after the infection.[joint and muscle pain](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-body-aches/) and [headaches](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-symptom-headache/). Women who have a milder case of COVID tend to notice fewer changes to their period.[2](https://ada.com/covid/can-covid-affect-your-period/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
Concerned that you or a loved one may have COVID-19? Start your symptom assessment in the [app](https://ada.com/app/) first.
## The COVID vaccine and your menstrual cycle
There’s not only a link between COVID-19 and your period but also between the COVID vaccine and your period[1](https://ada.com/covid/can-covid-affect-your-period/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") [3](https://ada.com/covid/can-covid-affect-your-period/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
  * Early menstruation
  * Late menstruation
  * Bleeding in between 2 periods
  * Heavier menstrual bleeding
  * Lighter menstrual bleeding
  * Shorter period
  * Longer period   
  
The most common way that COVID shots affect your period is by temporarily increasing the length of your cycle. However, other changes to the menstrual cycle are reported frequently as well. These menstrual cycle changes are similar across different types of vaccines.[4](https://ada.com/covid/can-covid-affect-your-period/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")


## How long do menstrual changes persist after COVID infection?
Slight changes in menstruation after COVID-19 or COVID vaccination usually resolve within the next cycle.[5](https://ada.com/covid/can-covid-affect-your-period/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
## The effect of COVID treatment on your period
Different [COVID treatments](https://ada.com/covid/treatment-guide/) are available, depending on your [risk profile](https://ada.com/covid/covid-19-high-risk-groups/) and the severity of your symptoms. If you’ve been hospitalized due to your COVID-19 infection, then it may be that you’ve been treated with dexamethasone[6](https://ada.com/covid/can-covid-affect-your-period/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
## Wrapping up
COVID-19 can affect your period in multiple ways. The infection, the stress and anxiety related to it, and vaccination may cause changes in your menstrual cycle. Luckily, these changes usually do not last long and are not a cause for concern in most cases. 
## Find out more about your symptoms
## FAQs
Q: How does COVID affect your period?   
A: COVID can affect your period by disrupting your hormonal system or binding to ACE-2 receptors in the ovaries or the endometrium. Stress caused by COVID-19 can also be an essential factor for menstrual changes. 
Q: How long can COVID affect your period?   
A: The changes in your menstrual cycle usually only last for one cycle, after which they usually return to normal. If your symptoms persist, then it’s recommended to consult your healthcare provider. 
Q: Is it normal if I have COVID that my period is late?   
A: COVID can cause a number of changes to the menstrual cycle, such as a late period, but also an early period, bleeding in between periods, heavier or lighter menstrual bleeding and a shorter or a longer period.

# Glomerulonefritis postestreptocócica
Escrito por nuestro [Equipo de Profesionales Médicos](https://ada.com/es/team/medical/)
Actualizado el 25 de julio de 2022, 8:33 EET
## En esta página
  * [Resumen](https://ada.com/es/conditions/post-streptococcal-glomerulonephritis/#resumen)
  * [Riesgos](https://ada.com/es/conditions/post-streptococcal-glomerulonephritis/#riesgos)
  * [Síntomas](https://ada.com/es/conditions/post-streptococcal-glomerulonephritis/#sintomas)
  * [Diagnóstico](https://ada.com/es/conditions/post-streptococcal-glomerulonephritis/#diagnostico)
  * [Tratamiento](https://ada.com/es/conditions/post-streptococcal-glomerulonephritis/#tratamiento)
  * [Prevención](https://ada.com/es/conditions/post-streptococcal-glomerulonephritis/#prevencion)
  * [Pronóstico](https://ada.com/es/conditions/post-streptococcal-glomerulonephritis/#pronostico)
  * [Otras denominaciones](https://ada.com/es/conditions/post-streptococcal-glomerulonephritis/#otras-denominaciones)


* * *
Comparte este artículo:
## Resumen
La glomerulonefritis posestreptocócica es un problema renal que se presenta después de una infección con una bacteria llamada Streptococcus. Generalmente la bacteria estreptocócica causa infecciones de las amígdalas y la piel. Este problema tiende a afectar a niños entre los cinco y doce años y a adultos mayores de sesenta. Los síntomas son hinchazón de las piernas, manos y cara, la aparición de sangre en la orina y la mayoría de las personas también presenta presión arterial alta. Generalmente no existe un tratamiento específico, pero la infección se debe tratar y es posible que se tengan que tomar medidas para asistir los riñones mientras se recuperan. Los niños suelen recuperarse muy bien en unas seis a ocho semanas. Los adultos tienen más probabilidades de presentar complicaciones, incluso presión arterial alta y daño renal.
¿Te sientes mal? Revisa tus síntomas con la app verificador de síntomas antes de probar nuestra app.
## Riesgos
Los riñones son dos órganos ubicados en la espalda, debajo de las costillas, y son responsables de filtrar las toxinas de la sangre y mantener el equilibrio de líquidos y electrolitos. En la glomerulonefritis, se produce inflamación e hinchazón de las unidades de filtración del riñón (los glomérulos). Puede aparecer después de una infección, aunque existen varias causas posibles, incluyendo condiciones autonimunes (cuando el sistema inmunitario comienza a atacar por error los tejidos sanos del cuerpo), diabetes y algunos tipos de cáncer. La glomerulonefritis después de una infección con la bacteria estreptococo es una de las causas más comunes de enfermedad renal en niños de todo el mundo, aunque es poco frecuente en países con buen acceso a la atención médica. El estreptococo frecuentemente causa amigdalitis e infecciones de la piel, y se cree que causa glomerulonefritis porque el sistema inmune confunde las células del riñón con la bacteria estreptocócica. Esta condición es más común en niños de cinco a doce años y en adultos mayores de sesenta, y tiende a afectar a hombres y mujeres por igual.
## Síntomas
Los síntomas pueden variar de persona a persona dependiendo de la gravedad, los más comunes son orina roja o marrón e hinchazón de los pies y las piernas. En las personas con glomerulonefritis la presión arterial aumenta, pero esto no suele causar síntomas. Otras molestias como dolor en el costado, una sensación de debilidad y orinar cantidades pequeñas pueden acompañar los síntomas mencionados. Algunas personas pueden sentir dificultad para respirar o tener tos. Los síntomas comienzan dentro de las tres semanas de una infección bacteriana.
## Diagnóstico
El diagnóstico se puede sospechar en base a los síntomas y un examen físico en una persona que recientemente se sintió mal debido a una infección bacteriana. Los análisis de sangre y orina ayudan a confirmar el diagnóstico y son necesarios para vigilar la función renal y la recuperación. También se suele realizar una ecografía de los riñones. Si el diagnóstico es incierto, es posible que sea necesario tomar una muestra pequeña del riñón para analizarla (biopsia) en busca de la causa de los problemas renales.
## Tratamiento
El tratamiento de la glomerulonefritis posestreptocócica suele implicar tratar la infección bacteriana (si es necesario), los síntomas y a su vez vigilar y asistir el funcionamiento renal. No existe un tratamiento específico para estos casos y se pueden usar medicamentos diuréticos para reducir la cantidad de líquido del cuerpo, junto a otros medicamentos para bajar la presión arterial. Si hubo un daño renal severo, es posible que sea necesario realizar diálisis para ayudar a la persona mientras se recuperan los riñones.
## Prevención
El diagnóstico y el tratamiento de la amigdalitis bacteriana pueden ayudar a impedir que algunas personas desenvuelvan glomerulonefritis posestreptocócica.
## Pronóstico
Este tipo de glomerulonefritis suele mejorar en seis a ocho semanas y la mayoría de las personas se recupera sin quedar con un daño renal duradero. Los adultos y los niños que tienen episodios recurrentes de esta glomerulonefritis tienen más probabilidades de desarrollar problemas renales y presión arterial alta, incluso muchos años después del episodio original de glomerulonefritis.
## Otras denominaciones
  * inflamación del riñón luego de una infección bacteriana

# What are my GDPR privacy rights?
The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) governs data collected by companies within the European Economic Area since May 25, 2018. Through GDPR, Ada ensures the responsible management of your data, offering you greater control over your privacy preferences and rights regarding its processing.
When you create an Ada account, your data is securely stored. If you [delete your account](https://ada.com/help/how-to-delete-account/), your data will be permanently removed. However, in compliance with legal obligations, certain assessment data is retained even after account deactivation. Rest assured, this data is not stored with information directly identifying you and is used solely to monitor the performance of our medical device. 
Moreover, you have the right to inquire about Ada's data processing and obtain a copy of the information you've shared with us. You may make this request at any time via [our website](https://ada.com/contact/support/) or via email at 
Have more questions? [Submit a request](https://ada.com/contact/support/)

# Política de Privacidad de Datos de Salud del Consumidor de Ada Health, Inc.
19 de marzo de 2025
## En esta página
  * [1. Categorías de Datos de Salud del Consumidor que recopilamos](https://ada.com/es/us/consumer-health-data-privacy-policy/#section-1)
  * [2. ¿Cuáles son las fuentes donde recopilamos Datos de Salud del Consumidor?](https://ada.com/es/us/consumer-health-data-privacy-policy/#section-2)
  * [3. ¿Con qué propósitos recopilamos tus Datos de Salud del Consumidor?](https://ada.com/es/us/consumer-health-data-privacy-policy/#section-3)
  * [4. ¿Qué categorías de Datos de Salud del Consumidor compartimos?](https://ada.com/es/us/consumer-health-data-privacy-policy/#section-4)
  * [5. Cómo ejercer tus derechos con respecto a tus Datos de Salud del Consumidor](https://ada.com/es/us/consumer-health-data-privacy-policy/#section-5)
  * [6. Actualizaciones a esta Política](https://ada.com/es/us/consumer-health-data-privacy-policy/#section-6)
  * [7. Contáctanos](https://ada.com/es/us/consumer-health-data-privacy-policy/#section-7)


Ada Health, Inc. (“Ada”), su empresa matriz, Ada Health GmbH, y sus afiliadas se comprometen a procesar, usar, transferir y gestionar la información personal de acuerdo con las leyes de privacidad aplicables y esta Política. Esta Política de Privacidad de Datos de Salud del Consumidor (“Política”) detalla cómo Ada recopila, usa, transfiere y comparte tus “Datos de Salud del Consumidor” según la definición de la Ley de Washington Mi Salud Mis Datos (“MHMDA”), la Ley de Privacidad de Datos de Salud del Consumidor de Nevada (“NCHDPA”), la Ley de Privacidad de Datos de Connecticut (“CDPA”) u otras leyes de privacidad de la salud de EE. UU. Esta Política modifica la Política de Privacidad general de Ada.
Esta Política se aplica a los Datos de Salud del Consumidor que obtenemos cuando interactúas con Ada usando nuestra evaluación de salud y síntomas digital (“Ada Assess”) y otros servicios en línea o cuando te conectas con nosotros de cualquier otra manera (colectivamente, los “Servicios”).
En esta Política, "nosotros" y "nuestro/a/os/as" se refieren a Ada, y "tú y "tus” se refieren a cualquier individuo sobre quien recopilamos información personal.
## 1. Categorías de Datos de Salud del Consumidor que recopilamos
Los servicios de Ada son de naturaleza médica y dependen de que tú nos proporciones tus Datos de Salud del Consumidor. Cuando usas nuestros Servicios, recopilaremos las siguientes categorías de Datos de Salud del Consumidor al interactuar con nosotros.
  * Información sobre tu salud que proporcionas al usar nuestros Servicios, p. ej., descripción de tus síntomas, alergias, medicamentos, historial médico y quirúrgico, etc.
  * Información sobre tu salud que proporcionas cuando nos das tu opinión, presentas una queja o te pones en contacto con nosotros por cualquier otro motivo.
  * Información sobre tu condición física (p. ej., altura, peso, edad).
  * Información sobre factores de riesgo relacionados con tu salud (tabaquismo, diabetes, estado de embarazo, hipertensión, etc.).
  * Información sobre tu salud que generamos basándonos en los datos que ingresas, p. ej., posibles causas de tus síntomas, estado de riesgo, estado de elegibilidad para un tratamiento, consejos médicos, etc.
  * Cualquier información adicional relacionada contigo que nos proporciones directamente a través de nuestros Servicios o por otros medios, como por teléfono, correo electrónico o en persona.
  * Información que nos proporcionas a través de comentarios o encuestas voluntarias.


## 2. ¿Cuáles son las fuentes donde recopilamos Datos de Salud del Consumidor?
Solo recopilamos tus Datos de Salud del Consumidor a través de nuestros Servicios. Basándonos en la información que ingresas, generamos Datos de Salud del Consumidor adicionales, como posibles causas de tus síntomas, tu estado de riesgo o de aptitud para un tratamiento, u otra información sobre tu estado de salud física o mental pasado, presente o futuro.
## 3. ¿Con qué propósitos recopilamos tus Datos de Salud del Consumidor?
Ada recopila y usa los Datos de Salud del Consumidor con los siguientes propósitos:
  * Para proporcionarte los Servicios que solicitas.
  * Para contactarte con el fin de hacer un seguimiento sobre tu uso de nuestros Servicios o para proporcionarte actualizaciones relevantes sobre tu evaluación de salud.
  * Para asegurar que nuestros Servicios funcionen correctamente y sean seguros.
  * Para control de calidad, administración, y para ayudarnos a desarrollar productos y Servicios nuevos y mejorados.
  * Para cumplir con cualquier requisito de cualquier estatuto, regulación, norma y/o buena práctica aplicable.
  * Para responder a tus solicitudes, preguntas, quejas y otras consultas generales.
  * Para contactarte si se necesita información adicional para realizar la evaluación que solicitaste o si tu evaluación presenta resultados anómalos.
  * Para investigar, desarrollar y expandir nuestros Servicios.
  * Usos realizados bajo tu dirección y con tu consentimiento.
  * Para prevenir o detectar el abuso de nuestros Servicios o de cualquiera de nuestros derechos (y los intentos de hacerlo), y para hacer cumplir o aplicar esta Política y/o cualquier otro acuerdo, y para proteger nuestra propiedad o derechos (o los de otros).


## 4. ¿Qué categorías de Datos de Salud del Consumidor compartimos?
No compartimos tus Datos de Salud del Consumidor. Pondremos tus Datos de Salud del Consumidor a disposición de nuestros proveedores de servicios que procesan datos para Ada bajo los fines mencionados anteriormente. Esto incluye a la empresa matriz de Ada, Ada Health GmbH, y a otras afiliadas de Ada. Todos nuestros proveedores de servicios han firmado un acuerdo que garantiza que el procesamiento de datos se realice únicamente según las instrucciones de Ada.
Nos reservamos el derecho de divulgar tu información personal según lo exija la ley, cuando creamos que la divulgación es necesaria o apropiada para cumplir con un requisito regulatorio, un procedimiento judicial, una orden judicial, una solicitud gubernamental o un proceso legal que se nos haya notificado, o para proteger la seguridad, los derechos o la propiedad de nuestros clientes, el público, nosotros u otros.
Nos reservamos el derecho de transferir la información que mantenemos en caso de que vendamos o transfiramos la totalidad o una parte de nuestro negocio o activos. Si participamos en dicha venta o transferencia, haremos esfuerzos razonables para indicarle al destinatario que use tus Datos de Salud del Consumidor de una manera que sea consistente con esta Política. Después de dicha venta o transferencia, puedes contactar al destinatario con cualquier pregunta sobre sus prácticas de privacidad.
## 5. Cómo ejercer tus derechos con respecto a tus Datos de Salud del Consumidor
Como residente de Washington, Nevada, Connecticut o cualquier otro estado cuyas leyes de privacidad de datos de salud se apliquen a los servicios de Ada, puedes tener ciertos derechos con respecto al procesamiento de tus Datos de Salud del Consumidor:
  * El derecho a confirmar si Ada está recopilando, compartiendo o vendiendo tus datos de salud del consumidor, y a acceder a estos datos, incluida una lista de todos los terceros y afiliados con quienes Ada ha compartido o vendido los datos de salud del consumidor y un contacto para estos terceros (correo electrónico u otro).
  * El derecho a retirar tu consentimiento para la recopilación, el uso compartido y la venta de tus datos de salud del consumidor (cuando aplique).
  * El derecho a que se eliminen tus Datos de Salud del Consumidor.


Puedes ejercer tus derechos contactándonos por correo electrónico a 
Cuando ejerzas estos derechos y nos envíes una solicitud, verificaremos tu identidad pidiéndote que la verifiques a través de procedimientos de autenticación estándar. Por ejemplo, podemos pedirte tu dirección de correo electrónico, nombre completo, etc. También podemos usar un proveedor de verificación de terceros externo para verificar tu identidad. Ten en cuenta que en los Servicios que no requieren registro, es posible que Ada no pueda identificar y autenticar a los usuarios individuales. En estos casos, Ada no puede ni está obligada por ley a atender tu solicitud para ejercer los derechos descritos anteriormente.
En caso de que nos neguemos a ejercer tus derechos, puedes apelar esa decisión por correo electrónico a 
  * Fiscal General del Estado de Washington en 
  * Fiscal General del Estado de Nevada en 


## 6. Actualizaciones a esta Política
Ada puede modificar esta Política de vez en cuando, con o sin previo aviso. Te recomendamos que visites nuestros Servicios regularmente para mantenerte al día con cualquier cambio. También intentaremos informarte sobre los cambios importantes en esta Política (por ejemplo, publicando un aviso en nuestro sitio web).

# Was kann ich tun, wenn ich ein Symptom oder eine Krankheit nicht finde? 
Ada weiß bereits eine Menge, aber sie lernt nie aus. Unser Ärzteteam arbeitet jeden Tag daran, Adas medizinisches Wissen zu erweitern und stets auf den neuesten Stand zu bringen. Wenn du ein Symptom oder eine Krankheit nicht finden kannst, dann schreibe uns an hello@ada.com und hilf uns, Ada noch besser zu machen. 
Du hast weitere Fragen? [Stelle uns eine Frage](https://ada.com/de/contact/support/)

# Hypothermie
Verfasst von [Adas medizinischem Fachpersonal](https://ada.com/de/team/medical/)

## Was ist Hypothermie?
Hypothermie bezeichnet eine Körperkerntemperatur, die unter 35 °C liegt. Umgangsprachlich kann dies auch als Untertemperatur bezeichnet werden. Dies kann lebensbedrohlich sein und ist als Notfall zu betrachten.
Typische Symptome von Untertemperatur sind Zittern, Verwirrung, eine Veränderung der Atemfrequenz und des Pulses, blaue Lippen, Finger und Zehen. Wird sie zeitnah behandelt, erholen sich die meisten Menschen gut von einer Hypothermie. Komplikationen können Koma und Gehirnschäden bis hin zum Tode sein. [1](https://ada.com/de/conditions/hypothermia/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
Finde mehr über Deine Symptome heraus.
## Risiken für eine Untertemperatur
Eine Hypothermie wird gewöhnlich durch kalte Temperaturen ausgelöst,
Für einige Personen besteht ein höheres Risiko eine Hypothermie zu entwickeln, dazu gehören:
  * ältere oder sehr junge Menschen,
  * Personen mit psychischen Problemen, unter Alkohol- oder Drogeneinfluss oder mit bestimmten Krankheiten (wie Hypothyreose, Anorexia Nervosa usw.). 


Hast Du oder eine andere Person Symptome, die auf diese Erkrankung hinweisen könnten? Starte jetzt eine kostenlose Symptomanalyse mit der 
## Hypothermie Symptome
Die verschiedenen Stadien einer Untertemperatur verursachen unterschiedliche Symptome.
Eine leichte Hypothermie
  * Zittern,
  * Schwindel,
  * Übelkeit,
  * schneller Atmung,
  * Herzrasen und
  * Müdigkeit.


Wenn Du Dir unsicher bist, ob diese Beschwerden auf Dich zutreffen, starte eine 
Personen mit einer mittel- bis schweren Hypothermie
  * werden schwerfällig und verwirrt,
  * entwickeln Sprachschwierigkeiten,
  * atmen langsam,
  * zeigen eine Schläfrigkeit und
  * einen schnellen oder unregelmäßigen Puls.


Oft sind sich betroffene Personen über den Schweregrad ihrer Erkrankung nicht bewusst. [2](https://ada.com/de/conditions/hypothermia/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
## Hypothermie-Diagnose
Die Diagnose wird durch einen Arzt gestellt, der die Symptome bewertet, den Patienten untersucht und die Körperkerntemperatur misst. [3](https://ada.com/de/conditions/hypothermia/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3")
## Behandlung der Untertemperatur
Erste-Hilfe-Maßnahmen sind bei einer Hypothermie sehr wichtig.
Ist die Person nass, so ist die nasse Kleidung auszuziehen. Ist die Person in der Lage zu trinken, so sollte sie warme Getränke zu sich nehmen. Heizkissen und -strahler können auch nützlich sein.
Personen, die einen schwachen Puls sowie eine langsame Atmung haben und bewusstlos sind, müssen möglicherweise wiederbelebt werden. Weitere Sofortmaßnahmen umfassen (in der Reihenfolge der Dringlichkeit): warme Luft, Gabe warmer Flüssigkeiten über einen Tropf und die Blutentnahme zu Erwärmung des Blutes.
## Hypothermie-Prognose
Eine schwere Hypothermie kann lebensbedrohlich seinLeichte bis mittelschwere Episoden einer Hypothermie haben in der Regel keine dauerhaften Folgen.
## Vorsorge
Am besten vermeidet man eine Hypothermie, indem man sich bei kaltem Wetter an warmen Orten und nicht zu lange in der Kälte aufhält. Außerdem sollte in kalten Umgebungen kein Alkohol getrunken werden.

# Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on January 31, 2022 at 11:16 AM GMT+2
## On this page
  * [What is developmental dysplasia of the hip?](https://ada.com/conditions/developmental-dysplasia-of-the-hip/#what-is-developmental-dysplasia-of-the-hip)
  * [Risks](https://ada.com/conditions/developmental-dysplasia-of-the-hip/#risks)
  * [Symptoms](https://ada.com/conditions/developmental-dysplasia-of-the-hip/#symptoms)
  * [Diagnosis](https://ada.com/conditions/developmental-dysplasia-of-the-hip/#diagnosis)
  * [Treatment](https://ada.com/conditions/developmental-dysplasia-of-the-hip/#treatment)
  * [Other names for developmental dysplasia of the hip](https://ada.com/conditions/developmental-dysplasia-of-the-hip/#other-names-for-developmental-dysplasia-of-the-hip)


* * *
Share this article:
## What is developmental dysplasia of the hip?
Developmental dysplasia of the hip, or simply hip dysplasia, is a failure for the normal hip joint to form before birth. It may be caused by poor positioning of the legs in the womb. This doesn't cause any pain to young children, but can cause a limp and osteoarthritis as the child grows. Hip dysplasia can be successfully treated, especially if diagnosed and treated in babies or young children.
## Risks
In a normal hip, the upper end of the thigh bone (femur) is surrounded by the hip socket (acetabulum). In a dysplastic hip, there is an abnormality in the formation of either the head of the femur, the acetabulum, or the other supportive soft tissues. As a result, the contact between the femur and the acetabulum is loose and unstable, [causing frequent hip dislocations](https://ada.com/conditions/subluxation-and-dislocation-of-the-hip/). Hip dysplasia is more common in girls and people with who have family members with the condition. Within certain ethnic groups this condition tends to be more common, such as Native Americans and Laplanders. Other risk factors include being the first-born child or a breech baby.
## Symptoms
Babies will usually have no symptoms of hip dysplasia, though it might be possible to see a difference in the length or appearance of their legs, hips and buttocks. Toddlers with hip dysplasia may walk later than other children, and children with hip dysplasia who have not been diagnosed may suffer hip pain and walk with a waddle, limp or bowed legs.
## Diagnosis
All babies should be tested for hip dysplasia in the first weeks of their life. This is usually done by a doctor assessing the movement of the hips, or, increasingly, by ultrasound. X-rays of the hip joint can help to determine hip dysplasia in cases where there is uncertainty.
## Treatment
Hip dysplasia is treated by placing the baby in a harness or brace for a period of a few months to keep the legs in the correct position to allow the hips to form normally. If this is not successful or the developmental dysplasia of the hip is diagnosed later in life, surgery is necessary to reconstruct the hip joint.
## Other names for developmental dysplasia of the hip
  * Congenital hip dislocation
  * Congenital dysplasia of the hip
  * Congenital hip dysplasia
  * Hip dysplasia

# Migraña
Escrito por nuestro [Equipo de Profesionales Médicos](https://ada.com/es/team/medical/)
Actualizado el 15 de febrero de 2022, 10:01 EET
## En esta página
  * [Resumen](https://ada.com/es/conditions/migraine/#resumen)
  * [Riesgos](https://ada.com/es/conditions/migraine/#riesgos)
  * [Síntomas](https://ada.com/es/conditions/migraine/#sintomas)
  * [Diagnóstico](https://ada.com/es/conditions/migraine/#diagnostico)
  * [Tratamiento](https://ada.com/es/conditions/migraine/#tratamiento)
  * [Prevención](https://ada.com/es/conditions/migraine/#prevencion)
  * [Pronóstico](https://ada.com/es/conditions/migraine/#pronostico)


* * *
Comparte este artículo:
## Resumen
Las migrañas son dolores de cabeza fuertes y recurrentes. Es un problema frecuente que suele afectar a adultos jóvenes (desde la adolescencia hasta la mediana edad) y tiende a afectar a mujeres con más frecuencia que a hombres. Las migrañas suelen estar acompañadas por náuseas y sensibilidad a la luz (fotofobia) y al sonido (fonofobia). Muchas personas experimentan un aura antes de la migraña. Si bien se conocen numerosos desencadenantes, la causa de las migrañas no se comprende bien. Las migrañas pueden controlarse haciendo reposo y tomando medicamentos para el dolor de cabeza. Aunque muchas personas experimentan migrañas recurrentes la mayoría puede manejar sus síntomas.
## Riesgos
Las migrañas afectan mayormente a adultos jóvenes (desde la adolescencia hasta la mediana edad y son más comunes en mujeres que en hombres. Las personas con sobrepeso y fumadoras podrían ser más propensas a sufrir migrañas.
## Síntomas
El síntoma típico de la migraña es un dolor de cabeza intenso (a menudo en un solo lado de la cabeza) con náuseas, vómitos y sensibilidad a la luz (fotofobia) y al sonido (fonofobia). Los síntomas aparecen rápidamente y pueden permanecer entre 6 a 12 horas. Además, algunas personas pueden presentar síntomas adicionales antes del dolor de cabeza, conocidos como aura. Los síntomas del Aura envuelven hiperactividad, cambios en la visión, hormigueo en las manos, los pies o la cara u otras sensaciones inusuales. Muchas personas se sienten muy cansadas después de una jaqueca.
## Diagnóstico
El diagnóstico de migraña se basa en los síntomas y un examen físico. Puede ser necesario realizar una tomografía computarizada (TC) de la cabeza para descartar otras condiciones que puedan causar síntomas similares a los dolores de cabeza tipo migraña.
## Tratamiento
Muchas personas encuentran que hacer reposo en un ambiente oscuro y tranquilo las ayuda a manejar los síntomas de una migraña. Los medicamentos antiinflamatorios (ibuprofeno, aspirina) pueden ayudar a reducir el dolor. Para las personas que tienen dolor de cabeza intenso los triptanes podrían ser más adecuados. Las personas que sufren migrañas severas y recurrentes (más de dos por mes) podrían beneficiarse de medicamentos adicionales para reducir la frecuencia e intensidad de los dolores de cabeza.
## Prevención
Evitar los factores que desencadenan las migrañas puede ayudar a prevenir algunos episodios. Estos factores varían de una persona a otra, pero algunos desencadenantes comunes son: estrés emocional, no comer, algunos olores, determinados climas, alteraciones del sueño, alcohol, fumar, etc. Las personas que sufren migrañas severas y recurrentes (más de dos por mes) podrían utilizar medicamentos que reduzcan la frecuencia e intensidad de los dolores de cabeza.
## Pronóstico
Las migrañas suelen ser recurrentes. Si son ocasionales, la mayor parte de las personas pueden controlar los síntomas durante una migraña. Si son frecuentes, hay medicamentos que tomados regularmente pueden ayudar a reducir el número de días afectados por migrañas y mejorar la calidad de vida.

# LDL Cholesterol
Written by [Ada’s Medical Knowledge Team](https://ada.com/team/medical/)
Updated on June 20, 2025 at 11:59 AM GMT+3
## On this page
  * [What is LDL or LDL cholesterol?](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#what-is-ldl-or-ldl-cholesterol)
  * [Why is LDL cholesterol “bad”?](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#why-is-ldl-cholesterol-bad)
  * [What is the normal LDL cholesterol range?](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#what-is-the-normal-ldl-cholesterol-range)
  * [How to lower LDL cholesterol?](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#how-to-lower-ldl-cholesterol)
  * [Wrapping up](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#wrapping-up)
  * [FAQs](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#faqs)


* * *
Share this article:
You may already know that lowering cholesterol is vital for maintaining a healthy heart and blood vessels
Introducing LDL cholesterol. This is the type your doctor refers to when they talk about the importance of lowering your cholesterol levels.But what exactly is LDL cholesterol, and what makes it "bad?” And what do you need to do to decrease your LDL cholesterol levels?
Let's find out.
Do you think that your LDL Cholesterol levels might be too low or too highsymptom checker works before you try it for yourself.
## What is LDL or LDL cholesterol?
Your body needs a certain amount of cholesterol to function normally
Your liver produces molecules called lipoproteins to transport that cholesterol around the body. [1](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1") These particles consist of fats and proteins that bind to cholesterol so your blood can transport it around your body. [2](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#fn:2 "See Footnote 2")
Your liver produces 2 main types of lipoprotein: [1](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#fn:1 "See Footnote 1")
  * **[High-density lipoproteins](https://ada.com/biomarkers/hdl-cholesterol/) (HDLs), or "good cholesterol"**
  * Low-density lipoproteins (LDLs), or "bad cholesterol"


Having too much LDL cholesterol can lead to a variety of health problems. But what is it that makes LDL cholesterol "bad"?
## Why is LDL cholesterol “bad”?
When your LDL cholesterol levels get too high, fatty buildups begin to form in the walls of your arteries. [3](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#fn:3 "See Footnote 3") Eventually, these buildups turn to plaques, narrowing your arteries and making it difficult for blood to flow through[4](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#fn:4 "See Footnote 4")
This narrowing can increase your chances of developing [cardiovascular disease](https://ada.com/cardiovascular/) and complications including: [5](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#fn:5 "See Footnote 5")
  * Heart attack
  * [Stroke](https://ada.com/signs-of-stroke/)
  * Chronic kidney disease
  * [Coronary artery disease](https://ada.com/conditions/coronary-artery-disease/)
  * Peripheral artery disease
  * High blood pressure


That said, your body does need a small amount of LDL cholesterol for cell repair. [6](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#fn:6 "See Footnote 6")
So what is the right amount of LDL cholesterol?
## What is the normal LDL cholesterol range?
A healthy LDL cholesterol range[7](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7") The target level should be 50-70 mg/dL to prevent plaque formation in your arteries. [7](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7") The risk of plaque buildup is increased by [diabetes](https://ada.com/conditions/diabetes/), high blood pressure, smoking, or a pre-existing [atherosclerosis](https://ada.com/conditions/atherosclerosis/).
An LDL cholesterol level of 130-159 mg/dL would be considered borderline[7](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7") 160-189 mg/dL is highvery high[7](https://ada.com/biomarkers/ldl-cholesterol/#fn:7 "See Footnote 7")
You should regularly check your LDL cholesterol levels. Ask your doctor about getting a lipid profile test at your next checkup.
Reducing your LDL cholesterol levels is linked to reduced cardiovascular risk. So what can you do to lower your levels?
Do you think that your LDL Cholesterol levels
## How to lower LDL cholesterol?
The best way to reduce your LDL cholesterol levels
This can include: 
  * Eating a balanced diet
  * Losing weight
  * Exercising regularly
  * Avoiding or quitting smoking
  * Reducing alcohol consumption


There are also medications
## Wrapping up
Maintaining healthy, low levels of LDL cholesterol is important for your health.So remember to stay active, eat healthy foods, and regularly check your blood cholesterol levels. Be sure to read our [“How to lower cholesterol”](https://ada.com/editorial/how-to-lower-cholesterol/) article to get the full story on cholesterol.
## Find out more about your symptoms
## LDL Cholesterol FAQs
Q: When should I test my LDL cholesterol levels?  
A: LDL cholesterol levels are measured as part of a lipid profile test. This should be done every 4-6 years.
Q: Can I feel it when my LDL levels get too high?  
A: You won’t experience symptoms if your LDL cholesterol levels get too high. That’s why it’s essential to get your levels checked regularly.
Q: Can I test my LDL cholesterol at home?  
A: Your doctor can measure your LDL cholesterol levels as part of a lipid profile test. You can also check them yourself at home using a finger-prick test.
Q: Do I need to fast before an LDL cholesterol test?  
A: Your doctor may advise you to fast for 10-12 hours before a cholesterol level test. That means avoiding any food or drink except water.
